#6290. Older adults get tailored plans for fall prevention, but a simple leaflet may work just as well

Across 110 trials, tailored fall prevention plans for older people worked no better than basic advice, and people on them fell slightly more often.

A doctor who worries that an older patient might fall can order the full workup. Balance, eyesight and medicines get checked, someone looks at the loose rugs at home, and a plan is then built around those findings. It sounds like the gold standard of fall prevention.

However, pooled across the trials that have tested it, that tailored plan probably prevents no more falls than a leaflet of good advice. People on the plans actually fell slightly more often.

The result comes from a new Cochrane review, a kind of study that gathers every reliable trial on a question and pools the numbers. This one covered 110 trials and 48,919 people aged 60 and over. All participants were living at home rather than in care.

Lianne Wood and Cynthia Swarnalatha of the University of Exeter led the review. The co-authors were at the University of Oxford and the University of Sydney.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wood said the next job is to work out what the tailored programs contain that plain advice doesn’t.

“At the moment we are not sure why the results show that education is possibly more effective than tailored interventions,” she said.

Researchers call the tailored approach a multifactorial program. A health professional checks a person for two or more risks that can be changed, then treats or refers each one.

That might mean an exercise class for weak legs, a medicine review, or a handrail for the bathroom.

Seven trials with 9,901 people compared that approach with falls advice or education alone. The advice side was deliberately basic, often a standard leaflet such as Age U.K.’s Staying Steady, sent by post or handed over in a session.

People on the tailored plans had about 9 percent more falls per year than people given advice. The review rated that evidence as moderately certain. The chance of falling at least once, and of falling two or more times, was the same in both groups.

Against usual care, meaning no special fall prevention at all, the tailored plans did better, but not by much. Across 29 trials and 9,442 people, they cut the number of falls by about a quarter. In 17 trials, the risk of falling two or more times was about 13 percent lower.

The chance of falling at least once barely moved, across 38 trials and 12,774 people. Fall-related fractures and hospital stays didn’t change either.

The review rated all of those results as low-certainty evidence. This was because results varied from trial to trial and many trials had weaknesses in design.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most once the trials were pooled, Wood said it was what did not happen.

“We were surprised that there were no other big changes to the previous review, despite adding many more people and trials of higher quality,” she said. “Much of the pooled results are very similar to the 2018 review with low quality evidence.”

The review also tested the untailored version, called a multiple component program, in which everyone gets the same bundle, regardless of their own risks. Forty-four trials used that design, and one tested both approaches.

Against usual care, those bundles made little or no difference to the number of falls, though they may have lowered the chance of falling at least once by about 12 percent. Against exercise alone, and against advice alone, they made little or no difference on any measure.

Side effects were generally mild, mostly short-lived aches from exercise, and serious ones were rare.

The components themselves were familiar. Of the 66 tailored-program trials, 53 included home safety changes or assistive equipment, 49 included exercise, and 36 included a medicine review.

Wood was asked what a health service that runs these programs should do on Monday morning.

“So, until we know more, we’d advise people to continue as normal,” she told Earth.com.

Asked what the best evidence does support, she named two things. “We know that falls prevention education and advice to start with exercise appears to be effective, so this may be the area we need to put more emphasis on.”

Her view fits the direction guidelines have already taken. The 2025 guidance in the United Kingdom puts strength and balance training at the center of prevention, and the 2022 World Falls Guidelines call exercise a core intervention.

Exercise and standard advice may also take less time and money to roll out across a whole population than individual assessments.

The review pooled every tailored program together, so it can’t say whether some combinations of components work better than others. The authors wrote that this question needs a different kind of analysis.

In most trials, participants knew which group they were in, and most relied on people reporting their own falls. Six of the comparisons showed signs that trials with weak results were less likely to have been published.

Trials that counted harder outcomes, such as fractures, have generally shown disappointing results, the authors wrote.

The evidence also comes from a narrow slice of the world. The tailored-program trials came from 22 countries, but most were run in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Only 17 of those 66 trials reported participants’ ethnicity, and some trials excluded people with dementia.

“There still remains a real lack of studies in low to middle income countries and people of different ethnicities, so understanding the effects of treatments in these groups remains a real priority,” Wood said.

About one in three people over 65 fall at least once a year. In the United States alone, falls in that age group led to about 4.5 million emergency department visits in 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Previous falls, muscle weakness and poor balance all raise the risk. A fall can also leave a fear of falling again, which the review links to faster physical decline and a retreat from social life.

Co-author Sarah Lamb of the University of Exeter said the results show how much is still unknown about why falls happen in the first place.

“We’re now conducting a major study to understand why people have unstable walking and are at higher risk of falls,” Lamb said.

“Combined with this review, it will help us design the best prevention programs in future, to reduce frailty and help people live well for as long as possible.”

Next, the authors want a single, large trial that tests home changes and exercise, alone and together, against usual care.

They also want wearable sensors recording falls instead of diaries. Until that trial runs, the pooled record says a tailored plan and a leaflet do about the same job, and nobody can yet say why.

The full study was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

#6289. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

#6288. The Mystery of Life’s Origin on Earth Just Got More Mysterious

Hydrogen cyanide was crucial for early Earth chemistry. A new study says comets almost certainly didn’t deliver it like we’d previously thought.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Since time immemorial, humanity’s greatest thinkers have wrestled with what is arguably the most burning question of our inquisitive species: Why are we here? Over the millennia, the proposed answers have meandered from the divine to the demonstrable. Then, in 1953, the famous Miller-Urey experiment made it seem increasingly plausible that life emerged from the complex chemistry of early Earth.

However, exactly where life’s building blocks came from remains an open question. Some scientists favor “panspermia,” the idea that life didn't begin on Earth at all. In this view, hardy microbes rode here aboard comets, asteroids, or rocky debris blasted off other worlds, survived the trip through space, and seeded our planet. A softer version of the idea says space rocks delivered life’s raw ingredients rather than life itself, in the form of organic molecules made in the protoplanetary disk around our young sun. Still others argue that Earth needed no outside help and produced everything life required on its own.

But just as important as pinpointing this much sought-after answer is ruling out a few choices. To that end, a new study led by scientists at the University of Cambridge and published in the journal Scientific Reports models the possibility that comets ferried chemicals, specifically hydrogen cyanide (HCN), to the planet’s surface during its infancy more than four billion years ago. A 2022 study found that cyanide on early Earth likely served as a critical reductant (an electron donor in a chemical reaction), and the cyanide also served as a vital intermediate in Stanley Miller and Harold Urey’s famous experiments by producing amino acids when exposed to electricity (possibly from volcanic lightning).

Cometary bombardment is one of the leading theories of how HCN arrived on Earth (though other studies explore whether Earth's own chemistry could have produced the molecule). So the Cambridge team, led by Richard Anslow, modeled whether comets could have delivered it. They found the opposite of what the theory predicts: The chances of comets delivering HCN intact to the surface are vanishingly small, bordering on impossible.

“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon- and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get-out-of-jail-free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” Anslow said in a press statement. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”

The theory that comets provided the chemical substrate of life runs head first into two major problems. Anslow’s previous work showed that “bouncing comets”—comets whose speeds are impacted by the gravitational influence of multiple planets—could arrive gently enough to deliver their fragile cargo intact. But these new models suggest that such a billiard-ball effect likely didn’t occur in Earth’s neighborhood. Using advances in comet-impact simulations and a better understanding of comet-atmosphere interactions, the researchers concluded that comets usually traveled too fast and at too sharp an angle. On the off chance that HCN did survive the journey, the concentrations would often be too low to be useful, and prebiotic chemistry would need to occur quickly upon arrival. Together, these two requirements push the comet-delivery theory from plausible to a “one-in-a-million” occurrence, Anslow says.

“We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way,” Anslow said in a press statement. “But it seems to be a really rare occurrence—at best, a one-off fluke.”

Strangely, Earth’s planetary neighbor Mars would’ve had an easier go of it because it’s smaller and its atmosphere is less thick. This would’ve increased the likelihood of comets actually reaching its surface in higher numbers, but the dissolution of the Red Planet’s magnetic field roughly four billion years ago doomed the world to a lifeless existence (as far as complex life goes, that is).

Neither Anslow’s previous work nor this new study rules out the possibility that comets helped deliver life’s ingredients elsewhere in the Milky Way or beyond. But when it comes to the age-old question of why we’re here, these icy wanderers are likely not the answer.

#6287. A new species of millipede that loves moisture has been discovered living in a surprisingly dry part of South Australia

A post-fire survey on Kangaroo Island turned up a millipede first collected in 1936 and left unnamed for 90 years.

In Australia, entomologists had only ever found millipedes from the moisture-loving family Dalodesmidae in the wetter east and southwest. So a male collected in 1936 on a dry stretch of South Australia’s coast didn’t fit.

Ninety years later, that millipede finally has a name, Colobothrix deckeri. It’s the first of its family known from such a dry part of the country.

Robert Mesibov, a millipede specialist in Ulverstone, Tasmania, described the new genus and species after finding fresh specimens on nearby Kangaroo Island.

Until now, scientists had not described any dalodesmid anywhere in a stretch of more than 1,240 miles (2,000 kilometers) between western Victoria and southwest Western Australia.

Most of the southern half of the country inside that gap gets less than 16 inches (400 millimeters) of rain a year.

The entomologist Herbert Womersley collected the millipede on the lower Yorke Peninsula in April 1936, during a little-known scientific expedition based at Marion Bay.

The specimen went into the South Australian Museum as an unidentified millipede.

The millipede stayed unidentified until 2015. That year, the German millipede researcher Peter Decker borrowed many of the museum’s specimens for his Ph.D. work on a different millipede family.

He was then at the Senckenberg Museum of Natural History in Görlitz. Among the loaned specimens were fragments of Womersley’s male.

Decker recognized the male as a dalodesmid and sent microscope images to Mesibov, who specializes in that family. The new species carries Decker’s name for that reason.

A 2012 study used the term shelf life for the wait between collecting a new species and describing it. For Colobothrix deckeri, Mesibov wrote, that wait was 90 years.

In the southern winters of 2016 and 2017, Mesibov searched forest, woodland and scrub within about 12 miles (20 kilometers) of Marion Bay. He didn’t find the millipede, though the trips did produce a different new species.

By then, entomologists had already collected the animal somewhere else. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were collecting spiders and other small animals on Kangaroo Island, about 31 miles (50 kilometers) south of Marion Bay.

At one site in the island’s relatively wet northwest corner, they found a new species of assassin spider.

Rix and Harms also collected two male and seven female millipedes there. The animals went to the Western Australian Museum. There Catherine Car, a specialist in millipedes and centipedes, identified them as dalodesmids.

They weren’t matched to the 1936 specimen for years.

Bushfires swept Kangaroo Island in 2020 and burned out the 2010 site. The assassin spider, Zephyrarchea austini, had been described from that single spot, and there were fears the fires had left it close to extinction.

In 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh ran a targeted survey for the spider. She found two more on private land about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) west of the original site, and the small animals she collected along the way included the millipede.

This year, while searching online for dalodesmid records in southern Australia, Mesibov found the Rix and Harms specimens in the Western Australian Museum’s online records.

Curator Mark Harvey sent close-up photos of one male, and its body and reproductive structures matched Womersley’s specimen.

Mesibov then traveled to Kangaroo Island. He couldn’t find the millipede at the 2010 site. He did identify it among the animals Marsh had collected.

“Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”

An adult male Colobothrix deckeri is about 0.75 inches (19 millimeters) long, close to the width of a U.S. penny. Its yellowish-brown body is speckled with reddish brown. The feature that sets it apart is on the legs.

Mature males in this family, and in some other millipedes, carry tiny, ball-shaped structures called sphaerotrichomes. Normally, a long, pointed hair sticks out of each ball. In the new species, that hair is only a short, blunt rod, roughly a quarter the length of the ball.

So Mesibov named the genus Colobothrix, from Greek words meaning stunted hair. What the balls do in this group of millipedes is still unknown, he wrote.

Neither living nor preserved specimens gave off a strong smell. In Mesibov’s view, that suggests any defensive chemical the species makes releases only a little cyanide.

On Kangaroo Island, the millipede is known from five sites inside an area of about 23 square miles (60 square kilometers).

They’re in Flinders Chase National Park, in the Western River Wilderness Area and on private land along Snug Cove Road, and all of them have native woodland.

At the Flinders Chase site, modeled rainfall is about 32 inches (810 millimeters) a year.

Mesibov suggested that the species may once have lived across more of the island’s wetter western half. Farm clearing and frequent bushfires have removed or damaged much of the native woodland over the past two centuries, he wrote.

In the remaining patches near farms, introduced European millipedes now make up nearly all of the millipedes he has seen.

Mesibov’s paper also describes a second new species from the 2010 site, Notonesocambala adoceta. It’s a dark gray millipede up to about 2 inches (50 millimeters) long.

The biggest open question is whether Colobothrix deckeri still lives on the Yorke Peninsula.

Near Marion Bay, modeled rainfall is about 18 inches (450 millimeters) a year, well below the 24 to 31 inches (600 to 800 millimeters) modeled for northwestern Kangaroo Island.

“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface.”

He offered one possibility. “I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past,” he said.

“That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”

Researchers would have to find the millipede inside the rock to test that idea. Mesibov kept some of the new specimens for future genetic work.

He also wrote that other dalodesmids may still live on the nearby Fleurieu Peninsula.

He pointed to forest remnants in its wetter middle and to deep gullies in Deep Creek Conservation Park.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

#6285. Cotton plants in poor soil lean on two hormones to grab enough potassium

Two plant hormones, ethylene and jasmonate, work together to help cotton take in potassium, and sprays of both raised yields in potassium-poor field soil.

Ethylene is the gas that ripens bananas on a kitchen counter, but in cotton plants it has a second job. Together with a partner hormone called jasmonate, it turns on the machinery that pulls potassium into the plant when the soil runs short.

Spraying cotton leaves with versions of both hormones also raised yields in potassium-poor field soil.

A team led by Professors Zhaohu Li and Xiaoli Tian at China Agricultural University in Beijing worked out the steps in upland cotton, Gossypium hirsutum.

Scientists recently traced the species’ origin to Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. The team describes the work as a possible basis for helping crops use potassium more efficiently.

The team tested its idea in two ways: lab experiments on the plant’s genes and proteins, and field experiments on cotton grown in potassium-deficient soil.

It ran the field work only in that kind of soil, so the field results don’t say whether the sprays would help where potassium is already plentiful.

Potassium helps plants run photosynthesis, switch on enzymes, and balance water inside their cells. Cotton is one crop that needs a lot of it. Researchers have found that more potassium is leaving agricultural soils around the world than is going back in.

Yet scientists understand less about how plants take up potassium than about nitrogen and phosphorus. In crops, the way genes control the proteins that carry potassium into cells remains largely unexplored. Other researchers have searched cotton’s genes for ways to make the crop tolerate drought.

The team started with the protein that does the work. It’s a transporter that carries potassium into the plant’s cells. This one grabs potassium even when little is around, and the plant needs it to keep its potassium level steady during a shortage.

A control protein switches the transporter’s gene on by attaching to the DNA right beside it. Two other proteins, one from the jasmonate pathway and one from the ethylene pathway, each attach to the DNA beside the control protein’s gene and turn it up. Then the two link up, and as a pair they turn up the control protein more than either one does alone.

In cotton, then, the two hormones act as partners rather than as separate signals. Hormones do plenty of jobs besides telling plants when to grow. In one earlier study, a drought hormone helped plants block spider mites.

A plant with enough potassium doesn’t need the extra uptake, and the team found how the plant keeps the system off.

When potassium is plentiful, two proteins that hold others back grab the jasmonate-pathway protein and the control protein. In the team’s reading, that stops the plant from spending resources on a system it doesn’t need.

Crops run a similar shutoff for nitrogen. Researchers recently found a protein that tells crops to stop absorbing nitrogen even when plenty remains in the soil.

To see whether the finding could matter on a farm, the team ran field experiments in soil with a shortage of potassium. Each kilogram of that soil held less than 60 milligrams of available potassium (60 parts per million). The team calls that a moderate-to-severe shortage.

The team sprayed cotton leaves with methyl jasmonate, a form of jasmonate, or with ACC, a compound plants turn into ethylene. Either spray raised the potassium level in the leaves and improved photosynthesis.

Using both did best. It raised seed cotton yield by 11.6% compared to unsprayed plants. Seed cotton is the crop as it comes off the plant, with the seeds still inside.

In the field, as in the lab, the two hormones worked best together.

The 11.6% gain came from soil with too little potassium, so it doesn’t show whether the sprays would help where potassium is already plentiful.

Anyone considering sprays like these on a working farm would first need to see the gain repeat across more fields and growing seasons.

The full study was published in the journal Science Bulletin.

#6284. NASA is searching for a way to protect future astronauts from inhaling Martian dust

NASA’s Perseverance rover found ultrafine Mars dust clinging to spacesuit samples for years, a challenge for protecting future astronauts.

Dust is usually something you can brush off. The finest dust on Mars, however, isn’t like that. On small squares of spacesuit fabric carried by NASA’s Perseverance rover, dust fine enough to reach deep into human lungs has stayed attached through years of driving and drilling.

Perseverance measured that dust over 1,645 Martian days, more than four years on an Earth calendar. Its readings came from PIXL, an X-ray instrument on the end of the rover’s robotic arm.

Scott VanBommel, a Perseverance scientist at Washington University in St. Louis, is the paper’s lead author.

“The existence of Mars dust at these ultrafine sizes has been predicted for a long time, and PIXL gave us the chance to measure it directly on Mars,” he said.

None of this fabric is part of a suit. Five swatches of spacesuit material, each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are mounted on a small panel.

The rover uses that panel to check the settings of another instrument, called SHERLOC. NASA sent the swatches to see how spacesuit materials hold up on the Martian surface.

PIXL has its own test panel, with one sample of Teflon and one of glass made from basalt, a dark volcanic rock. Teflon contains no elements PIXL can detect directly. So any signal the instrument picked up from that sample had to come from dust resting on it.

On SHERLOC’s panel, the team also checked swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits.

Earlier missions had measured Mars dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across. PIXL picked up two groups of even smaller ones.

Fine particles were less than 2.5 micrometers wide, and ultrafine particles were around 100 nanometers. A human hair is about 70 micrometers wide, so the ultrafine grains are roughly 700 times thinner than a hair.

Grain sizes varied from one surface to the next. Dust on PIXL’s Teflon and on SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers.

On the basalt glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, some grains were as small as about 100 to 300 nanometers.

“The larger clumps, the Martian dust bunnies, get shaken off over time. But the smallest particles stay behind, and those are the ones that pose the greatest challenge for human support systems,” VanBommel said.

Static electricity appears to explain which grains cling to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the test panels attracted grains of different sizes.

Plastics like Teflon are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust.

Some materials held less dust than others, which could guide the choice of materials and protective coatings for future suits and habitats.

Chemically, the dust matched what earlier missions had measured: rich in iron and sulfur. PIXL also found extra phosphorus and signs of calcium sulfate.

During NASA’s Apollo missions, lunar dust scratched visors, degraded the outer layers of spacesuits, and damaged their seals. Some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever.

Mars dust is different. Wind keeps knocking the grains into each other, which rounds them off, so they’re less abrasive than grains on the Moon.

They carry more sulfur, chlorine, iron and silica than lunar dust does. Regional and global dust storms can keep them circulating through the atmosphere.

On Earth, airborne particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers are tied to a range of health problems, because they can get deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

Studies have shown that ultrafine particles, those no larger than 100 nanometers, can travel from the nose to the brain along the nerve that carries smell.

Martian dust is mostly silicate minerals, and it carries reactive chemicals. Those include perchlorates, which can disrupt the thyroid, and reactive iron, which damages cells. Scientists think the health risk depends on how much dust a person takes in and for how long.

Perseverance measured dust stuck to small samples, not dust floating in the air of a crew’s living space. Researchers still don’t know how much of that dust would get indoors, or how much a person would breathe there.

NASA can use the results as it refines indoor dust limits for astronauts and works out ways to clean gear.

Some designs could keep dust out. A suitport lets an astronaut climb into a suit attached to the outside of a habitat. Airlocks with two chambers could also cut how much dust reaches living quarters.

NASA is already testing some fixes on the Moon. In March 2025, an Electrodynamic Dust Shield developed at Kennedy Space Center in Florida landed on the Moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1. It used electric fields to clear lunar soil from glass and radiator surfaces.

At Johnson Space Center in Houston, engineers use vacuum chambers and imitation Moon soil to test spacesuit parts and a handheld dust-removal tool ahead of Artemis missions.

Those lunar tests are the proving ground for gear that future crews will eventually need on Mars.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6283. Nov. 3, 1957: The flight of Laika

Less than a month after the launch of Sputnik 1, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2. The mission was readied quickly in order to keep the propaganda momentum from Sputnik 1 and to coincide with the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.

Carrying mixed-breed dog Laika, Sputnik 2 was the first flight to carry a living animal to Earth orbit. A small stray from the Moscow streets, Laika had undergone training to help her become accustomed her to the close quarters and gravity changes. Electrodes attached to the dog sent data back to Earth, for future research into the biological effects of space travel. Unfortunately, Laika died a few hours after takeoff – always the expected outcome of the mission, as the life-support systems on Sputnik 2 were imperfect and there was no plan for recovering the satellite or its passenger after launch. Sputnik 2 burned up on reentry in 1958, after its batteries died the previous year. In 2008, a statue commemorating Laika was erected in Moscow.

#6282. The Real Ark of the Covenant May Be Hiding in Ethiopia—and Only One Man Alive Is Allowed to See It

According to an ancient Ethiopian epic, the biblical relic was stolen in a 3,000-year-old temple heist—and now sits in a tiny chapel guarded by a single monk for life.

Next to the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in the ancient city of Axum, Ethiopia, stands a small, fenced-off sanctuary called the Chapel of the Tablet. Entry is forbidden to everyone on Earth except one man: a lone monk appointed for life to watch over its contents.

According to believers, he’s guarding one of history’s most sacred and sought-after relics: the Ark of the Covenant.

In the Hebrew Bible, the Ark is described in precise detail: a rectangular chest of acacia wood overlaid inside and out with gold, measuring roughly four feet long by two feet wide and high, and crowned with two golden cherubim with outstretched wings. Forged at Mount Sinai to house the Ten Commandments and serve as God’s literal throne on Earth, the Ark guided the Israelites through the wilderness, toppled enemy armies, and eventually became the sacred centerpiece of King Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem. Then, during the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.E., this ultimate seat of divine power vanished from the biblical record without a trace.

For millennia, its disappearance has fueled endless archaeological quests, conspiracy theories, and pop-culture touchstones like 1981’s Raiders of the Lost Ark. Yet according to the Kebra Nagast (“The Glory of the Kings”), a revered 14th-century Ethiopian national epic, the Ark was never lost at all. Instead, it was smuggled out of Jerusalem nearly 3,000 years ago by Menelik I, the son of King Solomon and Makeda—better known outside Ethiopia as the Queen of Sheba.

According to the epic, Menelik grew up in Ethiopia before traveling to Jerusalem in his early twenties to meet his father, carrying a royal ring Solomon had left with his mother as proof of his lineage. Solomon recognized the young man immediately—he was the spitting image of his grandfather, King David—and begged his favored son to stay and inherit the throne of Israel.

Menelik insisted on returning home to rule his mother’s kingdom. Reluctantly, Solomon agreed, but on one condition. The firstborn sons of Jerusalem’s highest-ranking nobles, priests, and military commanders were ordered to accompany Menelik as his new royal court to establish a “second Israel” in Ethiopia.

That decree sealed the Ark’s fate. Devastated at the thought of leaving the presence of God behind, the young elites conspired to pull off an ancient inside job. The heist was masterminded by Azariah, son of the High Priest Zadok. Prompted by an angel in a vision, Azariah commissioned an exact wooden replica of the Ark. Under cover of night, he and his co-conspirators slipped into the Temple, swapped the genuine Ark for the decoy, and hid the real relic in their luggage.

When Menelik’s caravan departed the next day, the Kebra Nagast claims the Ark’s power lifted their wagons and animals off the ground, propelling them toward Ethiopia at supernatural speed. By the time Zadok discovered the counterfeit and Solomon’s army gave frantic chase, the Ethiopians were long gone.

Christianity was still centuries away, so as tradition has it, the relic was first kept on Tana Qirqos, a remote island on Ethiopia’s Lake Tana, where priests guarded it for 800 years. Then around 340 C.E., when King Ezana of the Aksumite Empire converted to Christianity, the Ark was ceremoniously moved to the newly built Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum, permanently linking the ancient Israelite covenant with Ethiopian Christianity.

Over the centuries, whenever invaders threatened Axum—including Queen Gudit’s forces in the 10th century and the devastating Adal War in the 16th century—monks spirited the Ark away to mountain strongholds and island refuges until the cathedral could be rebuilt. In the 1960s, Empress Menen Asfaw, wife of Emperor Haile Selassie, funded the dedicated Chapel of the Tablet next door. According to local monastic lore, the move was necessary because a divine “heat” radiating from the Ark was cracking the ancient stone walls of its previous sanctum.

Because the Ethiopian Orthodox Church forbids anyone—including scholars, archaeologists, and even the church’s own patriarch—from laying eyes on the relic, its authenticity remains impossible to verify scientifically. Only one outsider in modern history has claimed to get a look. In 1941, British army officer Edward Ullendorff—later a prominent professor of Ethiopian studies—allegedly used his military clout and fluency in classical Ge’ez to talk his way inside the sanctuary. In a 1992 interview, Ullendorff claimed the chest he saw was merely a “middle- to late-medieval construction.”

However, Ethiopian officials and historians quickly pointed out a flaw in Ullendorff’s scoop: every church in Ethiopia keeps a replica of the Ark, known as a tabot, for ceremonial use. If Ullendorff saw a medieval wooden box, believers argue, he was simply fooled by a decoy—the exact same trick Azariah used on King Solomon 3,000 years ago.

And so, while treasure hunters continue to scour subterranean tunnels in Jerusalem and desert caves across the Middle East, millions of Ethiopians believe the search is already over. The world’s most famous lost treasure isn’t buried in a secret vault—it’s sitting right on a street corner in Axum, hiding in plain sight.

#6281. Scientists poured dye into a sinkhole at the bottom of a Florida lake, and it surfaced 35 days later at a famous spring 19 miles away

A pink dye test revealed an underground connection between Florida's Lake Jackson and five natural springs.

On September 19, 2017, scientists poured a pink tracer dye called Rhodamine WT into a sinkhole in the bed of Lake Jackson, about 5 miles (8 kilometers) north of Tallahassee, Florida.

Thirty-five days later, the main peaks of that dye turned up at Wakulla Spring, about 19 miles (30.6 kilometers) to the south.

Traces of the dye reached five separate natural springs in all. The results show a connection between the lake and those springs through underground channels in the limestone.

Only a small amount of dye seems to have made the full trip, and the scientists suspect most of it spread into the porous rock along the way.

Lake Jackson sits in a closed basin of 27,000 acres (10,900 hectares), or 42 square miles (109 square kilometers). Several large sinkholes open in its bed, including Lime Sink in the north and Porter Hole Sink in the south.

The lake’s original name, Okeeheepkee, means “disappearing waters.” Every so often it drains away through the bottom, in events known as dry-downs.

Major or partial dry-downs have been recorded in 1907, 1909, 1932, 1935, 1936, 1957 and 1982, and several times since 1999. In the final stages, the lake appears to drain rapidly, as though someone pulled the plug from a bathtub.

A dry-down can follow a combination of below-average rainfall, low groundwater levels and high evapotranspiration. Heavy storms can refill the lake quickly.

Water that leaves through the lakebed eventually enters the upper Floridan aquifer, according to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.

Researchers think some of that water may travel to Wakulla Spring, though the agency notes that the timing and flow path still need investigation.

Seán E. McGlynn, technical director of McGlynn Laboratories Inc., carried out the study with co-author Alan W. Niedoroda.

They used fluorescent dye tracing to test whether a subterranean flow between Lake Jackson and Wakulla Spring could be positively demonstrated.

They injected the dye into the lake-bottom sinkhole for six and a half minutes.

Water-quality sondes at Wakulla Spring and nearby Sally Ward Spring recorded the main peaks after 35 days.

Charcoal packs, which absorb dye from passing water, were placed at those two springs and three others nearby. They also picked up dye within time windows that matched the peaks recorded by the sondes.

Each breakthrough event was brief, lasting from one minute to 100 minutes.

In slides for a Florida State University karst symposium, McGlynn put the peak travel time at 35.21 days over 19.1 miles (30.7 kilometers), or 2,864 feet (873 meters) a day.

The results point to a conduit-like system in the aquifer dominated by advection, meaning the dye was carried along by the moving water. On average, it traveled about half a mile (0.8 kilometers) a day.

Because dye showed up at five well-separated springs, the authors conclude that the conduit system is both braided and branching.

The paper describes a leaky conduit, in which much of the dye moving through the channels dispersed into the surrounding limestone matrix.

The study was exploratory, and its authors caution that it allows only conjectural statements about how much of the dye ended up where.

The study’s authors call Wakulla Spring a renowned first-magnitude spring. Its limestone holds many interconnected holes that feed a network of conduits, and it discharges about 300 million gallons (1.1 billion liters) a day, according to Florida State Parks.

Its cave system is the longest mapped underwater cave system in the United States, with conduits extending both north and south of the spring. More than 22 miles (35 kilometers) of passage lie deeper than 190 feet (58 meters).

Earlier dye traces in the Wakulla Spring watershed had already shown that water entering four major swallets later flows out at the spring.

The area’s many sinkholes are developed in the St. Marks Formation, a fossil-rich sandy limestone 20 to 23 million years old.

The 2024 study points to a leaky-conduit flow able to carry nutrients and pollutants rapidly over long distances. The same weakness leaves cave groundwater vulnerable to pollution in other karst regions.

In August 2021, the Florida Geological Survey announced a second trace at Porter Hole Sink, using green fluorescein dye, to confirm the earlier connection.

The dye release was timed to low water and the approach of Tropical Storm Fred, whose rain was expected to push the dye toward 23 monitoring sites. The agency said results could take weeks or months.

“Confirming this connection will help resource managers develop more informed strategies for managing our water resources,” said Guy Means, then acting director of the survey and Florida’s state geologist.

The upper Floridan aquifer supplies drinking water to Leon and Wakulla counties and feeds Wakulla Spring.

The study was published in the journal Journal of Cave and Karst Studies.

Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

The new toothbrush still needs to be tested in further safety trials.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Lu, Y., Song, J., Chi, X., Li, W., Wu, L., Guo, Y., Cui, Q., Zheng, X., Bai, Y., Heng, B. C., Han, X., Zhang, X., & Deng, X. (2026). Self-charged toothbrush facilitates tooth healthcare maintenance. Science Advances, 12, Article eaeg5744. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg5744

#6278. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6277. The Sky Today on Wednesday, November 4: Venus and Spica stand close

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon high above them in Leo, creating a gorgeous sight that early risers won’t want to miss.

By 6 A.M. local time (roughly half an hour before sunrise), the sky is growing bright and Venus and Spica are about 8° high in the east. Venus, at magnitude –4.4, far outshines the magnitude 1.0 star, which sits just to the planet’s upper left. A waning crescent Moon, just over 20% lit, hangs high above the pair, to their upper right. Through a telescope, Venus’ large, 58”-wide disk is also a crescent, now 5% lit. In the coming days, Venus’ phase will start to grow as its diameter slowly shrinks.

Also glance to Venus and Spica’s upper left, where you’ll spot magnitude –0.1 Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes the Herdsman, which borders Virgo to the north.

#6276. Darwin’s finches face a deadly threat hiding in their nests

A DNA study traces how vampire flies spread across the Galápagos, offering clues to protecting Darwin’s finches from the deadly parasites.

A fly’s larvae can kill every chick in a Darwin’s finch nest by feeding on their blood and tissue.

That fly, the avian vampire fly, is now considered the greatest threat to land birds in the Galápagos Islands.

The finches evolved far from any continent, but the fly came from the mainland.

A new DNA study suggests it most likely got in through San Cristóbal, the island closest to mainland Ecuador and historically the first stop for cargo ships.

From there, the flies appear to have spread west. Knowing that route gives conservation teams a clearer idea of where to focus their efforts.

Abbie Hay, a PhD student, and Rachael Dudaniec, an associate professor, led the study at Macquarie University’s School of Natural Sciences in Australia.

They worked with scientists from the Charles Darwin Foundation and other groups to compare island flies with flies from mainland Ecuador, where the species is native.

Scientists know the vampire fly as Philornis downsi. It probably reached the islands with human help sometime before 1964, but it wasn’t identified in finch nests until 1997.

The fly’s larvae feed on growing chicks and sometimes on their mothers.

The fly has been found on 15 of the 17 Galápagos islands where scientists have checked, and it attacks at least 11 species of Darwin’s finches.

Island species can be especially vulnerable to new parasites. Species that evolved in isolation often lack defenses against these newcomers, the authors wrote.

Sonia Kleindorfer, now at the University of Vienna, has led more than two decades of research on the fly and the finches, and this study builds on that work.

The researchers collected flies during the 2024 bird breeding season, from January to April, on five islands: Santa Cruz, Isabela, Floreana, San Cristóbal and Santiago. Santiago is the only one of the five without a human settlement.

Some adult flies were caught in traps. Others were collected from nests as pupae, the stage between larva and adult, after the birds had finished nesting.

In all, the team gathered 235 island flies and 39 mainland flies.

After removing poor-quality samples and close relatives, they compared 169 island flies at more than 33,000 points in their DNA where a single letter varied.

The DNA differences let the team work out which groups had been mixing, without following individual flies between islands.

Groups that mix tend to become genetically similar, while groups that stay apart gradually become more different.

The island flies had much less genetic variety than the mainland flies, and the two formed separate genetic groups.

That fits a genetic bottleneck, where a population starts with just a few founders and carries only part of the original group’s variety.

San Cristóbal stood apart from the other islands. Its flies were the most genetically different from the rest, yet they also had the most genetic variety.

Isabela showed the opposite pattern. Even though it’s by far the largest island in the study, its flies had the least genetic variety.

Three neighboring islands, Isabela, Santa Cruz and Santiago, are just 10 to 17 miles (16 to 27 kilometers) apart, and their flies mixed a lot.

Santa Cruz and Santiago seemed to exchange the most flies, both with each other and with nearby islands.

When the team estimated which way fly genes were moving between islands, only San Cristóbal showed a clear one-way pattern. More of its genes moved out toward the other islands than came back in.

Westward is also the way the wind blows. The southeast trade winds carry air from South America northwest across the islands, which puts San Cristóbal upwind of the others.

Cargo has traveled the same way. Ships from the port of Guayaquil historically stopped at San Cristóbal first, and the cargo then went to Santa Cruz and on to Isabela and Floreana.

Adult flies feed on fruit and vegetables, so shipments of fresh produce could carry them between islands.

“Our results suggest that the fly may be traveling from the mainland to San Cristóbal with human assistance, and from there to other islands through a combination of human activity and natural dispersal,” Dudaniec said.

Adult vampire flies have been found riding on tourist boats between islands. A related species, the stable fly, has been reported to travel up to 140 miles (225 kilometers) on the wind.

That’s farther than San Cristóbal is from any of the other four islands, but how far the vampire fly itself can fly between islands hasn’t been documented.

Right now, conservation workers fight the fly by applying insecticide by hand and by using self-fumigating nesting material.

A wasp called Conura annulifera, which attacks only this fly, looks promising as a natural enemy that could be released to keep it in check.

Choosing where to start matters. Pests with more genetic variety are more likely to evolve resistance to a control agent, the authors wrote, which makes isolated islands that receive fewer new flies better starting points.

“By identifying which populations are genetically connected, we can better understand where flies may be coming from and where control efforts could have the greatest impact,” Dudaniec said.

San Cristóbal presents a challenge. Its flies are the most genetically distinct, but they also have the most genetic variety, and new ones may still be arriving from the mainland.

The island may need several control methods at once, plus tighter checks on what arrives.

Floreana may be an easier place to begin. The team suggested that the island, home to just 111 people, could be a more efficient site for a control trial.

San Cristóbal had the smallest sample in the study, just 21 flies, mostly from nests in one small area. With so few flies, the researchers may have underestimated the island’s genetic variety.

The one-way movement out of San Cristóbal also has two possible explanations.

Flies may still be arriving there and spreading out today, or the DNA may reflect the route of the first flies to settle on the island.

None of the flies collected on other islands looked like a recent arrival from San Cristóbal.

Telling the two explanations apart will take a separate study of the population’s history, the authors wrote.

The mainland source is a mystery, too. Flies from all three mainland sites differed genetically from the island flies, so none of them looks like the population that started the invasion.

One of those sites was a forest about 9 miles (15 kilometers) from the port of Guayaquil. Flies may be reaching the port from somewhere else before they board ships.

The authors wrote that testing flies from places that ship fresh produce to Guayaquil could help trace the invasion back to its source.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Ecology.
