#6213. Eurostar Premier (First Class) Review: Better Than Flying, But Hardly A Luxury Experience

My first Eurostar Premier journey took me from Brussels to Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, where I connected to a KLM flight to Los Angeles. The train itself felt older than I expected, but the quiet carriage and productive journey made it a pleasant alternative to flying.

I sometimes enjoy trying a new travel experience without researching every detail beforehand. There is a certain irony in that, considering how much of this blog is devoted to helping others know what to expect. Eurostar was one of those experiences. I had long wanted to try it, and an award booking provided the opportunity.

I booked Brussels to Los Angeles through Air France/KLM Flying Blue for 60,000 miles in business class (plus $478.13 in taxes and fees). The itinerary included a Eurostar train from Brussels-Midi to Amsterdam Schiphol, followed by KLM World Business Class to Los Angeles. I could have booked a departure from Brussels Airport for the same mileage price, but chose the rail connection to try something different.

The cabin description was confusing. My ticket indicated business class, while KLM’s Air&Rail information referred to a “premium” experience for those connecting in business class. Eurostar’s actual classes are Standard, Plus, and Premier. At check-in, the agent confirmed I was booked into Premier.

Rather than use the actual Eurostar check-in desk, Brussels-Midi has an Air France-KLM ticketing office and rail check-in counter located in the rear of the station.

My train departed at 5:53 am and I showed up at 5:15 am to check-in…where I found a massive line and only one agent on duty. One passenger in the front of the line was traveling on SNCF to Paris but had a ticketing issue which the lone agent was trying to resolve. But time was ticking and the line grew longer.

Finally at 5:30 am I walked to the front of the line to ask for assistance, noting my train departed in 20 minutes. I did not mean to be the ugly American, but it was just what the agent needed to ask the frazzled traveler from Côte d’Ivoire (I noticed her passport) to step aside. Within a few minutes she had cleared the line and I was on my way upstairs to the rail platform.

There was a Eurostar lounge in Brussels, but it did not open until 6:00 am during my visit, so I could not use it…though I would have access to it had my train departed an hour later.  Not that I ended up having a lot of time to spare, but it woudld have been nice to have a cup of coffee there before the train departed.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in Coach 11, the very last cabin designated as Premier.

Stepping onboard felt more like entering an older TGV first class carriage than the sleek, modern interior I had imagined. Old is, not necessarily a bad thing, but the cabin showed wear. My footrest was broken and the cabin just look tattered and well past its prime.

In the very rear of the cabin was a compartment with seating of four that remained empty throughout the journey.

The bigger advantage on this particular departure was how quiet it was: there was only one other passenger in my carriage and even as we neared Amsterdam there was never more than five in the cabin.

A nearly empty premium cabin is not something you can count in Premier, but it made this an especially pleasant setting to work ahead of a long flight in which I did not want to open my computer.

The lavatories in the Premier cabin were very typical European train toilets with metal toilets, a small sink, but fairly spacious.

We departed on time, and an attendant welcomed us and offered me breakfast menu shortly after pushback, along with a packaged moist towelette.

Sandwich IGP Bayonne ham, AOP Comté cheese, with dill picked cucumbers

Fruit Kampot pepper and verbena apples, gala melon, watermelon

Both were accompanied by yogurt, a croissant, juice, and coffee. I chose the fruit, though I would have liked both (and my request for both was politely declined).

It was a modest meal, but I enjoyed it. The fruit was good and the coffee was decent, as was the croissant.

I preferred this breakfast to the catering KLM serves on its short intra-European flights and the presentation was far nicer. It did not need to be elaborate to be satisfying at that hour and I had a second cup of coffee and some cold pressed berry juice prior to arrival at AMS.

The onboard internet worked well, allowing me to be productive during the ride. For this trip, I valued that more than a particularly luxurious cabin, though I was initially concerned that I would be capped at 500 MB of data.

Thankfully, even though I quickly exceeded the cap the internet continued working…

In-seat power was also available so I arrived in AMS with my devices fully charged.

The attendant’s welcome and breakfast service provided a pleasant start to the morning. Sure, it would have been nice to have the sandwich as well (I was still hungry and the cabin was empty), but she denied my request in a very kind way!

At one point I took a walk through the train to check out the Café Car which offers food and drinks for purchase.

Looking at the menu, I’d say I would have been fine with a falafel wrap and Lavazza coffee had I been booked in coach.

My destination was Schiphol Airport, not Amsterdam Centraa, whcih thankfully meant no backtracking a regional train to the airport.

Next came my KLM lounge visit and onward flight to Los Angeles.

For my itinerary, I was happy to have Premier included in the Flying Blue award.

Whether I would pay a substantial premium for it separately is another question and the answer is probably not. Eurostar lists extra-spacious seating and lounge access among Premier’s benefits, but I could not use the Brussels lounge on this departure.

It is also important to compare the correct route. Eurostar’s class descriptions distinguish between London services and continental routes. For example, the included meal in Premier on a London-route would have included a multi-course hot meal.

For a separate purchase, I would compare the actual fare difference and the benefits available for the particular trip (like the lounge), probably paying no more than €50 for the upgrade on this particular route.

Eurostar Premier was less polished than I expected, but I enjoyed the journey. The worn interior and broken footrest deserved attention, while breakfast and reliable internet helped make the ride worthwhile. For this Brussels–Schiphol connection, I was glad I chose the train. It gave me a quiet, productive start to the trip home and left me interested in trying Eurostar again.

Eurostar to/from London requires going through security and passport control, and is in a completely different part of the train station, and a lot more like getting in a flight. Overall. I’d recommend Plus. The price difference is rarely huge with economy, and you get more or less the same as Premium but without the lounge access or meal. Overall, it’s a good review and reflective of the experience. Fingers crossed the new rolling stock freshens things up when it arrives, and I’m glad you could try things in this part of Europe.

#6212. KLM Forced Into 'Painful' €1B Financial Overhaul

KLM has announced a widespread restructuring and consolidation program as it looks to improve its earnings in what is an increasingly challenging operational environment. This year, more than most, has seen airlines around the world come to terms with various external pressures, such as the airspace closures and fuel price hikes related to the ongoing geopolitical instability in the Middle East.

With this in mind, KLM is looking to improve its annual earnings by €1 billion (€1 = $1.12). Such a boost, it says, "is needed to invest in the fleet, customer experience, and KLM's people." However, this will come at a cost, with both its network and workforce consolidating to save money. Most notably, thousands of employee positions are being reorganized, with the total workforce set to drop by around 15%.

In a statement released earlier today by the Dutch flag carrier and SkyTeam member, KLM explained that it has made good financial progress in recent years, with existing efforts having already resulted in "structural improvements of more than €750 million." Having got its pilot and maintenance staff shortage under control, the airline has outsourced catering and maintenance ops and trimmed its office work.

However, with external pressures mounting, these efforts, alone, are not enough to provide long-term financial security for the airline. With this in mind, KLM has now announced further measures that it says will "strengthen its position and keep the Netherlands connected to the world." It found that delaying such actions "would further limit KLM's strategic options," with President and CEO Marjan Rintel saying that:

"The environment we operate in is becoming increasingly complex, with global instability, high fuel prices, and growing pressure on the industry. That’s why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we’re taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures."

KLM wants to improve its annual earnings by €1 billion to a total of €1.4 billion. This growth will come at a human cost, with 5,000 positions being reorganized as KLM cuts its workforce by 15%. Of these 5,000 positions, 1,000 will be lost through "structural productivity improvements," while the remainder in catering, ground services, and customer contact have been or will be outsourced or transferred.

The airline says that, via "natural attrition, voluntary arrangements, and transfers to other positions," it hopes that it will be able to limit the overall impact of this reorganization. President and CEO Marjan Rintel says that this difficult choice is the right one, adding that "doing nothing would ultimately have even more painful consequences, both for jobs and for our country's connections to the rest of the world."

Consolidation is also expected at the network level, particularly in terms of European routes. KLM believes that it can restore regional and short-haul profitability by focusing its capacity "on routes that contribute most to passenger connectivity and the nonstop network from Schiphol." On the fleet side, KLM Cityhopper will play a more important role, with its smaller jets allowing the airline to better align capacity.

The regional airline is increasing capacity in the E195-E2’s economy cabin by adding four additional seats.

Elsewhere in its operations, KLM believes that increased operational efficiency is also set to make a big difference as it targets earnings increases. In ground services alone, it has identified three key pillars on this front. Firstly, passenger services will rely more heavily on digital technology, allowing flyers to have more control over their bookings while employees turn their attention to hospitality.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Secondly, KLM will look to work more closely with external partners when it comes to apron and baggage services. On this front, the Dutch flag carrier says that such providers "can invest more and at a faster pace, while delivering services more efficiently and at a lower cost." Third and finally, technology and external collaboration will be used to streamline the Hub Control Center at Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS).

#6211. BermudAir Completes Move to New Florida Airport

BermudAir transferred flight operations to Orlando Sanford on Saturday after almost three years serving Orlando International.

The carrier now flies between Orlando Sanford and Hamilton, Bermuda. A second route, to Belize, will commence Dec. 21.

BermudAir announced the switch from MCO to SFB in June, saying Sanford is a more convenient and efficient gateway for flights to and from Bermuda, the Caribbean, and Central America.

The inaugural flight received a water cannon salute at Sanford on Saturday.

#6210. Alaska Airlines Cuts Jobs As $700 Million Loss Looms, CEO Admits Overhead Costs Grew Too Fast

Alaska Air Group is cutting about 200 jobs as CEO Ben Minicucci warns the company could lose as much as $700 million this year if current conditions persist. Higher fuel prices are the immediate problem, but Minicucci also acknowledged that overhead has grown too quickly. That is a sobering backdrop for an airline pursuing an ambitious international expansion.

According to Reuters, which reviewed Minicucci’s employee memo, the reductions affect non-contract positions, including 125 in Washington and 48 in Hawaii. No frontline, non-management positions are being eliminated. Affected employees will finish working November 13 but continue receiving pay through December 31, with severance and other support.

The cuts represent less than 1% of the group’s roughly 32,500 employees. That makes them relatively small across the company, but certainly not small to the people losing their jobs…

Minicucci warned employees that, if conditions persist, Alaska Air Group could record its first adjusted pretax annual loss outside the pandemic since 2003. That is a warning about a potential full-year result, not a $700 million loss already reported. It also concerns the parent group, which includes Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

In its October 20 earnings release, Alaska forecast a full-year adjusted loss of $5.00–$5.50 per share and said fuel would cost $1.8 billion more than its original annual plan. Its fourth-quarter forecast assumes fuel at $4.65–$4.85 per gallon. Third-quarter revenue rose 14% to $4.3 billion, but that commercial growth has not been enough to deliver the annual profit management expected.

Those numbers help explain why simply selling more tickets is not solving the problem.

There was another revealing part of Minicucci’s message:

“We must return to the financial discipline that has long been a key competitive advantage.”

He also acknowledged that overhead expenses had grown disproportionately to revenue in recent years, adding these costs had “grown at a disproportionate rate to revenue.”

Fuel prices are largely beyond an airline’s control, but the size and cost of its management structure are not. The question is why overhead was allowed to grow that way and whether these reductions address the problem or merely provide some near-term savings. Cutting 200 positions cannot will certainly not offset a fuel bill running $1.8 billion above plan.

It also puts management in the uncomfortable position of asking employees to absorb the consequences of spending decisions those employees may have had no role in making.

I have been following Alaska’s efforts to become a more substantial global competitor, including its latest European expansion to Athens and Paris and investment in premium cabins and lounges.

These job cuts do not automatically mean that strategy is wrong, though Alaska cannot cut its way to growth. It needs a product passengers will choose and a network that gives them a reason to return. Pulling back on customer investments when conditions deteriorate could leave Alaska with the costs of expansion but less ability to earn a premium.

Still, growth deserves scrutiny when the company is losing money. Management must be willing to adjust if demand or achievable fares do not justify the investment. Ambition is useful, but it cannot become an excuse to keep spending on something that is not working, though with every investment, it takes time for a sappling to grow into a tree and the “no pain, no gain” mantra certainly applies here too.

Minicucci intends to continue investing in the fleet, customer experience, and network while tightening spending elsewhere. That is a defensible approach…and it could be that these jobs are no longer needed with AI and simply a low-hanging fruit to trim unnecessary expense in order to focus on what is more important.

Alaska Air Group is cutting about 200 jobs while warning of a potential $700 million annual loss. Fuel costs explain much of the pressure, but management’s acknowledgment that overhead grew too quickly deserves attention too.

I want Alaska’s expansion to succeed. Heck, I want JetBlue and Alaska to merge. A stronger competitor is good for passengers. But the company needs to demonstrate that its growth can produce sustainable earnings, and employees losing their jobs should not be the only ones held accountable for restoring financial discipline.

Earlier this year, JetBlue raised its checked bag fees and kicked off a wave of fee hikes across the industry. United followed. Then Delta, American and Southwest.

Seven months later, JetBlue is leading the fee-hiking charge again.

The carrier on Tuesday raised its bag fees for the second time in 2026.

Going forward, customers will pay at least $50 per bag. That’s a 28% jump from the lowest fee the airline previously charged its customers.

Passengers who don’t pre-pay for their bag will pay $60 for their first piece of checked luggage.

And because JetBlue uses a dynamic baggage-pricing system, flyers will pay even more for their checked baggage on peak travel days.

In a statement about the airline's second bag-fee hike this year, the carrier pointed to rising fuel and operating costs.

“This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one,” a spokesperson said.

Here’s how JetBlue’s bag fees will shake out, going forward.

These fees will apply to flights booked starting Nov. 3.

So if you had already purchased a JetBlue flight prior to Nov. 3 — including trips for the holidays — the previous fees would apply to your trip.

As noted above, JetBlue also raised the fees customers will pay for their second checked bag, too.

Here are the days where JetBlue's "peak" baggage fees will apply, through October 2027.

JetBlue does continue to offer free baggage perks as a benefit of certain cobranded credit cards. Plus, its Mosaic elite status members each get at least one free bag.

Customers flying in JetBlue’s premium Mint cabin are still entitled to their first bag free. The same goes for flyers who book the carrier’s new domestic first-class (BlueFirst) seats, which are set to debut on some flights next month.

As JetBlue raises its baggage fees, the biggest question for consumers is how the rest of the airline industry respond.

If history is any indication, we’re about to see another wave of fee hikes across the industry.

After JetBlue raised its bag fees in late March, it took only weeks for nearly every major U.S. carrier to follow with their own fee hikes.

This would be the latest case of sticker shock for travelers, who are simultaneously battling surging fares.

Even budget airline Frontier last week reported customers had paid 71% more in fares over the prior quarter.

All of this comes as airlines have had to contend with sky-high jet fuel costs in 2026 — which they’ve aggressively passed onto customers.

But while jet fuel costs may eventually fall, it’s unlikely flyers will see any future relief when it comes to baggage fees — typically, once those go up, they don’t come back down.

While JetBlue has raised its baggage fees, it is worth noting that passengers do have freedom to bring a full-size carry-on bag on JetBlue flights, regardless of the fare type. The airline no longer bars its Blue Basic (basic economy) passengers from using the overhead bins.

Of course, the belongings packed in any carry-on bag must meet the Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy.

#6208. United Airlines CEO Insists He Runs The “World’s Best” Airline. Does That Title Even Matter?

Scott Kirby believes United Airlines is the best airline in the world (he has for quite some time). I understand his argument, and there are aspects of United that compare favorably with just about any competitor. But the claim raises a more interesting question: what actually makes an airline the best? The answer depends on much more than the seat or the route map or any other single quality…and maybe that’s asking the wrong question anyway.

In his recent Cheeky Pint interview with John Collison and Ben Thompson, Kirby made a case for United that deserves more than an eye roll.

His argument is not that United serves the best food or offers the most luxurious seats. He acknowledges that Asian and Middle Eastern competitors do better on the physical product and probably service. He also identifies schedule as the primary reason people choose an airline. But he believes United’s technology changes the overall assessment:

“I say schedule is the number one reason people pick an airline. But, everything else matters for brand-loyal customers. It’s service, product, reliability, and technology. The Asian and Middle East carriers do better than the US airlines on product for sure, and probably service too. I think we do a really good job, but they have different cultures for service, so they do better on that. But I think technology is the differentiator.

“United, that’s why I now believe that United in totality is the best airline in the world, and it’s because of technology. It’s exponentially getting better. Things like being able to do this for customers when there’s a delay and tell them what’s going on. We started it this summer. AI allows us to institutionalize this. But if you’re going to have a delay, like sending customers weather radar maps. In Chicago, there was a day where the weather was over the horizon, but you had to fly. It was sunny at the airport, but you had to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and so the routes were closed. You couldn’t—

“We sent half the people the normal weather delay, which they think you’re lying… Because it’s sunny outside. You must be lying to me. We sent half a picture with the radar map, and you have to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and the routes are closed because of outside. The people with a 1-hour delay, I think the numbers were negative 60 NPS on the normal way of sending it, plus 60 when we send a picture of the map. A 120-point difference.”

His case for United rests on technology: better tools for managing travel, clearer communication during disruptions, and connectivity that makes time onboard more useful. For example, he describes sending passengers radar maps to explain why distant thunderstorms were delaying flights even though the weather at their airport looked fine. His point is that passengers respond much better when they understand what is happening.

Thus, Kirby is acknowledging that competitors outperform it in some traditional measures of onboard quality, but arguing that United’s technological advantages outweigh those shortcomings.

I think he is right that these things matter. I am less convinced that they settle the question.

Start with the most obvious consideration: an airline is not particularly useful if it cannot conveniently take you where you need to go. I love trying new products and will sometimes take an absurd routing to do so. Most travelers understandably do not approach their trips that way.

A nonstop flight at a convenient time can be more valuable than a better seat reached through a connection. Frequency matters too. An airline with several flights a day gives you more options, particularly when something goes wrong.

This is a substantial part of United’s appeal. Its network gives me reasons to fly it that have nothing to do with whether another airline serves better Champagne.

But the best network for me may be largely irrelevant to someone living elsewhere. A traveler in Taipei and a traveler in Chicago are starting with very different choices. There is no universal route map that works best for everyone.

Emirates is a good example of why an airline’s reputation may need to be separated from the particular experience you are buying.

Mention Emirates and many people think of luxury (massive first class suites, showers, and bars onboard with beautiful flight attendants serving you extensive food and beverage offerings). That “halo effect” reputation is understandable.

But someone booking business class on an older Boeing 777 may encounter a product that falls well short of that image. The retrofitted 777s improve the situation with a 1-2-1 layout and direct aisle access, but I would not put that seat ahead of the leading business class products elsewhere.

Singapore Airlines illustrates this as well. Its reputation for service, built in part around the Singapore Girl branding, is extraordinary. Yet some travelers strongly dislike its longhaul business class seats, particularly their sleeping position.

A beautifully presented meal and gracious service cannot entirely compensate for a bed in which you struggle to get comfortable. Singapore’s new cabin reveal on Friday, November 6, will be particularly interesting for that reason.

My recent Emirates 777 first class flight demonstrated the reverse problem: a superb suite paired with service that did not live up to it. I loved the space, but the experience still fell short.

So what about Kirby’s argument that technology is most important?

We sometimes talk about technology as if it is separate from the passenger experience. But an app that lets you solve a problem without standing in line is providing service. A clear explanation of a delay is providing service. Working internet can determine whether a long daytime flight is productive or frustrating.

US airlines deserve credit here. Their digital tools can be excellent, and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it. But even the Alaska, American, and Delta apps are–comparatively speaking–much better than their non-US peers.

To be clear, that does not mean every American airline leads every foreign airline or that an attractive app excuses indifferent employees. It does mean that evaluating service solely by how someone pours your wine misses a large part of what an airline does for its customers.

Connectivity is especially important to me. Extra legroom and a better meal are welcome, but painfully slow or non-functioning Wi-Fi can materially change how I feel about a flight. For someone hoping to disconnect and sleep, it may barely register. The features can be measured. The importance each passenger assigns to them cannot be universal.

I also recognize the limitations of my own perspective. Much of my coverage focuses on premium cabins, and those experiences influence my preferences. But what does the airline offer someone in economy?

Some Asian carriers offer a more appealing combination of legroom, meals, and attentive service than their US counterparts. That deserves weight, even if the business class cabin lacks the latest suite.

At the same time, the aircraft still matters. So do the fare restrictions, baggage allowance, and cost of choosing a seat. A generous meal does not tell us whether the ticket represents good value.

For a family paying for several tickets, the best airline may be the one offering a tolerable nonstop journey at an affordable total price. For a tall passenger, a little more legroom may matter far more than the entertainment selection.

An airline cannot claim superiority for everyone based on what it provides a small number of passengers at the front of the aircraft.

A great airline should operate reliably and treat passengers well when it fails.

Those are related, but separate, expectations. I want to arrive on time. When that is impossible, I want an honest explanation and practical assistance.

No airline can prevent every weather delay or mechanical problem. But how it prepares, communicates, and recovers tells me much more than a polished promotional video.

American Airlines is a useful example from my own flying. I would argue that some of my recent meals on American have been the best among the US network carriers. Its free Wi-Fi has also tends to work very well for me. Those are real strengths.

Nevertheless, my experiences with inconsistent service and operational problems place American well below Delta and United in my overall assessment. That is not a claim that every American flight is bad or every Delta flight is good. It is the cumulative effect of repeated experiences. A carrier earns my confidence over time, and it can lose it the same way.

The loyalty program belongs in this discussion too.

Award availability, redemption prices, and the usefulness of elite benefits all affect how much value I receive from an airline. A good program can persuade me to choose one carrier when the alternatives are otherwise similar.

But I try to separate the airline I enjoy most from the program in which I find the most value.

An excellent redemption does not make an uncomfortable seat comfortable. Status does not make a canceled flight depart. Conversely, a wonderful airline can have a loyalty program that gives me little reason to engage with it. Ideally, the program reinforces a relationship the airline has already earned through its service.

Qatar Airways and STARLUX are among my favorites because I have found their overall experiences so compelling. The appeal extends beyond a seat or a meal: I look forward to flying them because of the reliable Wi-Fi, excellent service, and quality in everything.

Air France has also come such a long way. Its newer business class seat is excellent, and the addition of Starlink on equipped aircraft addresses something that matters greatly to me. Combined with the food and service I enjoy, that makes it an increasingly attractive choice.

Yet I still have many reasons to fly United. Its network and technology have practical value in my life that an exceptional flight on another carrier cannot always replace.

That is why my favorite airline and the airline I choose for a particular trip need not be the same…maybe the point is that talking about which carrier is “best” is ultimately futile and our focus instead should be rewarding carriers who do things well and not patronizing those that continually disappoint.

Kirby’s claim is worth discussing because he recognizes that being the best involves more than having the fanciest cabin. Technology and network utility deserve more credit than they sometimes receive.

But I would not crown United the best airline in the world on that basis alone. The seat still matters. So does the person serving you, the reliability of the operation, and what happens when your plans unravel.

For me, the best airlines are the ones that bring those elements together consistently, but at the same time I realize how arbitrary my own evaluation can be. Thus, I tend to think asking “who is best” is the wrong question versus asking “who does X,Y, and Z well?”

What makes an airline the best for you—and which airline comes closest?

#6207. JetBlue Raises Baggage Fees Again, Now Charges Up To $140 Roundtrip For One Checked Bag

JetBlue has raised checked baggage fees again, and bringing one ordinary suitcase can now add as much as $140 to a roundtrip ticket. With holiday travel approaching, this is another reminder that the fare you see when shopping may be far removed from what your trip actually costs.

JetBlue has increased baggage charges for new bookings made on or after November 3, 2026. The airline’s updated fee schedule lists a first checked bag starting at $50 each way. The price depends on when you travel and when you pay.

For passengers without an included baggage allowance or waiver, these are the new charges within the United States, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Canada. All amounts are per bag, each way:

You can see more particulars here, including pricing for Mosaic elites.

Upcoming peak periods include November 19–January 18. If you booked before November 3, check your reservation for the applicable charges (old rates apply). Here’s the full chart of peak dates over the next year:

That means one suitcase costs $100 roundtrip even at the lowest new rate. On peak dates, it costs $110 when paid in advance or $140 when purchased within 24 hours of each departure.

Consider a family of four traveling over Thanksgiving, with each person checking one suitcase and no baggage benefits.

Pay sufficiently early and the roundtrip baggage bill is $440. Wait until check-in for both flights and it becomes $560.

When does it become cheaper just to buy new clothes at your destination? We certainly try to pack efficiently when traveling with our children, but one standard checked bag per person hardly strikes me as an extravagant amount of luggage, especially for a longer holiday trip.

At these prices, baggage can materially change which airline offers the best deal. A cheaper JetBlue ticket may cease to be cheaper once you add the luggage you actually need…though it would not surprise me to see others follow.

Mosaic 1 members receive one checked bag, while Mosaic 2–4 members receive two. Eligible JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders receive one bag. Premium-cabin allowances depend on the fare purchased: Base fares include one bag, while standard and Flex premium fares include two.

Those benefits become more valuable every time the underlying fees rise, though it’s still not a loyalty program or credit card product I can get enthusiastic about.

JetBlue’s latest increase pushes the cost of one checked suitcase to $100–$140 roundtrip for passengers without an exemption. For families, the additional expense can reach hundreds of dollars.

Compare the total cost before booking, and if you know you will check a bag, pay more than 24 hours before departure. I want JetBlue to succeed, but charging passengers more to bring their belongings does little to make it an airline people actively want to choose. Quote the contrary, JetBlue is doing a great job of alienating passengers during its great time of need.

#6206. Why United Airlines' Unusual Boeing 767-400ER Seats With 43 Inches Of Pitch Aren't For Passengers

Lokyo Multimedia JP | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

United Airlines operates some of the most unusual economy seats in the industry, and passengers lucky enough to find them can enjoy an experience that rivals premium economy. Hidden toward the back of the carrier's Boeing 767 aircraft are four seats offering an impressive 43 inches of pitch, extendable leg rests, footrests, and additional recline. With an entire foot more pitch than United's standard economy seats, these unusual accommodations are the most spacious options available in the airline's economy cabin.

However, these seats don’t exist for passenger comfort; rather, they serve as dedicated inflight crew-rest accommodations, giving flight attendants somewhere to relax during longer international journeys. United occasionally makes them available for passenger reservations when the aircraft operates shorter routes that do not require dedicated crew-rest facilities, creating an unusual opportunity for travelers to secure some of the most spacious seats in the cabin.

Tucked into the back of the economy cabin on all of United’s 16 Boeing 767-400ER aircraft are two pairs of four seats unlike any other on the aircraft. Located in rows 52 and 53 in the A and B positions on the left side of the cabin, these four seats offer a whopping 43 inches of seat pitch. That means these seats offer an entire foot of additional pitch compared to the 31 inches that come standard in United’s economy cabin.

Pitch, also known as the distance between a point on one seat and the same point on the seat in front, is the most impressive number here because these seats take up a much larger footprint. On the left side of the aircraft, in the same space where United has just two rows on the right side, the airline fits three rows of standard economy seats, reflecting just how special the set of four seats truly are. Compared with economy plus, United’s extra-legroom offering, the seats boast nine additional inches of legroom and even offer five additional inches of pitch compared with premium economy toward the front of the aircraft.

The additional improvements don’t stop at seat pitch, however. They also include additional cushioning, greater recline (approximately seven inches), and extendable leg rests and footrests, bringing these seats closer to what one can expect in premium economy rather than standard economy. Additionally, these seats have curtains that can be drawn around the seating area. When available to passengers, seats 52A, 52B, 53A and 53B are easily among the best in the economy cabin.

With an incredible amount of legroom and the additional amenities in rows 52 and 53, it raises the question of why United chose to install these special seating pairs. The reasoning behind this has nothing to do with the passengers at all. Rather, the unusual configuration exists because flight attendants need somewhere to rest sufficiently during long international flights, like Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Sao Paulo Viracopos International Airport (GRU) or Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Barcelona-El Prat Airport (BCN), the 767-400ER frequently operates.

The design of the seats hints at the true purpose they serve. Rather than installing a dedicated bunk compartment like those found on many larger long-haul aircraft, United instead uses these specially modified seats to increase overhead bin and galley space. United’s agreements with its flight attendants formally require two rows of two seats, providing enough room for two flight attendants to rest during scheduled crew breaks.

United’s 56-seat-economy 767 shows how far the airline is pushing premium.

The availability of the four seats ultimately depends on whether United needs them for its flight attendants. On long-haul international services, typically those longer than eight hours, flight attendants must take rest breaks inflight. In those scenarios, United blocks off its additional economy seats to serve as the crew rest area when inflight. This means passengers cannot select them even if they are willing to pay for additional legroom. The curtains and specialized features that come with the seat are there to support the crew first, not create another passenger seating category.

However, when United’s 767-400ERs operate shorter domestic services, often transcontinental flights between major hubs, the flight usually is not long enough to require a mandated crew rest period, meaning United can release the seats for passenger use. This situation is when lucky passengers may find them listed as Economy Plus on the airline’s booking platform. The Points Guy has previously reported that United generally blocks these positions well in advance and may release them about 24 to 48 hours before departure when not required for crew rest.

While most travelers booked in United economy would have to upgrade to Economy Plus in order to be able to select these seats, United elite status holders have an advantage when seats are released. United’s lowest elite status holders, those with Silver Premier status, can select Economy Plus seats for free at check-in. All other United elites, including Gold, Platinum, 1K and Global Services, can move to Economy Plus for free at booking, although most will have to wait to select the crew rest seats until they become available a few days before departure.

Passengers hoping to find the unusual seats will first need to identify the correct aircraft and seating configuration. Luckily for travelers, all of United’s Boeing 767 aircraft are equipped with four special seats at the rear of the economy cabin, even the carrier’s Boeing 767-300ER airframes. The retrofitted 767-400ER, now the only configuration of the type in United’s fleet, features a three-cabin configuration with 231 seats in total, including 34 United Polaris business-class seats, 24 Premium Plus seats and 173 Economy and Economy Plus seats.

When looking at United’s online booking or check-in platform, there are several recognizable characteristics that can help confirm the aircraft type. Aside from a designator present at the top of the seat map specifying what type of aircraft is operating the route, the most noticeable way to tell a 767 apart from United’s other widebody aircraft is the 2-3-2 seating configuration in economy. On the 767-400ER, the four crew-reset positions are located in the final two rows, making seats 52A, 52B, 53A and 53B the ones to look out for on these aircraft.

United’s 767-300s, which also feature the specialized crew rest seats, have a similar overall layout to the 767-400ER, albeit with less length. Given this, the unique seats can instead be found in rows 43 and 44, with 43A, 43B, 44A and 44B all containing the leg rests, footrests and additional recline. Online seat map databases, like aeroLOPA and Simple Flying’s own seat map database, can provide further insight into the position of each seat.

An unstable approach forced the 757 into a go-around with low fuel remaining.

While United’s Boeing 767 aircraft are the carrier’s only widebody aircraft without a dedicated cabin crew rest area, United also operates countless long-haul or transoceanic routes onboard smaller narrowbody aircraft, including the Boeing 757, Boeing 737 and soon, the Airbus A321XLR. On these single-aisle aircraft, airlines generally have much less space to install dedicated crew-rest compartments, so blocked-off passenger seats can serve a similar purpose.

On the Boeing 757, United frequently blocks off at least one Polaris business class seat for one of the three pilots operating long-haul flights to take a break inflight. For flight attendants on these routes, a curtained-off row of economy seats towards the rear of the aircraft is standard. A similar strategy is used for Boeing 737 flights long enough to require crew rest breaks. On routes like United’s famous island hopper, the airline blocks off two first class recliners to provide space for the crew to rest, as well as a row of economy seats in most scenarios.

Looking ahead, the Airbus A321XLR further demonstrates how airlines are being forced to adapt to these arrangements as narrowbody aircraft increasingly operate longer international routes. American Airlines, for example, has detailed plans to block off two rows of seats, 33 ABC and 34 DEF, to serve as a couch of sorts, with a sleeper pad and curtains for its flight attendants on long flights. Several other innovative solutions, like Diehl Aviation’s crew rest compartment, can be installed to provide a module with two beds dedicated to crew breaks. Ultimately, crew-rest arrangements depend on the aircraft and length of operations, with United’s four enhanced 767 seats providing a relatively simple solution to a potentially complex and expensive problem.

Providing adequate rest facilities is a crucial part of long-haul flight planning, especially those that operate overnight or cross multiple time zones. Flight attendants have numerous safety responsibilities throughout the journey, including monitoring the cabin, assisting passengers who need assistance, and responding to inflight emergencies. Having an appropriate place to rest during designated breaks is therefore an important part of managing extended operations.

Crew-rest requirements also influence how airlines schedule their flights and configure their aircraft. For aircraft like United’s 767s or other narrowbodies, without crew rest compartments built into either the overhead or cargo hold, longer flights mean having to block off seats that could be filled with revenue-generating customers.

For United, the four unusual seats aboard its Boeing 767-400ER represent one solution to this challenge. Their extra cushioning, 43-inch pitch, leg rests, and footrests make them far more comfortable than conventional economy seats, but these features exist mainly to support the airline's flight attendants. Passengers may occasionally benefit when United releases the seats on shorter services, but their availability will always depend on the airline's operational requirements. Ultimately, the unusual configuration highlights how commercial aircraft cabins must balance passenger capacity with the needs of the people responsible for operating flights safely.

A lot of these stylish, boutique hotels enter the points world through curated hotel collections that participate in loyalty programs, giving hotels a wider reach of potential guests without having to adhere to strict brand standards that change the spirit of the property.

One of the pioneers in this space is Design Hotels, a collection of hundreds of independently-owned hotels and resorts dotting the globe, each with its own identity, personality and approach to hospitality.

"Every hotel is picked for its originality [and] the vision that's behind it," Stijn Oyen, managing director at Design Hotels, told TPG, adding that each property has "a strong point of view and cultural connection."

And it's not necessarily easy to make the cut for this collection: According to Oyen, only about 5% of the hotels that apply to join Design Hotels are accepted in an effort to "stay true to the original roots and values of what makes a design hotel."

Then there's the loyalty twist: Marriott actually owns Design Hotels, and many (but not all) of the collection's properties participate in Marriott Bonvoy.

Here's a quick guide to everything you need to know about Design Hotels, plus a few standout properties where you can earn and burn Marriott Bonvoy points.

Related: 12 new boutique hotels worth redeeming your points for

Founded in the early 1990s, Design Hotels was created to bring together independently owned, design-forward hotels that shared a commitment to originality, creativity and local culture.

Today, that collection is more than 300 members strong, with new properties regularly joining. What differentiates the collection is the individuality of each property — each one has its own unique point of view, rather than a prescribed set of standards travelers will see at more traditional hotel brands.

"We're set up around design," Oyen explained. "It's about the vision. It's about being independent with a voice."

Design Hotels became part of Marriott's portfolio following the hotel giant's acquisition of Starwood Hotels & Resorts in 2016, giving Marriott a majority stake in the company. By 2021, Marriott had acquired full ownership of Design Hotels, though the collection continues to operate as a separate entity, with member hotels retaining their individual identities and independence.

The company describes its properties as "design-driven hotels that function as social hubs and spaces for purposeful experiences."

But what does that actually mean? To start, getting into the collection isn't easy, and Design Hotels is looking for one distinguishing factor before choosing a new member: "the originality in its concept."

According to Oyen, only about 5% of applicants pass the test. Hotels are also evaluated on everything from design and sustainability to cultural programming and the property's connection to its local community.

"It's a strong, strong sense of place," Oyen explained, adding that beyond their physical design, the hotels should have vibrant public spaces that attract locals and feel like an extension of the neighborhoods they call home.

It's also about the people. According to Oyen, about 60% of Design Hotels owners are first-time hoteliers, bringing fresh perspectives and new approaches to hospitality. The company calls the creative minds behind its properties "Originals," describing them as "the engines behind pioneering design and revolutionary hospitality," according to the brand's website.

Without rigid brand standards dictating every detail, these hoteliers have the freedom to pursue projects that seasoned hospitality pros might consider too risky. That might be as simple as removing TVs from guest rooms or as dramatic as building a hotel accessible only by cable car, like Vigilius Mountain Resort in Italy's Dolomites.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, Design Hotels offers a truly independent, boutique-like stay while still allowing them to earn and burn points. Something that, frankly, a lot of people don't realize is available to them in the loyalty world.

Just don't forget: Not all Design Hotels participate in Marriott Bonvoy. To see a full list of the 120-plus participating hotels, visit Marriott's dedicated Design Hotels landing page.

For Design Hotels, according to Oyen, the relationship with Marriott is a win-win situation: Hotels gain access to nearly 300 million loyalty members while maintaining their "complete independence."

But because these properties operate differently from traditional Marriott hotels, Bonvoy elite members shouldn't expect all their usual perks to apply.

Here's what members can expect based on their status.

The following Marriott Bonvoy benefits are excluded at Design Hotels:

Set near the beach in Casablanca, Villa Sahrai pays respect to "Casablanca’s Art Deco tradition" across its 56 rooms and public spaces. Be sure to take advantage of the spa and its Moroccan hammam before settling down for food at one of two restaurants or a nightcap at the bar.

How to book: Cash rates from around $160 per night or 34,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

To get to Vigilius Mountain Resort, guests must ascend a private cable car that travels between the mountain hotel and the village it soars above. But once up at the top, guests are treated to beautiful Dolomite views, architecture that incorporates nature and wellness experiences around every stylish corner.

How to book: Cash rates from about $341 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

At The Austin Proper Hotel, patterns, textures and colors combine in unexpected and beautiful ways from the moment guests step inside until their head hits the pillow. The hotel is as cool as Austin itself, but also full of surprises: You can grab classic Tex-Mex to eat or opt for a French Japanese tasting menu or soak up the sun at the rooftop pool before a lymphatic drain at the Verbena Spa.

How to book: Cash rates from $350 or 54,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

Kyoto is no stranger to incredible hotels, but Genji Kyoto offers an intimate experience with just 20 rooms that feel distinctly Japanese and totally sleek and fresh. As serene as they come, spend a day getting lost in Kyoto's ancient history before heading to the rooftop bar and garden to unwind.

How to book: Cash rates from about $227 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

Condesa is one of Mexico City's trendiest neighborhoods, so it only makes sense to stay in a hotel that also fits the description. At this hotel, enjoy rooftop sushi or French-Mexican fusion food; relax in the hydrotherapy pool or kick back on the patio and watch the city's cosmopolitan set roam the area.

How to book: Cash rates from $339 per night or 42,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

As major hotel companies continue to expand their portfolios beyond traditional hotels, from independent boutique properties to outdoor-focused experiences, collections like Design Hotels are helping diversify what travelers can experience with points and miles.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, that means more opportunities to stay somewhere truly unique without giving up the ability to earn and redeem points. And while the elite benefits might look a little different, the chance to experience a hotel with its own distinct personality might just be worth the trade-off.

#6204. Denver Air Connection Plans First Florida Service

Denver Air Connection will launch its first-ever service to Florida, and it will be outside the scope of any Essential Air Service (EAS) contract. The only other place in the carrier’s network that isn’t directly part of an EAS contract is its service to Telluride, Colorado, from both Denver and Phoenix.

Beginning January 9, 2027, DAC will begin nonstop flights from Muskegon, Michigan, to Orlando Sanford, with service operating on Saturdays using the 50-seat Embraer E145XR.

While Muskegon itself only has one other destination, Chicago O’Hare, which is also operated by DAC under the EAS contract, DAC will compete indirectly with Allegiant, as it has a sizable operation and a base in Grand Rapids, Michigan, which is located only about 45 minutes east of Muskegon.

The 1,030-mile route from Muskegon to Orlando Sanford on the E145 will become the longest at-risk flight operated by any EAS carrier, and one of the longest commercial airline flights operated by an Embraer E145 in the country, overtaking the current record holder, United’s 830-mile route from Washington Dulles to Mobile, Alabama, by almost 200 miles.

That record for the E145 is a little bit of a technicality, as JSX does operate a handful of flights over 1,000 miles with its Embraer E145s, but the carrier is not considered a commercial airline, and is instead classified as a “public charter operation.”

Muskegon Airport director Ken Efting did have something to say about this new service: “This is a historic milestone for MKG and the communities we serve…This is exactly the kind of opportunity we’ve been working toward, and it’s a testament to our growing community support and strong partnership with Denver Air Connection.”

This isn’t the first time an EAS carrier has operated at-risk service to the state of Florida from an EAS community. These smaller carriers sometimes begin flights to leisure destinations like Florida and other leisure-heavy destinations to entice higher passenger numbers that boost the communities they serve.

Muskegon will join the small but growing list of Essential Air Service communities that are now connected with nonstop flights to the state of Florida, but they will be the only EAS community in Michigan to have Florida flights.

#6203. Delta Air Lines CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow Move That Separates It From Virgin Atlantic

Delta Air Lines is fighting Heathrow Airport’s decision to move it away from Virgin Atlantic, warning that separating the partners will hurt passengers and undermine years of investment. I understand why Delta is upset. But whether that should entitle it to remain in Terminal 3 is a more complicated question.

Heathrow plans to move Delta from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, while Virgin Atlantic remains in Terminal 3. The decision would split an operation the two airlines have spent years integrating.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian issued an unusually pointed public statement on November 2, calling the decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.” He argued that sharing Terminal 3 supports convenient connections and a consistent premium experience. Delta intends to challenge the move, saying it “will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision.”

“Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers. For more than a decade, our airlines have served millions of customers through our co-located operation in Terminal 3, offering travelers convenient connections, premium amenities and access to an expanded global network.

“Delta and Virgin Atlantic provide UK consumers with a valuable competitive alternative across the Atlantic. Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal. We are committed to preserving the seamless travel experience for which Delta and Virgin Atlantic are known and will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision. We urge Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider their decision in favor of a more prudent and thoughtful outcome that puts travelers first and allows competition to flourish at Heathrow.”

Terminal assignments can sound like an obscure airport planning issue until you are the passenger trying to make a connection.

A traveler arriving on Delta and continuing on Virgin Atlantic would face a terminal transfer that is unnecessary today. The same applies in reverse. Unfortunately, terminal transfers are not easy at LHR and moving between terminals introduces another step and more opportunity for something to go wrong.

For someone simply flying Delta to London and heading into the city, the effect may be less consequential. But Delta and Virgin sell their partnership as an integrated travel experience. Separating their airport operations makes that promise harder to deliver.

There is also the premium experience. Eligible Delta passengers currently benefit from Virgin Atlantic’s Terminal 3 facilities, including its Clubhouse. Those facilities are part of what makes the partnership attractive, especially when choosing between similarly priced business class tickets.

If the move happens, I would assume that a Delta flight departing from Terminal 4 will not include access to Virgin’s Terminal 3 facilities, at least in any practical capacity. However as I mentioned in my earlier story, integrating with Air France/KLM in Terminal 4 makes a lot of sense (far more connecting itineraries) and the lounge is not bad at all.

Still, replacing something that already works well requires money and effort. I can understand why Delta would prefer not to start over.

Heathrow’s decision follows a three-year terminal review. The airport says the changes will improve its use of existing capacity and operational resilience, while creating room for growth.

Heathrow also says airlines representing 81% of its passengers support the outcome (that is a share of passenger traffic represented by supportive airlines, not a survey showing that 81% of travelers approve).

Delta is not the only carrier being asked to move. The wider reshuffle also affects Finnair, Japan Airlines, LATAM, and China Southern.

An airport cannot necessarily give every airline its preferred location. Keeping one partnership together may mean imposing constraints or additional costs elsewhere. Delta’s investment deserves consideration, but it should not automatically settle how Heathrow should allocate scarce terminal space.

Bastian also presents the shared terminal as supporting competition across the Atlantic. I accept that a more cumbersome ground experience could make Delta and Virgin less attractive to some travelers. A passenger comparing connections may reasonably prefer an itinerary that avoids a terminal transfer.

But claims that the move will weaken competition or drive up fares need more support than the fact that Delta dislikes it. Heathrow is changing where Delta operates, rather than announcing that it must stop serving London or taking slots away. Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult. That deserves a substantive answer but there’s undeniable logic in the shuffling.

Delta has good reason to challenge a Heathrow move that would separate it from Virgin Atlantic. Sharing Terminal 3 offers practical benefits, and I understand Bastian’s anger. But Heathrow must manage the airport as a whole. I would be more persuaded by a clear account of what this reshuffle improves and why those gains outweigh the disruption.

For now, this is a dispute over a planned 2028 change..itt does not mean your next Delta flight has moved to Terminal 4. I hope the eventual outcome preserves as much of the current passenger experience as possible, but I’m still not convinced Delta is being unfairly picked on by LHR and I am convinced that whether Delta wins or loses this battle, its passengers will enjoy a great ground product at Heathrow for many years to come.

I doubt they have anything to gain by being co-located with AF/KL rather than VS. Also T4 is worse than the T2/T3 complex for ground transport or self-connecting options.

Is terminal 4 underutilized or are they shifting the problem of crowding from T3 to T4? With LHR ruling out the prospect of new slots at LHR in 2028 when Heathrow’s Management says this move will lead to gains the question they haven’t answered is gains for who, for which airline.

Terminal 4 is much more modern than Terminal 3 so there should be little complaint on that one.

Yep. This was the obvious move by LHR if that’s your end game. End of the day this will be about compensating DL/VS for the move to T4. But VS(/DL) gets no brownie points for renovating the current Clubhouse in a transparent attempt to forestall this. LHR told VS/DL that this was the likely outcome – if VS(/DL) wanted to waste their money playing a game of chicken, that’s on them.

Are there really that many people connecting in LHR to Asia on Virgin?

While the clubhouse is nice I wasn’t overly wowed by it. And since flights are day time west, it’s not as important having a lounge meal like eastbound when you’re trying to maximize sleep. The Air France lounge in T4 looks nice enough anyways. I think the biggest loss for anyone flying D1 is the arrivals lounge, especially if you’re heading straight into the office.

Maybe Delta should have listened to their pilots a few years ago and stopped outsourcing so much of their international flying to partners…

” Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult.”

Heathrow is proposing to level the playing field between the two major US-UK Joint Ventures at the airport. Virgin had the chance to move, as well. It’s not as though Delta doesn’t have the cash to build a reasonable ground experience at T4. LHR isn’t even anything close to a transfer hub for DL. Those hubs are AMS and CDG — CDG, an airport where DL/AF customers have to change terminals and clear security between terminals. what a concept for Delta.

I get why Delta is upset but it doesn’t seem very persuasive to be mad about “connections” when LHR isn’t much of a connecting airport for their Joint Venture. But as usual… Delta and Virgin Atlanta love to cry foul when asked to do what AA/BA do today…

#6202. Flying Blue Delays 50% SAF XP Price Hike After Admitting “We Didn’t Handle The Rollout Well”

Flying Blue has postponed an abrupt devaluation to the elite status credit members earn through sustainable aviation fuel and charitable contributions. I remain skeptical of the underlying scheme, but program chief Tiffany Funk deserves credit for acknowledging the botched rollout, listening to members, and giving them time to adjust.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue initially changed its earning rates on November 2, 2026, without advance notice. For cash contributions toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the cost increased from €10 per XP to €15 per XP, a 50% increase.

XP, or Experience Points, determine Flying Blue elite status. Members who had incorporated these contributions into their qualification plans suddenly faced a more expensive path to their goal.

Now, as One Mile At A Time also reports, Flying Blue has postponed the changes until December 1, 2026. The previous earning rates return effective November 4, and contributions made since November 2 will also receive credit at the prior rates.

Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, addressed the reprieve:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I appreciate the candor. Funk acknowledges that Flying Blue handled the rollout poorly and offers a practical correction. Members now have a transition period, including protection for contributions made during the initial rollout.

To be candid, I consider this arrangement a greenwashing revenue-generating measure. Awarding elite status credit for an environmental contribution is a convenient way to monetize the pursuit of status while wrapping the transaction in a sustainability message, a win-win for both Flying Blue and frequent travelers but probably not for the environment.

We don’t have to litigate that here and I readily acknowledge SAF can play a role in reducing aviation’s lifecycle emissions, but purchasing a contribution does not make a passenger’s flight emissions disappear. And I suspect the additional XP is the deciding factor for many members who participate, not altruism for Mother Earth.

Flying Blue certainly understands the appeal. Someone approaching a qualification deadline may find paying for a contribution far more convenient than taking another flight. But my skepticism about the arrangement does not diminish the importance of treating participating members fairly. Flying Blue offered an opportunity, and members planned around it. Their reliance was entirely foreseeable.

Flying Blue owes no one a permanent opportunity to acquire additional XP at a particular rate. It can decide that the existing formula is too generous or that it wants a different balance between flying and other qualification methods. Members can then decide whether the revised offer is worthwhile.

My larger objection, as with most devaluations, concerns candid communication and advance notice. Tell us what is changing. Give us time to adjust plans made under the existing rules. Please spare us the suggestion that a reduction in benefits is an “enhancement” inspired by member feedback.

Funk avoids that familiar gaslighting here. She does not claim members asked to pay more for their XP. She acknowledges that feedback exposed a problem with the rollout and explains what Flying Blue will do about it.

That is a much more credible use of member feedback.

Consider someone who booked travel expecting to earn a certain number of XP from flights and make up the remainder through SAF contributions. An overnight change can upset that calculation after the flights have already been purchased.

That member is not necessarily demanding that the rules remain unchanged forever. The objection is that a plan made in good faith has become more expensive without warning.

The additional time gives members an opportunity to complete contributions at the previous rate or reconsider their qualification strategy. Crediting contributions made since November 2 at the old rate also avoids penalizing those who happened to transact during the botched rollout.

Neither measure eliminates the devaluation. Both make its introduction fairer.

I commend Funk for listening and adjusting. Management can respond to criticism without abandoning the underlying business decision. Here, a relatively straightforward concession makes loyal customers  feel heard rather than taken for granted.

I remain skeptical of Flying Blue’s SAF contribution scheme, and the higher cost per XP will make it less attractive. Heck, I remain skeptical of status in general as a proud free agent for two years running. But the program has corrected the avoidable failure of introducing that change without clear communication or notice.

Funk acknowledged what went wrong and gave members time to prepare. Flying Blue is entitled to revise its earning rates. Members who planned around those rates deserve a reasonable transition, and they now have one. That is a welcome response…I never thought Funk would make the program more generous as other loyalty programs cut and devalue, but measured and clear changes with advance notice to members are all anyone can ask for.
