#6201. The Key Differences Between Economy, Premium Economy, Business & First Class

Boarding a plane today means stepping into a highly structured, carefully designed world. If you’re a frequent traveler or just interested in aviation, you probably spend your walk down the aisle analyzing exactly how airlines divide up the limited space inside their aluminum — nowadays also composite — tubes with wings. Understanding the real differences between economy class, premium economy, business class, and first class goes beyond just picking a ticket — it’s actually a masterclass in clever cabin design and airline economics that extends far beyond what we as passengers could ever imagine. In this guide, we’ll break down exactly what you get for your money across all four cabin zones.

To understand today's LOPAs (acronym for Layout of Passenger Accommodations), you have to look at how much flying has changed. During the "Golden Age" of the 1950s and 60s, just being on an airplane was a luxury, and even standard "coach" seats offered generous legroom and a sophisticated onboard service. Today, the industry is highly competitive, data-driven, and built on optimizing every single square inch. While we might miss the spaciousness of the past, this high-density approach is exactly what made flying affordable for millions, creating a sliding scale of comfort that fits just about every budget.

Economy class, often called "coach", "standard seating," or "the back of the bus," is the undisputed backbone of the global commercial aviation industry. As someone who spends a lot of time thinking about airplane seats, I look at the economy cabin not only as the cramped space — and barely acceptable experience — that it is, but as an incredible feat of modern engineering and logistics. This is where the vast majority of travelers sit, and it’s the cabin that makes it possible for airlines to transport hundreds of people across the globe at affordable prices. While it often gets a deserved bad reputation for tight legroom and shrinking seat sizes, economy class is actually a masterclass in efficiency, allowing carriers to maximize passenger count while still meeting strict global safety regulations.

The main defining feature of modern economy class is space optimization, which is measured primarily by "seat pitch," the distance from any point on one seat to the exact same point on the seat in front of it. A few decades ago, standard pitch was around 34 inches (about 86cm), but today, most major carriers offer between 30 and 31 inches, with some ultra-low-cost carriers tightening it to 28 inches (about 71 cm). To make up for this lost space, seat manufacturers have developed "slimline" designs, stripping out bulky padding and using lightweight composite materials to carve out a little extra knee room for the passenger. Even with less physical space, today's modern long-haul economy seats often come with a crisp, on-demand entertainment screen, USB power outlets and a very limited recline, which tries to compensate for the uncomfortable and claustrophobic passenger experience that has become standard on almost every airline around the globe.

Despite the obvious physical limitations, economy class delivers exactly what it promises: safe, reliable transport that gets you to your destination at the exact same time as the people paying thousands of dollars at the front of the plane. For the budget-conscious traveler or the weekend adventurer, flying coach is a highly practical decision that leaves more money in your pocket for your actual vacation. Plus, when you consider that a modern twin-engine jet like the Airbus A350 or Boeing 787 is pressurizing the cabin to a more comfortable altitude and pumping in more humidity than older jets, the actual physiological experience of flying in economy today is arguably better than it was twenty years ago — but the truth is that the physical experience isn't.

If you've booked a long-haul flight recently, you've probably noticed that premium economy has become one of the most popular cabin choices available. Introduced back in the early 1990s by airlines like EVA Air and Virgin Atlanticpremium economy was designed to sit — literally — right in the middle of standard economy and business class, filling a massive gap in the market. As business class tickets got more expensive and economy seats got tighter, a whole new demographic of travelers emerged: people who wanted just a bit more comfort and space, but couldn't justify the sky-high prices of a lie-flat bed. Premium economy essentially brings back the standard of comfort from the older days of flying, repackaging it as an upgraded experience for the modern era.

The physical differences when you upgrade to premium economy have a surprisingly big impact on a long flight. You usually get a wider seat — often 19 or 19.5 inches compared to the standard 17 to 18 inches in economy — and the seat pitch is bumped up to a very comfortable 38 inches, giving you plenty of room to stretch your legs and have a decent amount of recline. The seats also feature wider armrests that you don't have to fight your neighbor for, and usually a fold-out footrest or leg rest to help you sleep better. On top of the physical seat, airlines elevate the "soft product" as well, meaning you might get priority boarding, an upgraded amenity kit, and meals served on real ceramic dishware with metal cutlery instead of plastic trays.

From an airline business perspective, premium economy is an absolute home run. Industry data shows that this cabin often generates the highest profit margins per square foot of any zone on the aircraft, because it only takes up slightly more floor space than standard economy but sells for significantly more money — close to two times the price of an economy ticket. It’s the perfect product for small business owners, corporate employees whose travel policies won't pay for business class, or leisure travelers who want to start their vacation feeling rested.

The seat is the foundation of premium economy comfort. Airlines can add better amenities, but none of those compensate for an uncomfortable seat.

The constant push for innovation in business class seating has been amazing to watch in the last 10 years. We went from "angle-flat" seats that tended to slide you downward while you slept, to 180-degree fully lie-flat beds, and now to direct-aisle-access layouts where nobody has to climb over their neighbor to go to the restroom or the galley. Carriers like Qatar Airways with its famous Qsuites, or Japan Airlines with its brand new A350-1000 suites, have added sliding doors to the seats, turning them into private mini-rooms. Inside these suites, you’re treated to massive 4K entertainment screens, multiple storage compartments, designer bedding, and Michelin Star restaurant-quality dining that you can order on demand.

The reason business class has become so luxurious is simply that airlines have realized what premium passengers value most: uninterrupted sleep. Business travelers are paying a premium to avoid a day of lost productivity due to jet lag and back pain. By providing a true bed and a quiet, private environment, airlines are selling time and well-being rather than just transportation, making it the most important competitive product in their entire lineup.

While business class is focused on comfort and productivity, first class is all about pure, undeniable exclusivity and personalized service. It’s the highest tier of commercial air travel — and almost better than flying on a private jet in every aspect — as it is a space usually reserved for ultra-wealthy individuals, celebrities, or very dedicated travel hackers who have saved up millions of credit card points. First Class goes beyond just giving you a bed; it tries to replicate the experience of a five-star luxury hotel, making you forget that you are actually flying on an airplane at 35,000 feet.

The biggest difference between first and business class today comes down to real estate and the passenger-to-crew ratio. A Business Class cabin might have 40 to 60 seats, but a true first class cabin on a plane like the B777 or A380 usually only has six to eight massive suites and in smaller aircraft like the A350, between three and six. The space you get in first class is just incredible, sometimes featuring a separate leather armchair alongside an actual, standalone bed, rather than a seat that mechanically folds down. This is where airlines pull out all the stops: Emirates has its famous onboard shower spas exclusively dedicated to first class customers, Singapore Airlines offers double beds if you're traveling with a partner, and Etihad Airwaysgoes even one step further with their "Residence" — which features an incredible wide sofa for up to two passengers together with a private bathroom that even has a shower, and to round up the experience a queen-sized bed onboard their A380s. The food for first class passengers on most premium airlines is almost always prepared by a dedicated onboard chef, featuring caviar and high-end vintage champagnes, and every single luxury you could expect for a seating experience that almost never goes below the staggering price of 5,000 US dollars on a one-way ticket, and that can sometimes reach 30,000 or 35,000 US dollars for an ultra-long-haul return ticket.

However, despite how amazing it looks, international first class is actually becoming pretty rare. Because business class has gotten so good with lie-flat beds and sliding doors, most passengers and companies simply aren't willing to pay three or four times the price for first class. As a result, many airlines have completely removed first class from their fleets, using that valuable floor space to install more business and premium economy seats instead. Today, first class is mostly kept around as a "halo product" — something that looks great on billboards and social media to build brand prestige, even if very few people can actually afford to fly in it. For this reason, the only airlines still offering a true first class product are the following:

One of the most common questions I hear from friends and readers is, "Should I pay for the upgrade?" The answer is actually very complicated and depends heavily on how airlines price their tickets and how you value your own comfort. Deciding whether to upgrade from economy to a premium cabin is a personal choice that involves considering your budget, the length of the flight, and the condition you need to be in when you land. Here is a chart with all the key differences between the different classes:

Upgraded menu, real china and metal cutlery

On-demand fine dining, caviar, exclusive wines

Exclusive lounges, tarmac transfers, escorts

If you want to look at it logically, try breaking down the upgrade cost by the hour. For example, if you're taking a six-hour daytime flight from New York to London, sitting in Economy is completely fine for most people; paying an extra $2,500 to upgrade means you're spending over $400 an hour just to have a wider seat while you watch movies. On the other hand, if you're flying 15 hours on a red-eye from Los Angeles to Sydney, the math changes completely. On ultra-long-haul flights, upgrading to a lie-flat bed isn't just a luxury; it's an investment in your physical well-being, meaning you won't lose the first two days of your trip to exhaustion and jet lag — but only if you can afford it.

It’s also helpful to know how airlines handle these upgrades today. In the past, you might have gotten lucky by dressing nicely and asking the gate agent, but today, upgrades are controlled by complex algorithms. Airlines use yield management software to try to sell empty premium seats for cash right up until departure. Many carriers now use digital bidding systems that let you offer a specific amount of money for an upgrade a few days before the flight. It turns the whole process into a silent auction, allowing the airline to squeeze a bit more revenue out of the seat while giving you a chance to fly better for less than the standard fare.

When you really think about it, walking through the different cabins of an airplane shows us how many different ways there are to experience the exact same journey. Whether you are drinking champagne in a massive First Class suite or settling into a window seat in the very last row of Economy, the core product is identical: you are flying through the air at 600 miles per hour, crossing oceans and continents in a matter of hours, from point A to point B. The segmentation of the cabin simply reflects the different priorities of travelers, allowing the people who pay the most expensive tickets at the front to essentially subsidize the more affordable tickets in the back, making global travel possible for everyone.

Looking at the industry today, it's incredible to see how far we've come in terms of safety, technology, and cabin design. We take it for granted that we can watch live TV and browse the internet while miles above the ocean. But as a seat designer, I'm always thinking about what comes next. Airlines will always look for ways to optimize space and increase revenue, but there is a growing demand from passengers for better ergonomics, smarter storage, and more creative uses of the cabin space that doesn't solely rely on standard horizontal rows.

As we look toward the next generation of aircraft and the future of commercial aviation, the big challenge will be balancing airline economics with the passenger experience. With new aircraft materials and potential shifts in fuselage shapes on the horizon, will we continue to just tweak the traditional rows of seats, or is it finally time to completely rethink the three-dimensional space of the cabin to give every passenger — regardless of their ticket class — a better way to fly?

“Coach” is what we called economy for decades. There was a big difference between coach of the past and coach class of today. For one, everyone was fed. The seats were thick and heavily cushioned and the flight attendants were always at one’s service. There was actually leg room between seats. This happened until the late 1990’s early 2000’s. So it can be done. Coach passengers are now treated as an afterthought and shame on you passengers for not buying a better class ticket.

#6199. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

#6198. But Our Flag Was Still There

Imagine a time when Americans could be arrested by soldiers and imprisoned without the ordinary opportunity to challenge their detention before a judge. When a former congressman could be tried by a military commission for a political speech, then banished from the country. When newspaper offices could be occupied by troops and publication stopped. Imagine an editor imprisoned in the very fortress his grandfather had immortalized in a song about American freedom.

O say, can you see By the dawn’s early light

I woke up this morning thinking about the question at the beginning of our national anthem.

After an election, we tend to look for answers. This morning, I find myself more interested in what we can still see.

I see a country in which people cast ballots and those ballots have consequences. A country in which officeholders can be challenged and voters can change the direction of government. I see people who care enough to argue, sometimes bitterly, about the future of a place they still believe is worth fighting for.

That is an exhausting way to govern ourselves, but what a remarkable inheritance!

What so proudly we hailed At the twilight’s last gleaming

The president in those opening examples was Abraham Lincoln.

His administration’s restrictions on civil liberties are part of our history, even if they sit uncomfortably alongside the achievements for which we rightly honor him.

Beginning in 1861, Lincoln authorized the suspension of habeas corpus, the means by which a detainee can ask a court to examine the legality of detention. The Constitution permits suspension in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it. Whether the president could exercise that authority without Congress was fiercely contested. The practical consequence was that people could be held by military authorities without the ordinary judicial protection against unlawful imprisonment.

In September 1862, his proclamation, circulated by the War Department as General Orders No. 141, subjected people discouraging enlistment or engaging in broadly described disloyal practices aiding the rebellion to military trial. It also suspended habeas corpus for those detained by military authority.

These were sweeping powers, with consequences far beyond the battlefield.

Whose broad stripes and bright stars Through the perilous fight

In 1863, a former Ohio congressman was arrested after delivering an antiwar speech, tried by a military commission, and convicted. Lincoln changed his punishment from imprisonment to banishment into Confederate territory.

Another critic, a Baltimore newspaper editor, had been arrested in 1861 and confined at Fort McHenry. His grandfather was Francis Scott Key. Think about that for a moment. The grandson of the man who wrote the words we sing about the land of the free became a political prisoner inside the fort associated with those words.

He was a Southern sympathizer. The former congressman’s politics were deeply objectionable in their defense of a slaveholding order. But we do not need to admire either man’s cause to take seriously the government’s treatment of him. Constitutional protections have little substance if they depend on our approval of the person invoking them.

O’er the ramparts we watched Were so gallantly streaming

General Ambrose Burnside ordered the suppression of the Chicago Times in 1863. Lincoln intervened to have that order revoked. That correction belongs in the account as much as the original abuse.

But in 1864, after the New York World and Journal of Commerce published a forged presidential proclamation, Lincoln himself ordered military action against the papers, including seizure of their printing establishments and the arrest of their editors and publishers.

The forgery was serious. So was the use of military power against newspapers.

All of this happened while the country was fighting a rebellion rooted in slavery, with its survival genuinely in doubt. That context is essential to understanding Lincoln’s decisions. Even so, it does not place those decisions beyond scrutiny and reminds us today there is nothing new under the sun.

I can regard Lincoln as a great president and still recoil at some of the powers exercised under his administration. An honest affection for America must leave room for that.

And the rockets’ red glare The bombs bursting in air

Our anthem was born of an actual bombardment. The danger was physical, and the outcome could not yet be known.

We sometimes speak of our own political moment as though we alone have discovered uncertainty. Every alarming development becomes unprecedented. Every election becomes the final opportunity to save the country.

Some warnings deserve our attention. Rights can erode, and institutions can fail. History offers plenty of evidence for the absolute necessity vigilance.

This country has been torn apart by civil war. It has tolerated profound injustice while congratulating itself on liberty. It has denied the protection of its promises to people who had every right to claim them.

And Americans have challenged those failures…often at great personal cost and against a majority quite comfortable with the way things were.

The work has never been easy, and progress has never been secure. The end of slavery did not prevent the injustices that followed. A constitutional promise could exist for generations before people received anything approaching its protection.

But the promise gave people something to demand. It still does.

Gave proof through the night That our flag was still there

I won’t comment on the outcome itself, but I have great hope after an election like this. The system is working. Imperfectly, unevenly, and with people understandably dissatisfied by its results. Yet democracy remains alive. Voters can register disapproval and impose consequences. Political power remains something that must answer to the public.

One election cannot certify the health of an entire republic. It can, however, demonstrate that the mechanisms of accountability still operate. I think we should allow ourselves to recognize that today, across political lines.

I spend much of my life traveling beyond our borders. That has made me more conscious of how much I value the ability to criticize my government openly and expect another opportunity to vote. Neither should be taken for granted.

We have built something very special here. Its failures are real, and so is its capacity for correction.

Repairing what is broken will require patient work long after the election coverage ends. Some damage will take years to undo. Some losses cannot be restored to the people who suffered them.

Still, Americans before us have undertaken that work under circumstances far more desperate than ours. We can honor them by continuing it.

This morning, I feel grateful that the country remains ours to shape. Grateful that disappointment can find expression at a ballot box. And I’m hopeful that we retain enough humility to recognize our mistakes and enough resolve to address them.

The anthem ends with a question. After all this time, it remains a question worth asking ourselves.

O say, does that star-spangled banner yet wave O’er the land of the free and the home of the brave

#6197. United Airlines First Class Steak And Eggs: Great Steak, But Where Were The Eggs?

United Airlines served me excellent cubed steak for breakfast on a recent flight from Chicago to Houston. The problem with its steak and eggs dish? The missing eggs.

For this week’s Meal of the Week, I want to highlight a breakfast that I would happily order again, even though one part of it was very disappointing. On a recent flight from Chicago O’Hare (ORD) to Houston (IAH), I selected the steak and eggs, described on the menu as:

Steak and eggs with home fries and chimichurri sauce

The tray was nicely presented, with sliced steak topped with chimichurri, potatoes, and what I expected would be an egg soufflé.

The steak was excellent for airplane red meat. The chimichurri worked very well with the beef, and this was the highlight of the meal.

Unfortunately, instead of the egg soufflé I expected, I received something much closer to bread pudding…in fact, it was the same bread pudding I had out of Chicago a couple months ago. There may have been egg binding it together, but it had virtually no discernible egg texture or flavor. It was like eating bread.

You can see the bread cubes in the photo. This was not simply a soufflé that turned out a little firmer than expected. Bread dominated the portion that was supposed to provide the eggs in my steak and eggs.

That was disappointing, especially because the steak was so good and because I try to limit my carbs. I hope United can address this with its catering out of Chicago, as I’ve seen other reports of the same problem (this wasn’t a one-off). An actual egg component would make this a much more satisfying breakfast and match the menu…

The accompaniments were better. The chocolate croissant was served warm and was excellent. Between that and the bread pudding, I certainly had enough bread on the tray…

The fruit was ripe, and the Chobani vanilla Greek yogurt was decent. I would prefer a no-sugar-added Greek yogurt, but at least this one provided 10 grams of protein.

The coffee was strong, which was also appreciated. I also requested orange juice, though I must confess that was more to add color to the tray for the photo. I did not drink it.

I would order United’s steak and eggs again. The steak with chimichurri was excellent, and the warm chocolate croissant was great. But United needs to fix the egg issue out of ORD. There is a good breakfast here. It just needs the eggs its name promises.

#6196. Air Serbia Flight To Nowhere: A320 Forced To Return To Belgrade Over Mysterious Security Concern

An Air Serbia flight to Moscow made it as far as Lithuania before turning around and returning to Belgrade over a security concern involving one passenger. Serbian media identified that passenger as the country’s former intelligence chief, who allegedly boarded without completing security screening. He denies wrongdoing.

As flagged by One Mile At A Time, Air Serbia flight JU134 departed Belgrade for Moscow on November 3, 2026, but turned back over southern Lithuania. According to Serbian media, the Airbus A320 left at 6:48 PM and returned shortly before 10:00 PM. Passengers spent more than three hours flying only to end up where they started.

Air Serbia confirmed that airport authorities requested additional security checks concerning one passenger. The airline said it returned in accordance with the instructions it received, but did not publicly identify that passenger.

The passenger in question has since been identified as Aleksandar Vulin, Serbia’s former intelligence chief. It appears that someone helped him board without completing the required screening and that the airport’s corporate security director ordered the return after reviewing surveillance footage.

Vulin insists he completed the required checks, was carrying no prohibited items, and was being targeted for political reasons (his pro-Russian party lost in a snap election last month). He said his trip concerned negotiations over Serbia’s gas arrangement with Russia.

Passengers and their luggage underwent additional screening in Belgrade. The flight eventually continued to Moscow with a replacement crew, arriving about seven hours late.

If the reports are accurate, the obvious question is how someone was allowed to board without completing the required checks. Political prominence should not provide an exemption from an aviation security procedure, though I understand how easy it is to open an employee access door for a VIP).

But Vulin disputes that account, and the airline’s statement establishes only that authorities requested additional screening. That leaves important questions about what happened before departure and what prompted the return. Vulin was allowed to continue on the delayed flight to Moscow.

Belgrade’s Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has requested an investigation into the circumstances, including whether procedures were followed, who authorized the aircraft’s return, and what security assessment supported that decision.

That inquiry is appropriate. If someone bypassed screening, there should be accountability for how it happened. If the checks were properly completed, authorities need to explain why an aircraft full of passengers was brought back.

This is all may be Serbian domestic politics…

An alleged screening lapse involving a former intelligence chief turned a routine Air Serbia flight into a lengthy journey back to its starting point. The aircraft eventually reached Moscow, but the competing accounts of what happened remain unresolved.

I hope the investigation establishes whether someone received preferential treatment or whether there is another explanation for this extraordinary return. Either way, the passengers arrived very late into Moscow.

#6194. American Airlines Dropped Trump’s Name From West Palm Beach Gate Screens Ahead Of Midterm Elections

American Airlines quietly removed the Trump reference from its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The timing will invite speculation, but the simpler destination label is an improvement regardless of what prompted the change, which does not appear politically-motivated to me.

JonNYC reports that American has changed its destination displays from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

That reverses a change introduced after Palm Beach International Airport was renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport earlier this year.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ?

The change is likely not connected to this week’s election and occurred in August as part of a planned transition. The IATA code for the airport is still DJT after the July 9, 2026 change from PBI.

The original change was peculiar because American generally identifies destinations by city, adding airport names when useful to distinguish between airports serving the same destination.

American does not ordinarily add the presidential names associated with airports serving places like Little Rock (Bill Clinton) or Grand Rapids (Gerald Ford). The West Palm Beach label stood out. Then again, as I indicated above, other airports did not change their IATA code.

There is a very practical reason to distinguish New York JFK from New York LaGuardia or Washington Reagan (National) from Washington Dulles. Leading with presidential initials on a flight to West Palm Beach offers less obvious help to passengers.

There was no possibility of similar confusion when flying into West Palm Beach.

Of course people will notice that this reversal surfaced around the midterm elections, but as I mentioned this goes back to August. Even so, it is an irresistible invitation to speculate about corporate America adjusting to a changed political environment, which was becoming clear even over the summer.

But I think it’s safe to say that American’s leadership did not order a “political” retreat, no matter what some MAGA world may be suggesting this morning. This was more likely all part of the transition plan.

I would be equally cautious about declaring that the original wording was personally ordered by executives seeking favor with the administration, though that could well be the choice as well. It was an unusual choice. The reasoning behind it remains a separate question.

Still, American created an unnecessary distraction by departing from a straightforward city label in the first place. Once a company makes a conspicuous change involving a political figure, undoing it will inevitably attract attention too…especially now.

American Airlines has restored the West Palm Beach destination label on its gate monitors, removing the presidential reference it added earlier this year.

The timing will generate political interpretations. Without more information, I would leave those as speculation and it appears wholly unrelated. The practical result is easier to assess: passengers once again see the name of the place they are flying to. That works for me. Now it’s time to move DJT back to PBI…there was certainly no need for that change either, though that ship (plane?) has sailed.

#6193. Delta CEO Calls Heathrow Move ‘Short-Sighted’

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is pushing back against a planned terminal move at London Heathrow, calling the airport’s decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.”

In comments posted Monday on LinkedIn and published by Delta, Bastian objected to Heathrow’s decision to relocate the airline from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4. The move, planned for 2028, would separate Delta from joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which would remain in Terminal 3.

Bastian said the airlines’ shared operation has served millions of passengers for more than a decade, providing connections, premium amenities and access to their combined networks. He argued that splitting the carriers would undermine years of investment and the benefits of operating from the same terminal.

Delta will “pursue all available remedies to correct this decision,” he said, urging Heathrow to reconsider. Bastian did not outline specific legal or regulatory steps.

Virgin Atlantic has also challenged the plan. CEO Corneel Koster said separating the two airlines would complicate journeys, weaken competition and reduce passenger choice. The carrier is considering its options to contest the relocation, Sky News reported.

Heathrow says the changes will help ease congestion and make better use of its terminals. The airport began notifying airlines of the outcome of its terminal occupancy review on Oct. 27.

A Heathrow spokesperson told Sky News that the plan followed consultation with airline customers and would improve the passenger experience, strengthen operational resilience and provide room for growth.

Delta is one of five airlines slated to change terminals. Finnair and Japan Airlines would also move from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4, while LATAM would relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 2. China Southern would move from Terminal 4 to Terminal 5.

Delta consolidated its Heathrow operation in Terminal 3 in September 2016 to operate alongside Virgin Atlantic. In announcing that move, Delta cited easier connections and last-minute flight changes, along with access to Virgin Atlantic’s premium facilities for eligible passengers.

#6192. The Aircraft Set To Replace The Most Beloved Aircraft In The Sky In 2026

As the end of the era of quatjets approaches on the horizon, carriers around the world are still reworking fleet strategies to replace iconic aircraft like Airbus A380. The superjumbo still tops the charts as one of the most popular planes in the sky for its sheer scale as much as the features that a double-decker jetliner makes possible inside the cabin. Yet, with a shuttered assembly line, airlines like Emirates and Qantas must choose from a short list of next-gen twinjets for the successor to Airbus’ flying giant.

In general, there is not a single aircraft taking over the missions currently flown by the A380, and many are still slated to serve for years to come. The first of Qantas' replacement jets is not due until April 2027, and the Boeing 777X that Emirates is counting on at the end of the decade is yet to be certified. Thus, the fleet strategies made public represent a split. Instead of buying a new giant plane, airlines are replacing the A380’s mission rather than seats.

The primary drivers of this transition are advancements in engine technology, enabling large twin-jets to fly just as far as the A380 but with 25% lower fuel burn and substantially reduced maintenance. Boeing's 787 Dreamliner family is one of the smaller successors, seating anywhere from 180 to 430 depending on layout. The Airbus A350-900 and A350-1000 feature advanced carbon-composite fuselages, ultra-efficient engines, and seat between 350 and 450 passengers. Boeing 777X family comes with industry-first folding wingtips and a capacity equal to or greater than the -1000.

Australia’s flag carrier has moved up the formal retirement schedule for its A380 superjumbos. The accelerated timeline has already seen the end of operations from Melbourne Airport (MEL) and dictates that the remaining ten operating A380s will begin exiting the fleet sequentially in March 2028, with the final superjumbo flight projected for the same year. Driven by soaring heavy maintenance costs, worsening fuel price volatility, and recently affirmed delivery certainty for its next-gen planes, Qantas will be one of the industry's first full-scale A380 fleet divestments.

Rather than a simple 1-to-1 aircraft replacement, Qantas is executing two parallel replacement programs under the umbrella of ‘Project Fysh’ and ‘Project Sunrise.’ The combination of the two programs will see the introduction of 24 A350-1000s divided between 12 standard and 12 ultra-long-range 'Sunrise' variants, as well as 12 Dreamliners split between four 787-9s and eight 787-10s.

The downgrade in seat count of roughly 50% per hull will push prices up, but Qantas is betting on passenger demand for the time-savings of nonstop ultra-long-haul routes. Because the A380 is so massive, it can only fly between specialized mega-airports equipped with double-decker gates.

Next-gen twinjets can land anywhere, paving the way for point-to-point travel like Qantas' upcoming Project Sunrise flights. Instead of flying from Sydney to Dubai, waiting for a three-hour layover, and then flying to London, passengers fly completely nonstop, saving up to 4 hours of travel time. To combat the physical toll of ULH flying, Qantas' upcoming A350s will even feature a dedicated, mid-cabin ‘Wellbeing Zone’ for passengers to stretch and enjoy self-serve refreshments.

What will the Australian flag carrier choose?

Emirates is moving in the opposite direction. President Tim Clark told Aviation Week in 2025 that the active A380 fleet would grow from 95 or 96 aircraft to about 110 by the end of 2026, and that redesigned interiors built by the airline itself would reach every cabin within three years. Clark told CNN that Emirates plans to fly the A380 into the early 2040s, which is why it is spending billions on cabins and technology such as Starlink.

Cirium figures cited in CNN reporting show 101 flying and 15 stored, which leaves the airline some distance from the 110 goal by the end of the year. Meanwhile, the Centre for Aviation reported that Emirates reached 100 refurbished aircraft on July 14, made up of 53 'triple sevens' and 47 A380s, under a $5 billion retrofit program, with about 20 more due by the end of December. A further phase covering 60 A380s and 51 777s adds new economy seats, entertainment screens and Starlink connectivity, and the airline plans to install Starlink across all 232 of its in-service aircraft by mid-2027.

The Centre for Aviation also noted that Emirates has begun turning high-density two-class A380s into three-class aircraft with premium economy on the upper deck, with 15 planned by the end of this year. George Dimitroff, Cirium's global head of aircraft valuations, told CNN that carriers with small A380 fleets will retire them as the industry leans toward premium travel, and that the type will eventually be flown by Emirates alone.

CNN reported that the likeliest handoff to an Emirates-only operation falls between the early and middle 2030s. Emirates' long-term answer is the Boeing 777X. As of July, the airline holds orders for 235 777-9s and 35 777-8s, 270 in total, with the first expected in the second quarter of 2027. Boeing expects to complete certification and begin deliveries in 2027.

Even with a plan laid out for succession, the heir shrinks the aircraft. The 777-9 seats around 415 in Qatar's planned two-class layout, according to ch-aviation, against roughly 485 on a Qantas A380 for scale. The first is the delivery of Emirates' first 777-9 in the second quarter of 2027, which will show whether Boeing's 2027 certification target holds.

The Airbus A380 has staged an improbable comeback, serving as the ultimate canvas for aviation luxury.

Next-generation twinjets optimize airline profitability by reducing total seat counts to make room for larger, highly lucrative premium cabins. Instead of packing an aircraft with maximum economy seating, airlines use the advanced aerodynamics and space efficiency of twinjets like the A350-1000 and 777X to create spacious premium environments that generate higher revenue per square foot.

A passenger in economy pays a baseline fare, but a premium passenger pays three to five times more for a ticket while consuming only three to four times the space. By trading raw seat capacity for premium cabins, airlines can generate the same, or higher, flight revenue with far fewer people on board. This reduces the overall weight of passenger baggage and catering supplies, which lowers fuel burn. Qatar serves as the ultimate case study for this premium-heavy twinjet strategy, demonstrating how an airline can completely re-engineer its business model around high-yield real estate rather than raw passenger volume.

Under its fleet modernization campaign, the Doha-based carrier is explicitly using the wide fuselage dimensions of next-generation twinjets to blur the line between business class and first class. Qatar Airways pioneered the industry-wide shift in cabin economics with its Qsuite product. In a standard long-haul configuration, a single Qsuite mini-cabin takes up a massive amount of physical real estate, requiring a seat pitch of over 100 inches (2.5 meters) in a staggered 1-2-1 layout. A single one of these private suites consumes the floor space of roughly four economy seats.

A look at the challenges of operating a fleet of Airbus A380s today, and the future outlook on the type.

Qatar Airways deliberately caps the overall capacity of its flagship aircraft. On its premium-configured A350-1000s, the airline installs a massive block of 46 Qsuites up front. This choice forces the economy cabin down to just 281 seats, a total passenger capacity of 327. For context, some high-density airlines push that exact same airframe past 380 or even 400 seats by slashing the premium cabin.

Unlike its competitors, Qatar treats its eight airworthy A380s with data-driven pragmatism, employing them as a capacity bridge to the next-gen twin jets that are incoming. The airline aggressively shifts its superjumbo missions when twinjet operations become more profitable. Case in point, the airline permanently removed the A380 from its Sydney corridor in favor of the Boeing 777-300ER. Qatar also executed a similar withdrawal on its Singapore route, swapping the quadjet for the smaller A350-900.

The carrier's aircraft assignments fluctuate based on macroeconomic factors, evidenced by the recent grounding of the fleet following airspace constraints and fuel price volatility in the wake of Operation Epic Fury. That hiatus was followed by a swift reactivation to maximize passenger throughput at slot-constrained mega-hubs like London Heathrow and Bangkok. The A380s are ultimately expected to be systematically retired and sent to the scrapyard when Airbus satisfies the remainder of Qatar's A350-1000 order backlog, and Boeing begins deliveries of the delayed 777-9 widebody.

The 777X brings unique cabin architecture, larger windows, and more.

Lufthansa is performing a retrofit campaign for its eight active A380s to keep flying into the late 2030s, in a reversal of the pandemic-era plan to retire the jets early. This strategy shift stems from ongoing delivery delays for the airline's incoming Boeing 777X flagship fleet. To maximize efficiency, Lufthansa consolidated its entire superjumbo fleet at its Munich hub, separating them from the Boeing 747-8 fleet stationed in Frankfurt.

This modernization process is scheduled for completion by mid-2027, and Lufthansa has extended the operational window for these aircraft until the early 2030s. This will completely remove the older, business class cabins and replace them with modern XL seats, transforming the space into a direct aisle access layout.

Meanwhile, Korean Air is navigating a complex fleet strategy that has been significantly influenced by its merger with Asiana Airlines. The carrier originally intended to retire its ten A380s by 2026, but that timeline collapsed due to systemic bottlenecks at both Airbus and Boeing. Following the decommissioning of four older superjumbos earlier this year, Korean had just six remaining A380s, but the absorption of Asiana added six more to the fleet.

This sudden influx created a massive combined fleet of twelve superjumbos, presenting a split logistical burden as the two sub-fleets are equipped with different engine models. Facing a deficit of 40 long-haul widebodies due to assembly line delays, the merged carriers cannot afford to drop capacity. Thus, Korean has officially extended the lifespans of the A380s into the early 2030s, outsourcing heavy maintenance to facilities in the Philippines. The jet will be phased out gradually with the arrival of 20 A350-1000s and follow-on 787-10s, which are finally being delivered.

For anyone looking for a fun weekend getaway, Nashville almost always makes the short list of options. And for good reason, it’s a city packed with character, history, live music and excellent food.

I was lucky enough to grow up in the Nashville area, so the world of the Ryman Auditorium, the Grand Ole Opry and even excellent airport musicians will always feel like home. I recently went back for a short trip, and while I was there, I made sure to hit some of my favorite food spots — and check out some new ones while I was at it.

If you have Nashville on your list, don’t miss these favorite eateries. And for any food-focused trip, a card that earns on dining is worth having, like the Navy Federal Flagship Premier Visa Signature®. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases and 4 points per dollar on travel purchases, a strong combination for a trip like this, and all for just a $95 annual fee.

If you need a great travel and dining card, now is the perfect time to add the Flagship Premier card to your wallet. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 50,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 in the first 90 days from account opening. Offer ends Jan. 3, 2027.

Here’s how to use the card to make your food-focused weekend trip to Nashville even better.

I live on the West Coast now, so my go-to flight is usually a nonstop on Alaska Airlines, but I sometimes opt for another airline. With the Flagship Premier card earning on a wide range of travel purchases, I can compare prices and book whichever flight makes the most sense — no loyalty to one airline or travel portal required.

The Flagship Premier card can also help you save on your flight to Nashville with its $100 annual airline credit, which offsets the cost and gives you more flexibility when booking.

And when you’re at the airport, you’ll be thankful for Flagship Premier’s statement credit of up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck® to help you zip through security.

When it was time to choose my hotel, I knew I wanted to stay at The Thompson Nashville. It’s in the Gulch, making it within walking distance of many of my favorite dining and shopping spots.

Regardless of which hotel you choose, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar when you book on your Flagship Premier card. That means you’re free to pick whichever hotel you want, without worrying about staying within a single brand or portal to earn bonus points.

Flagship Premier tip: Earn 4 points per dollar on a wide range of travel spending — not just hotels and airfare. Ground transportation counts too, whether you’re in a rental car, on public transport or using rideshare services.

Nashville has quite the dining scene, and the list of standout spots seems to grow every day. To make sure I fit in as much as possible, I turned one day into my own food crawl, with a combination of old favorites and a few newer ones.

For a food-focused trip like this, the Flagship Premier card earns where it matters most. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, so you’ll earn bonus points wherever your taste buds take you.

Since moving away from Nashville, I’ve come to realize that few places make a better chicken biscuit than Biscuit Love. Biscuit Love is an iconic Nashville staple, but it was new to me, so I knew it would make the list when I saw it around the corner from my hotel.

It absolutely lived up to the hype. From the fun southern and country-music themed decor to the food worth writing home about, Biscuit Love has landed a permanent spot on my list of favorite Nashville eateries.

The menu spans southern staples like biscuits and gravy and shrimp and grits, as well as lighter options like oatmeal and omelets. I knew I wanted to try their Princess biscuit, a buttermilk biscuit topped with fried Nashville “Hot Chicken” and homemade pickles. I also added the summer special Sunshine latte to my order — an iced latte with tangerine, cinnamon and vanilla and topped with housemade salted honey cold foam. And, of course, a side of bacon.

The entire meal was excellent. The chicken was perfectly fried, the biscuit light and fluffy and the pickles delightfully tangy. And the sunshine latte, I discovered, is a favorite for a reason. It was the perfect morning treat to start the day.

After such a big breakfast, I had to wait a while before I could even think about lunch. But when the time finally came, I knew I was headed to Ladybird Taco for my favorite tacos in Nashville.

A location a few blocks from my hotel made it an easy walk. Wanting to pace myself a bit this time, I opted for just one brisket taco and a side of chips and queso.

While I haven’t been to all the taco joints Nashville has to offer, the Austin-inspired menu at Ladybird has been my favorite for years, and I was thrilled to be back for a taste. If you happen to be there for breakfast, be sure to check out their breakfast tacos and Crema coffee — I’m always surprised at how well their coffee and queso go together.

After lunch, I was ready for an afternoon pick-me-up. Living on the West Coast has raised my coffee standards pretty high, but Barista Parlor never disappoints.

I popped in for an iced whiskey-caramel latte as a post-lunch treat to keep me going through the rest of my day in Nashville.

While Jeni’s isn’t Nashville-exclusive, it's only available in select cities and is a spot I make sure to visit every time I’m in town for its creative, seasonal flavors. I originally went in for my favorite — Brambleberry Crisp — but was tempted by the new fall lineup on the menu, which included Pumpkin with Brown Sugar Blondies.

I took a risk and ordered a half scoop of each and was delighted to discover that they pair beautifully. (Just learn from my mistakes and be sure to eat your ice cream quickly if you happen to be there during a heat wave.)

To close out my food crawl day, I headed to The Optimist, a seafood restaurant from chef and restaurateur Ford Fry that was new to me. I love every restaurant of his I’ve been to, and so many of my friends had raved about this one that I wanted to see if it lived up to the hype.

One of my good friends joined me, and we set out to try some of the hottest dishes.

While we surveyed the menu, our server brought rolls for us to enjoy. They were soft and fluffy — and the perfect thing to snack on while deciding.

Per our server’s recommendations, we landed on the Alabama Blue Crab dip and a half dozen oysters, which were both an excellent start to the meal (and complement to our Champagne).

We then moved to the spicy kale salad, which was aptly named. While delicious, it was too spicy for either of us to enjoy more than a few bites.

For our main dish, we ordered the Crumbed Halibut (with brown butter, parsley and charred lemon) and a side of “Proper ‘Chips’” (with malt vinegar aioli). The Halibut was crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, and the brown butter made it sing. The fries were equally well-executed, and the aioli took them to the next level.

The verdict: The Optimist lives up to the hype. I’ll definitely prioritize going back the next time I’m in town.

Flagship Premier Tip: Earn 3 points per dollar on all dining, making this a great card to have handy when exploring local cuisines — from a nearby coffee stop to the splashiest seafood dinner in town.

A card that earns on both travel and dining makes a trip like this Nashville weekend a breeze, and that’s exactly what the Flagship Premier card does.

With the card, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar on your travel purchases — from hotels and flights to transportation while you’re there, without having to deal with booking through a travel portal.

The $100 annual airline credit and up to $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit (once every four years) take the edge off both the cost of flying and the airport experience.

No one likes to juggle multiple cards while traveling, and the Flagship Premier card keeps things simple. With 4 points per dollar on travel and 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, one card covers the two categories that matter most on a trip like this.

Plus, there are no limits on the rewards you can earn (other than your stomach at the end of your food crawl).

If you haven’t been to Nashville lately, be sure to add it to your list — along with these excellent food spots while you’re there.

And wherever your next trip takes you, the Navy Federal Flagship Premier card is worth bringing along, especially for trips centered on food and travel. Between the travel credits and elevated earning rates, it’s the perfect card for any trip.

Many of us here at TPG love to leverage our favorite credit cards to enhance our travels. From trying out the newest lie-flat product to relaxing in an airport lounge, these products can go a long way in unlocking memorable experiences.

But for many Americans, credit cards represent a tangible way to support their household’s bottom lines — especially in the face of rising costs and the unexpected hurdles that life can throw in their way.

Recently, TPG founder Brian Kelly sat down with three everyday families to help them maximize their wallets — and the conversations demonstrated the true power of making rewards work for you.

Here are some real-world stories that show just what credit cards can unlock for you.

One of the most under-the-radar benefits of credit cards is how they can build financial literacy and set your children up for success in the real world. No, this isn’t about giving teens or young adults unfettered access to a big credit limit. Instead, it’s the power of adding them as an authorized user to an existing credit card.

That’s exactly what we recommended to Seungah Jeong for her 14-year-old daughter, Emi. She just started high school and is starting to spend her own money. By becoming an authorized user on her mom’s card, she can start building up a credit history for when she’s ready to go off on her own.

Even better? Some cards allow you to set individual spending limits for your authorized users, so your kids can learn about budgeting in a controlled environment.

Everyone has different needs when it comes to credit cards, and making the most of your everyday spending requires two important items. Put simply, you need to know:

If you never eat out, a credit card with a bonus on dining purchases won’t do you any good. If you’re a frequent international traveler, you don’t want to swipe a card and incur foreign transaction fees. And if you focus on earning rewards with a single travel provider, you may be missing out on more flexible rewards.

We saw this play out with all the families we met.

Take the Goralczenkos. Parents Andrew and Tracy have quadruplets who are heading off to college, and both were laid off two years ago when the company they worked for suddenly went out of business. They had been collecting rewards on their favorite theme park credit card for years, but in their current situation, that’s not doing much for them.

Instead, they can shift their focus to cash-back rewards, picking up a new card that awards them 3% back on some of their biggest purchases — like gas and groceries.

It was a similar story with Seungah, whose 18-year-old son Oliver was heading off to Greece for college. Our recommendation was to get a new travel rewards card, specifically one that offers flexible rewards and waives foreign transaction fees. That means Oliver won’t be hit with up to 3% in fees every time he swipes the card in Europe.

Finally, there was Renee Lewis-Mance. She and her husband, Chris, are retired, but she’s very into the points game, focusing primarily on a single airline and a single hotel loyalty program. While these programs can be valuable, Renee is missing out on one of the biggest benefits of being retired: flexibility.

That’s why we recommended adding a new transferable rewards card to her wallet. Earning points or miles in one of these programs provides an array of redemption options when she’s planning a trip. She’s not locked into a single airline or hotel chain, which could limit her options.

Beyond earning with your everyday spending, most popular cards offer one-time bonuses for new applicants (subject to minimum spending requirements). This allows you to take home a big haul of points, miles or cash-back rewards up front while picking up a new card that better fits your spending habits.

This was particularly appealing for the Goralczenkos. The card we recommended came with a $100 welcome bonus, plus 3% back on some major everyday spending categories. That won’t get them a flight to Europe, but in their current situation, cash back is much more appealing.

Chris Mance found himself in a similar boat. He was able to grab a one-time, $200 cash-back bonus on a new card that was also a better fit for where he spends his money each month.

But even more importantly, this new card will help him address the final strategy ...

Here at TPG, we like to joke that there’s no “point” to using cash for your everyday purchases — but there’s certainly risk. Carrying around a bunch of cash leaves you vulnerable to theft, and even if you opt to swipe a debit card, you’re generally earning no rewards on those purchases.

That’s the exact situation that Chris Mance found himself in. While his wife (Renee) loves playing the points game, Chris usually pays cash or uses a debit card for his regular trips to Home Depot and the grocery store. However, by shifting those purchases to a cash-back credit card, he can unlock some significant rewards.

Based on our estimates, his grocery purchases alone could turn into $250 in cash back every year.

In addition, since Chris was spending a good chunk of money on home improvement purchases — tools, gardening supplies, plants — we recommended a card that will allow him to customize his rewards by picking a category to earn 6% back in the first year. That alone should net him around $300 in rewards.

The best part? This card had no annual fee.

In both cases, Chris isn’t spending more money than he already planned to spend. He’s just switching to a payment method that rewards him for his existing spending habits.

The world of credit cards features an array of products to meet the needs of virtually every American. Sure, there are options geared toward luxury travelers with a variety of benefits to help elevate their next trip. But many others can be a great fit for everyday pursuits, like shopping at the grocery store or building your child's credit history.

Ordinary families can easily take advantage of cash-back rewards to support their household bottom lines, and can boost their earnings by carefully analyzing their spending habits to select the best card(s) for their wallets.

And as long as you’re responsibly managing your credit and spending within your means, the only way to lose is by not participating at all.

#6189. British Airways Has Axed 8 Major A380 Routes From Heathrow: See Full List Now

British Airways is one of ten scheduled users of the Airbus A380. Mainly due to airframes being taken out of service to be retrofitted with just 421 seats, Cirium Diio shows that the carrier now only has the sixth-highest number of double-decker flights. Last November, it was second.

Ch-aviation shows that the oneworld member has 12 double-decker quadjets, the last of which was delivered in June 2016. While they currently have 469 seats, they're being retrofitted with new seats, with a higher premium offering. 88 economy seats are being removed, enabling 13 more business suites and 29 more premium economy seats. The equipment is, of course, used in high-volume and high-yielding markets.

The UK flag carrier's first commercial flight on the superjumbo took place in August 2013. The equipment was initially deployed to Frankfurt for crew training and familiarization. Many airlines have deployed their superjumbos on very short routes for this purpose. For example, Air France did so to London Heathrow Airport (LHR), while Singapore Airlines flew it to Kuala Lumpur. BA used the A380 to Frankfurt and Madrid in 2021 for the same reason, which was ahead of the type's reentry into service due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Comparing BA's schedule between August 2013 and October 2026 with what's planned from November 2026 through 2027 shows that the following eight routes no longer see the huge equipment. Singapore would also have featured, but BA reintroduced superjumbo service to Lion City two months ago: more on that later.

Notice Dubai. Ordinarily, BA would fly the 469-seater to the United Arab Emirates' massively popular destination during the winter, when the temperature is hot but not extraordinarily so. This is, therefore, the main tourist season. However, due to the ongoing war in Iran, the equipment is no longer deployed there. While no flights are currently scheduled through next October, the type may return next winter. BA only just returned to Dubai at the start of November 2026, with the Boeing 787-10 operating daily.

On September 6, BA11 left the UK's busiest airport for Singapore Changi Airport (SIN), having last been deployed to Lion City in early 2025. It is unclear if the return to SIN was influenced by the unease of passengers in connecting at Gulf hubs, although this seems to be dissipating. Whether coincidentally or not, other A380 operators have removed the type from SIN recently. Qatar Airways did so in March 2026, followed by Etihad three months later.

The return of BA's A380s to SIN is notable in various ways. First, it became the airline's sole remaining superjumbo destination in Asia, with only Hong Kong, Doha, and Dubai previously served. Second, LHR-SIN has three double-decker operators for the first time in 16 months, with BA joining Qantas and Singapore Airlines. It is now the only airport pair with three A380 operators.

Third, and just as significantly, if Emirates (the granddaddy of A380 operators) is excluded, LHR-SIN now has more superjumbo flights than any other airport pair, with four flights each day. SIN-Sydney comes close, but has three daily flights at times.

Five ended earlier this year, while one will do so later this month. Find out more here!

Like other Northern Hemisphere airlines, BA switched to winter schedules on Sunday, October 25, 2026, based on IATA slot seasons. It'll maintain winter operations through Saturday, March 27, 2027. In this period, and primarily reflecting aircraft undergoing reconfiguration, BA will only fly the double-decker on four routes from LHR: to Johannesburg (two daily), Miami (daily), San Francisco (daily), and SIN (daily).

Compared to last winter, superjumbo services have been reduced by 27%, which is why BA has temporarily fallen from being the second-largest operator by flights to sixth. At the time, six routes existed: LHR to Dubai (daily), Johannesburg (daily), Los Angeles (daily), Miami (two daily), San Francisco (daily), and Washington Dulles (daily through early November 2025). The equipment will return to Los Angeles in 2027, but it is unclear if Dubai will see it again.

#6188. Delta Plans Another Austin Route

Delta is expanding its Austin, Texas, network with a new daily route set to launch next spring.

The carrier will begin flights between Austin and Northwest Arkansas National Airport, which serves Fayetteville and the surrounding region, on March 7, 2027. SkyWest will operate the route under the Delta Connection brand using an Embraer E175.

Service from Northwest Arkansas to Austin begins March 8. Tickets are now on sale.

Flights will depart Austin at 8:59 p.m. and arrive in Northwest Arkansas at 10:49 p.m. The return flight will leave at 6 a.m. and arrive in Austin at 7:50 a.m. All times are local.

“Connecting Central Texas and Northwest Arkansas with new nonstop service brings two dynamic, growing regions closer together while giving our customers even more choice and convenience,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement.

Guitart described the addition as another example of the airline’s investment in Austin.

Delta has been building its Austin operation, with plans to offer more than 70 peak-day departures to approximately 30 destinations by summer 2027. That expansion includes new service to Paris and San Diego, a second daily flight to San Jose, California, and year-round service to Cancun, Mexico.

#6187. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6185. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6184. New Cathay Pacific “Halo Suites” First Class For Boeing 777-9s

In late 2024, Cathay Pacific unveiled its new Aria Suites business class, which is progressively being introduced on the carrier’s Boeing 777-300ER fleet. While we know Cathay Pacific is introducing a new first class product, it’ll take some time before we see that in service.

In light of everything going on — the introduction of Cathay Pacific’s new business class, the delays to the Boeing 777X, the products being introduced by competitors, etc. — I’d like to cover the latest when it comes to Cathay Pacific’s new first class.

We’ve known for years that Cathay Pacific plans to introduce new first and business class products on its Boeing 777-9s. The airline has 35 of these aircraft on order, and they’re expected to become the carrier’s flagship aircraft.

Note that not all Cathay Pacific 777-9s are expected to get first class. The expectation is that somewhere around 20 of them will feature the cabin, while the remaining will feature business class, premium economy, and economy.

Initially the aircraft was supposed to enter service as of 2020, though due to delays stemming from a variety of reasons, the plane is now slated to be delivered in 2027 at the earliest.

Many airlines were planning on introducing new “flagship” products on their 777-9s, though the seven year delay has obviously not been ideal for that, and has caused many airlines to fall behind with their premium products. I would imagine that Cathay Pacific was planning on debuting its new business class on 777-9s, but now decided to install it on 777-300ERs.

While Cathay Pacific has moved forward with introducing its new business class, the airline only plans to introduce a new first class as of 2027, on Boeing 777-9s. Understandably, one major concern here is when 777-9s will actually enter service for Cathay Pacific.

At this point, the aircraft will enter commercial service in the second half of 2027 at the absolute earliest, and Cathay Pacific isn’t even the launch customer. So it could very well be 2028 before we see the first Cathay Pacific 777-9.

In 2023, Cathay Pacific applied for a trademark for “The Aria Suites,” which is the carrier’s new business class. The airline also applied for a trademark for “The Halo Suites,” and this is specifically intended to cover “luxury and first class air transportation services.”

For what it’s worth, the two patents were filed just a few weeks apart. While we can’t say anything with certainty, I’d be willing to bet with that this will in fact be the name of Cathay Pacific’s new first class product.

We know that Cathay Pacific has been working on developing its new first class product for many years (it was supposed to be ready in 2020, based on the initial Boeing 777-9 delivery timeline). We also know that Cathay Pacific is planning something truly spectacular. However, there hasn’t been any official indication as to what we can expect (though rumor has it that we could get a “tease” in the coming months).

Back in 2019, Cathay Pacific applied for a patent for a new first class product, and… wow! Let me emphasize that I can’t guarantee this will be Cathay Pacific’s new first class, though I think it’s very possible. I’d highly recommend reading the whole application, as it actually contains a couple of different concepts.

Below is the diagram that’s displayed, and if I’m understanding this correctly, the plan is that figures five through eight reflect what Cathay Pacific is hoping to offer.

This appears to be based on Paperclip Design’s Peacock Suites concept. The below pictures should give you a sense of just how spectacular this product might be (though I’d expect Cathay Pacific to have a customized version of this, so don’t expect it to be exactly like this).

This product looks absolutely wild, and I’m in disbelief that we could see anything like this introduced. It almost looks more like The Etihad Residence than a standard first class product. Heck, it almost looks more like what you’d expect on a private jet.

A couple of years back, former Cathay Pacific Chairman Patrick Healy has called the new product “mindblowing,” and “a really, really special product and very impressive.”

This would likely blow away the best first class products in the world, like Air France’s 777 first class, Emirates’ 777 first class, and Japan Airlines’ A350 first class. In terms of other first class products on the horizon, we know that Singapore Airlines will be unveiling a new first class shortly, and Qatar Airways is working on a new first class, but it’s not a sure bet yet.

Due to ongoing delivery delays with the Boeing 777-9, the carrier’s plan to transition its fleet is proving to be anything but straightforward.

Cathay Pacific is currently retrofitting its 777-300ER fleet with the new Aria Suites business class. As the airline retrofits its 777-300ERs, it’s also removing first class from those planes (assuming they have them). We’re seeing a combination of three-cabin aircraft reconfigured (with business class, premium economy, and economy), along with some four-cabin aircraft (with first class).

At this point, Cathay Pacific has just six planes remaining with first class. In the past, the airline has acknowledged that it may hold off on reconfiguring some jets, so that it can maintain even a small fleet with first class seats, for markets where it’s really needed. However, with the extent of the delays, one wonders if Cathay Pacific really wants to put the fleet retrofit project on hold, just to preserve a few dozen first class seats.

Cathay Pacific’s first class is an excellent, spacious product. While this isn’t the world’s most private first class, it is one of my favorites. On top of that, the soft product is very good.

Cathay Pacific plans to introduce a new first class product, though only on the 777-9, and not on the 777-300ER. You can expect this product to be introduced as of late 2027 at the earliest, assuming the Boeing 777X actually gets certified (that’s a big “if”).

Based on some filings, it would appear that Cathay Pacific will name its new first class “The Halo Suites,” and some diagrams suggest that this will be an unbelievably good product. I can’t wait to learn more. Rumor has it that we could get our first official tease of this product in the coming months, though who knows, that may be delayed yet again.

What do you make of what we know about Cathay Pacific’s new first class?
