#6159. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6157. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

#6155. The Unproven Economics of the Weekend Cruise

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Cruise lines are moving some of their biggest ships onto shorter trips. Grok

Cruise lines are putting some of their biggest ships on shorter trips, but the financial evidence that those voyages generate better returns remains thin.

Cruise lines are moving some of their biggest ships onto three- and four-night trips, betting that shorter vacations will bring customers back more often. But more passengers are not the same as more profit. Norwegian shortened its average cruise this year, carried 24% more guests, and earned less revenue and gross margin per passenger-day. That does not prove short cruises are bad business, but it does mean the weekend math needs more scrutiny.

For decades, the industry sold seven-night vacations. As ships grew larger and added water parks, more restaurants, and bigger shows, short sailings went to older, smaller ships that sold for less.

Disney was already doing this with the Wish in 2022, and Virgin Voyages launched its first ship on four- and five-night Caribbean itineraries in 2021.

Royal Caribbean took the strategy to megaship scale in 2024 when it put Utopia of the Seas, a new Oasis-class ship, straight into t

Cruise lines are putting their newest and largest ships on three- and four-night itineraries, a break from the seven-night template the industry built its economics around. Royal Caribbean started it at megaship scale with Utopia of the Seas from Port Canaveral in 2024, and Carnival will follow with Mardi Gras on four- and five-day Bahamas sailings from the same port in May 2027. The logic is frequency: a ship running alternating short trips serves two sets of guests a week instead of one, doubling embarkations and the chance to sell drink packages, specialty dining, and excursions. Royal Caribbean Group CEO Jason Liberty said on the October 27 earnings call that half of the group's guests are millennials or younger, that they spend about as much on a short trip as on a seven-night cruise, and that onboard spending has beaten expectations. The filings are harder to read. Royal Caribbean's revenue per passenger-day rose only to about $320 from $315 in the first nine months of 2026, with ticket revenue per passenger-day flat, and its average voyage barely shortened, from 6.2 days to 6.1. Norwegian, which has cut its average cruise from about 8.6 days to 7.5, carried 24% more passengers but saw revenue per passenger-day fall from $401 to $385 and gross margin per passenger-day drop nearly 11%. Neither company reports results by cruise length, so the weekend model's profitability cannot be verified from public disclosures.

#6154. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

#6153. Clear expands e-gates to 53 airports, plans nearly full rollout by end of year

The next time you use Clear to get through airport security, it might be faster than you've come to expect.

Over the course of this year, Clear has been expanding its new "e-gates" to dozens of airports across the country.

It's a more streamlined setup that allows passengers to fly through without stopping at one of its famous blue kiosks.

As of this week, Clear had deployed its new automated gates to 53 airports across the country.

By the end of the year, the tech is expected to be in place at nearly all the airports where the company offers its flagship Clear Plus service.

That's certainly good news for travelers looking to speed through Transportation Security Administration checkpoints — especially as the busy holiday travel rush looms.

In the past, travelers hoping to use Clear at TSA would walk up to the checkpoint, then peel off to get their identity verified with a quick photo. Then, a Clear staffer would escort them to the front of the TSA line.

While it's obviously a shortcut, the service hasn't been without pain points.

Sometimes, flyers would arrive to find no open kiosks, or have to wait for Clear staffers to be free to assist them.

The new e-gate setup is intended to improve the flow of passengers.

I've used the Clear e-gates at a handful of airports this year, and am typically able to walk through pretty seamlessly — often pausing for just a few seconds to get my photo taken before the gates open.

The company touts identity verification in five seconds or less under the new design (but do let us know in the comments what your experience was like).

As of this week, Clear had installed e-gates at nearly 80% of the airports it serves — and noted the "vast majority" of its network would have the e-gates by the end of this year.

At those hubs, the company said 96% passengers were getting through in five minutes or less.

These improvements should make the service an even better shortcut at more airports.

Clear is a paid service that lets passengers effectively skip the TSA line and jump right to carry-on baggage screening. It's typically maximized in tandem with TSA PreCheck access.

Clear's flagship airport security service (known as Clear Plus) now costs $219 for an annual membership.

But some travel cards will offset the cost. For instance, I get a statement credit of up to $219 each year for my Clear+ membership fee by carrying the American Express Platinum Card®, which has an annual fee of $895 (see rates and fees). Enrollment required; subject to auto-renewal.

Plus, three major U.S. airlines partner with Clear to offer special pricing: Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

TPG Tip: If you want to try Clear and sign up using TPG's special offer, you can save $40 on the first year's membership.

Even as Clear expands its e-gates at TSA checkpoints, the program has also gotten some friendly competition from the TSA's newest security shortcut called TSA PreCheck Touchless ID.

That service, which allows members to pass through security without pulling out their ID or boarding pass, is now available at dozens of airports across the country. TSA Touchless has no extra cost for PreCheck (and Global Entry) members, though you have to opt in via your airline profile.

#6152. China Eastern’s Ex-Chairman Gets 14 Years For $10 Million In Bribes—He Didn’t Follow Xi Jinping’s Instructions

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison in a bribery case involving more than $10 million. The court says Liu Shaoyong sold favors over a period stretching from 2002 through 2023, using positions at both China Eastern and China Southern. He’d left China Eastern in 2022 with a glowing sendoff from the board. Three years later, the Communist Party announced it was investigating him. Corruption can be real, many state bureaucrats are at least a little corrupt Prosecuting often serves a political purpose. A conviction tells us what (who) the government decided to punish. So what’s always interesting in these cases is why this one, and why now. The Shenyang Intermediate People’s Court handed down its verdict on November 3. It found that Liu took more than 67.5 million yuan in bribes (US$10.1 million) in exchange for help with business operations, project contracts, and airline route management. He was also fined 4 million yuan (US$600,000) and disgorgement of his criminal proceeds. Liu admitted guilt at his July 24 trial. The court says it gave him a lighter sentence because he confessed and disclosed bribery facts investigators hadn’t yet uncovered. The party’s earlier disciplinary findings accused him of taking money for hiring favors, improperly holding shares in unlisted companies, helping relatives’ businesses including private equity funds, and accepting payments connected with aircraft leasing and flight management. There were also allegations about gifts, banquets, golf outings, resisting the investigation, and superstitious activities. A former pilot and deputy head of the country’s aviation regulator, Liu went on to lead China Southern before returning to China Eastern in 2008. He was credited with helping turn around both airlines. At China Eastern, his tenure included the Shanghai Airlines merger, entry into SkyTeam, and bringing private investors into parts of the business. The Party Was Already Looking At China Eastern I’ve written about this before with the detention of HNA’s leaders and the government’s takeover of Anbang Insurance. With Liu, there’s a more concrete place to start than guessing which faction he offended. A central party inspection team examined China Eastern from October through December 2023. A February 2025 report covered corruption leads and tightening controls over procurement. Liu was expelled from the party in January 2026. The report puts following Xi Jinping’s instructions, supporting Chinese aircraft, operating at Beijing Daxing, and strengthening party supervision alongside its discussion of corruption. So this was as much about carrying out the party’s priorities as about how he conducted business. The inspection records don’t tell us what finally triggered Liu’s prosecution. They do show specific problems during his tenure, and where running the airline could run into the party’s priorities: Party supervision and insider dealings. In 2015, inspectors reported executives setting up related companies in the same business, extensive use of cargo intermediaries, duplicative rewards for ticket agents, and large numbers of free or discounted tickets. Liu jointly headed the cleanup yet a 2019 inspection again flagged corruption and incomplete fixes. Bringing in private investors while maintaining party control. Liu’s 2017 restructuring of Eastern Air Logistics left China Eastern’s group with 45% ownership, outside investors with 45%, and employees with 10%. A 2020 report flagged shortcomings in integrating party leadership into companies with outside shareholders. It seems like Liu’s efforts at privatization may have provided insufficient Party control. Developing Beijing Daxing even when the airline had commercial reasons to prefer Capital airport. Reporting in 2019 described China Eastern resisting a wholesale move, with concerns about losing business travelers on routes like Beijing–Shanghai. Liu nevertheless publicly outlined plans for around 200 aircraft at Daxing. The government called for more capacity, a better route network, and faster construction of facilities supporting maintenance. By late 2024, party discipline officials were monitoring aircraft deployment and passenger numbers there. Liu resisted building up the Party’s showcase airport. Making Chinese aircraft succeed commercially. Liu was there when China Eastern signed its first firm order for five C919s in March 2021. The airline had also established a subsidiary to operate Chinese regional jets. The C919 only received its type certificate in September 2022, after he left. So Liu didn’t refuse Chinese planes. But the government called for broader route coverage, stronger marketing, and better operating support. They bought the planes but didn’t make the aircraft program work (and they can’t really blame the aircraft, so blame the airlines). Following Xi’s safety instructions. The report published in March 2020 described units giving insufficient attention to important safety and operating issues, failing to escalate major safety matters, and failing to act effectively on identified problems. It called for stronger safety oversight, clearer accountability, and changes involving flight operations, maintenance, and operational control. China Eastern had a crash after the report where the party said Liu’s airline needed to improve. China Eastern flight 5735 crashed in March 2022 and killed 132 people. Liu left the group’s top job four months later. In June 2025, a scholar suggested the crash helped trigger scrutiny of him. Prosecuting Liu enforces discipline over top leadership running Chinese state airlines. I don’t know which patron, rival, or specific transaction made Liu vulnerable. China Eastern’s August 2022 resignation filing said Liu had “faithfully and diligently performed his duties” and thanked him for his “outstanding contributions.” The court now says his bribery stretched through 2023—beyond that farewell. (HT: One Mile at a Time) Topics on this pageChina Eastern AirlinesChinese Communist PartyCommunist partyLiu ShaoyongXi JinpingBeijingBeijing Daxing International AirportChinaChina Southern AirlinesShanghaiShanghai AirlinesSkyTeam+7 more More From View from the Wing

The Shenyang Intermediate People’s Court handed down its verdict on November 3. It found that Liu took more than 67.5 million yuan in bribes (US$10.1 million) in exchange for help with business operations, project contracts, and airline route management. He was also fined 4 million yuan (US$600,000) and disgorgement of his criminal proceeds.

Liu admitted guilt at his July 24 trial. The court says it gave him a lighter sentence because he confessed and disclosed bribery facts investigators hadn’t yet uncovered.

The party’s earlier disciplinary findings accused him of taking money for hiring favors, improperly holding shares in unlisted companies, helping relatives’ businesses including private equity funds, and accepting payments connected with aircraft leasing and flight management. There were also allegations about gifts, banquets, golf outings, resisting the investigation, and superstitious activities.

A former pilot and deputy head of the country’s aviation regulator, Liu went on to lead China Southern before returning to China Eastern in 2008. He was credited with helping turn around both airlines. At China Eastern, his tenure included the Shanghai Airlines merger, entry into SkyTeam, and bringing private investors into parts of the business.

#6151. Former China Eastern Chairman Jailed In $10+ Million Bribery Scandal

The former chairman of China Eastern Airlines has been sentenced to 14 years in jail, as he accepted more than $10 million in bribes in his official role. Yowzers!

A court in China’s Liaoning Province has sentenced former China Eastern chairman Liu Shaoyong to prison. The court ruled that he accepted over $10 million in bribes in his official capacity as chairman of one of China’s largest airlines.

The court found that between 2002 and 2023, Liu abused his position at the airline to provide assistance to companies and individuals in business operations, project contracts, and flight route management. Liu has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and has been ordered to pay a fine of $600K, plus his illicit gains and related proceeds have to be recovered.

While the court ruled that his conduct constituted bribery “in an exceedingly large amount,” the sentence he got was actually lighter than it could’ve been, due to mitigating circumstances. These include his confession, voluntary disclosure of previously unknown offenses, and expression of remorse and cooperation in recovering illicit gains.

Make of this what you will, but it’s interesting to note that this is all part of China’s “anti-corruption campaign,” targeting officials at various levels, including executives of state-owned enterprises.

In June 2025, Liu had been placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision, for violations of party discipline and state laws. In January 2026, he was expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), after investigators found that he had abused his authority for personal gain, and he was formally charged in May 2026.

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, after he admitted to taking over $10 million in bribes in his official role. This came as part of a larger crackdown by the government, which also saw the executive expelled from the Communist Party of China.

Over the years we’ve seen a decent number of airline executives charged with corruption — after all, they control a lot of spending, and in some cases, might get influenced for the wrong reasons.

What do you make of this punishment for China Eastern’s former chairman?

Choice Hotels paid Barcelona-based Sercotel $24.3 million in September to exit an acquisition agreement, a person familiar with the transaction told Skift. Choice disclosed the payout in its latest quarterly filing without naming the company, noting it terminated the buy-out agreement on September 16. On the earnings call, CEO Dominic Dragisich said what began as an option to buy full ownership "eventually migrated to an obligation," and that Choice had expected the business to grow through franchise and management fees. Instead, growth increasingly came from leasing hotels. Dragisich described the leases as healthy but said the added lease exposure conflicted with Choice's asset-light strategy. The two companies have partnered on distribution since 2018, and Sercotel generated €170 million in revenue in 2025. The exit fee lands alongside Choice's push to recycle capital tied up in real estate: the company recently sold two hotels for about $34 million in estimated net cash proceeds while keeping their franchise contracts.

On the first Wednesday of each month, Atmos Rewards unveils new Members Day offers, including new Global Getaways destinations. Here's a look at the best November Members Day offers.

Atmos Rewards just launched its November Global Getaways offers. Each destination has its own eligible travel dates, but you must book by Nov. 7.

*Blackout dates to Hawaii are Dec. 17 to Dec. 30, 2026, and Feb. 12 through Feb. 15, 2027, and from Hawaii are Dec. 27, 2026, to Jan. 4, 2027, and Feb. 19 to Feb. 21, 2027.

One example of a route covered by this month's promotion is the following itinerary from Seattle to Venice. It costs just 25,000 points and $48 in taxes and fees. While writing this story, we saw 25,000-point award options for this route on many dates.

If you are an Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card holder, the taxes and fees on this award are only $27.60.

Prefer a trip to Singapore? We found awards from Los Angeles to Singapore on many dates for 30,000 points and $49 in taxes and fees (or $29 if you are an Alaska Summit cardholder).

Meanwhile, you can fly from Seattle to Honolulu on many dates for 11,500 points and $6 in taxes and fees.

You'll want to book quickly, though, as availability at the lowest rates will likely decrease as other members book. The Atmos Rewards cobranded credit cards are also a good way to accumulate points. You can earn points on purchases with these cards, but their welcome offers are also a way to quickly boost your account balance.

And through Nov. 7, you can buy up to 250,000 Atmos Rewards points with a bonus of up to 110%. The 110% bonus kicks in when you buy 30,000 points or more. So, you could buy 30,000 points and get 33,000 bonus points for $1,128.75 (a purchase rate of 1.79 cents per point).

Global Getaways are an excellent opportunity for travelers who want to book travel to the highlighted destinations, can book their flights within a few days and can travel during the specified time period. And if you are striving for Atmos Rewards status, keep in mind that you'll earn status points on Atmos Rewards award tickets.

#6146. American Airlines Says AAdvantage Is Its Edge—These 10 Changes Would Make That True

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom calls AAdvantage one of the airline’s strongest competitive advantages. I agree. I still find more value in American’s program than in most of its competitors. Alaska can be better for single-partner awards, including domestic American Airlines flights. American itself can offer terrific deals on its own flights, alongside some truly terrible ones. One of AAdvantage’s best features is that the partner award chart hasn’t been devalued since 2016. But a good price for an award you can’t book doesn’t get you very far. American improved its Million Miler program in 2025, and has more changes coming there. But that’s really the only real improvement I can think of in the past few years. In the meantime, it eliminated fixed-price mileage upgrades and took seat selection and upgrade benefits away from elites buying Basic Economy. Some of my major complaints about the program: American offers paid upgrades to anyone on the flight while elite members wait and usually do not get upgraded. Systemwide upgrades are nearly impossible to use. Upgrades were once the major benefit of status but can no longer meaningfully be factored, of course dependent on route and dates of travel. When you aren’t upgraded, at least elites can confirm extra legroom seats – but American has far too few of those. And when you exclude exit row seats (not eligible with young children), I often have to pick my flights carefully because there just aren’t extra legroom seats available. American says they’re adding more – but won’t start until 2028. When they first introduced Main Cabin Extra they did the whole fleet in a matter of months! Scarce partner business class awards. British Airways guarantees award space for those redeeming Avios (whether their own, Finnair’s, Qatar’s, etc.) but those guarantee seats are unavailable for AAdvantage redemption. Qantas reserves premium cabin awards for its own members (they didn’t before the pandemic). Cathay Pacific does the same. Qatar limits access to its own premium cabin awards to those redeeming their points or those in other Avios programs. Etihad heavily limits redemptions by partners, to name just a few. These are all new restrictions in the past few years that make AAdvantage miles less valuable. Same day changes are highly restrictive. Elites can confirm changes to their bookings, but can’t change the routing – they can’t connect through a different hub than their original reservation. What’s the use of having the best domestic network when customers aren’t allowed to use it? And from many cities there aren’t multiple flights to a given hub, effectively eliminating the benefit entirely. Here are ten changes that would make earning American miles and status more worthwhile. Most have precedents at other airlines. Some are things American has already done, and could simply bring back. Give the best customers better award pricing. American doesn’t offer a standing award discount for its top elites or credit card customers. They used to have extra availability at the saver level for Executive Platinums – by phone only – but they eliminated this when dropping the idea of saver awards for their ow flights and going all-dynamic pricing. They also used to offer an award option of a 15% redemption rebate at 175,000 Loyalty Points but they dropped this for 2024. It only applied to one American Airlines award trip, for up to two passengers, with a claim process after travel. Bring it back, make the rebate automatic, and let members use it on the awards they actually book. An annual mileage cap would control the cost without requiring a narrowly defined roundtrip. American still offers award rebates at million-plus Loyalty Point milestones. Delta and United have elite or cardmember redemption discounts. Delta mostly seemed to just raise prices on everybody else, while United’s has actually opened up more saver awards and discounts even compared to the old saver level at times. American doesn’t have anything comparable, but should. In my ideal – I don’t expect American to budget for this – I’d love to see Executive Platinum and ConciergeKey members have a limited number of opportunities to open award space each year. British Airways Gold Guest List members have “jokers” that can release awards from specified paid inventory. It doesn’t have to mean last seat avialability on every flight. It could be capacity controlled with a certain level of revenue inventory. Make partner awards easier to get, including when schedules first open American’s partner chart is very good (10 years ago the devaluation was brutal, but many airlines have devalued more since then). The challenge now is access to partner award space, with so many partners withholding inventory from American. British Airways shares revenue with American in a transatlantic joint venture that’s supposed to make them indifferent about whose aircraft a passenger flies. Yet Avios programs even outside the joint venture can get British Airways award space that American can’t. Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Qatar Airways and Etihad also give their own members or selected partners access that AAdvantage doesn’t get. American should negotiate for access, pay for additional inventory, and make reciprocal access part of its partnership discussions. Start with British Airways, despite draconian fuel surcharges that some other partners don’t even charge, simply because their close commercial relationship should produce a better result for customers – otherwise why are we allowing antitrust immunity in the first place? And keep the existing partner chart, don’t use this better inventory as an excuse to reprice the seats. American should also stop making members wait for its own booking calendar to open. American books up to 331 days ahead, while Finnair opens awards 360 days out. When a partner releases seats earlier, AAdvantage members should be able to book them then. Nearly a month’s head start matters when there are only a couple of business class awards. Many years ago that was the practice at Alaska Airlines – you could book the partner award right away, and call up later to add Alaska connecting flights when their own scheduled loaded. Give top elites priority for an empty middle seatI argued for this in 2020. It would be even more useful now, with complimentary upgrades harder to count on and not enough Main Cabin Extra seats. When a Platinum Pro, Executive Platinum or ConciergeKey member sits in a window or aisle seat in regular coach, hold the adjacent middle seat out from seat assignments. Have AgentAssist automatically release it at the gate when needed. The airline would keep selling the flight. It wouldn’t turn away a paying passenger to preserve an empty seat. Families who need to sit together and operational requirements could take priority. But when some middle seats are going to wind upempty anyway, ensuring the empty seat is beside the airline’s best customers simply makes sense. American could deliver a meaningful comfort benefit with very little displaced revenue. Make confirmed upgrades from paid premium economy a permanent option American has already tested this twice. In March and again in September, it offered promotions where a member could buy premium economy and apply a systemwide upgrade to confirm business class without the usual upgrade inventory. Make that a regular feature of systemwide upgrades: buy premium economy, spend a certificate, and confirm business class when a seat is still for sale. If American needs a short, published list of blackout dates, that’s fair enough. The existing ability to upgrade from coach should stay. This would give members an additional way to use their certificates, with certainty in exchange for buying a more expensive ticket. Give top elites 20% off paid upgrades, and let them earn upgrade creditsAmerican sells seats that once would have gone to complimentary upgrades. They value the tens of dollars more than rewarding the customer who spends tens of thousands. But upgrades were the key reason to earn status, which is the key driver of cobrand card spend. Give Platinum Pro and higher members 20% off the paid upgrade offers they see. American already has AA20 discounts for employees and eligible family members on airfare and awards. A comparable discount on upgrade offers for top customers isn’t an out of sample idea. The price before the discount needs to be the same offer the customer would otherwise receive. And American might collect more money from members who currently decline a buy-up because they’re waiting for a free upgrade. Some existing buyers would pay less while some people who never buy would start. Elites would get a better deal on excess premium inventory than once a year flyers. Add upgrade credits at Loyalty Point Reward milestones, usable toward these offers. That would provide something useful even when a systemwide upgrade won’t clear. Let top elites use the route network for same-day changes American has a huge network. Its same-day change rules prevent members from making full use of it. Under American’s rules, a replacement itinerary needs the same airports and routing. If you’re connecting through Charlotte, an earlier option through Dallas doesn’t necessarily help you. Neither does a nonstop replacing your connection. I was writing about this problem in 2015. The same-routing restriction already existed then, though agents had often been willing to waive it. Let Platinum Pro and higher members confirm a same-day change between the same origin and destination using any reasonable American routing with seats available in the cabin they’re entitled to occupy. Keep it to the day of travel, so this doesn’t become a way to buy a cheaper itinerary weeks ahead and immediately swap into an expensive one. Let an already-purchased upgrade carry over when the new flight has room in that cabin. A meeting ends early, the member gets home sooner, and American gives a frequent traveler a real benefit for their loyalty. Bring back stopovers on awards. Alaska allows free stopovers on one-way awards. Air France KLM’s Flying Blue offers them, too. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 additional points for an eligible stopover. American should let members stop at a connecting city on an international award that prices based on the partner redemption chart. Spend several days in Tokyo on the way to somewhere else in Asia, or visit Helsinki, London or Madrid before continuing through Europe. This should be free for top elites, but consider charging 5,000 miles for everyone else. Count award flights toward status and Million Miler balancesAmerican encourages members to earn miles through credit cards, shopping, hotels and other partners. When they finally redeem those miles and fly, the award trip doesn’t earn Loyalty Points. Publish a simple rate of Loyalty Points per mile redeemed. Include partner flights booked with AAdvantage miles. American issued the ticket and knows what the member redeemed. It could begin with its own flights if that’s easier to administer, but that shouldn’t be a permanent limit. Actual distance flown on awards should count toward Million Miler status as well. Delta already counts award travel toward its lifetime totals. Let elite households pool miles for free and share benefits easilyA family can collectively have enough miles for an award while each individual account comes up short. American should let an elite member establish a household pool, with no charge for combining miles. LifeMiles makes family pooling an elite benefit. Other programs manage pooling, too. Require verified members, put limits on how often people can join or leave, and give the household head redemption authority. Restricting the benefit to elites should make some forms of abuse less attractive, though it wouldn’t eliminate fraud. But the optimal amount of fraud is not zero anyway. American already lets members give someone status for a day. Make that benefit work like a trip benefit: select the traveler and reservation, then have the eligible seating and airport benefits apply immediately. The current terms require selecting the usage day at least seven days ahead Give Million Milers a benefit every yearAmerican deserves credit for adding lifetime Platinum Pro at four million miles and Executive Platinum at five million. It has also announced more choices for Million Miler milestone rewards. The next improvement should be something that arrives every year, including years when the member doesn’t cross another million mile threshold. Alaska gives Million Milers an annual head start toward status, which keeps them flying rather than retiring from engagement after they hit their threshold. American could also let a Million Miler share status with a designated household member, as competing programs do, or choose an annual benefit such as upgrade credit. Delta’s higher lifetime tiers bring recurring Choice Benefits. I’d start with the annual Loyalty Points. Someone who has already flown American a million miles shouldn’t have to begin every year’s pursuit of higher status at the same zero as someone who just joined. What do you feel American Airlines AAdvantage is missing, and how does it compare to other programs today? I see only Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards as comparable among U.S. airlines, believing both American and Alaska’s programs to be better than United’s. Some of you will disagree! And Alaska’s has its own challenges, including inventory for award redemption on its own flights and combining different partners on the same award ticket. Which of these changes I’ve suggested would move the needle for your own loyalty? And what am I missing from this list? One of AAdvantage’s best features is that the partner award chart hasn’t been devalued since 2016. But a good price for an award you can’t book doesn’t get you very far.

American improved its Million Miler program in 2025, and has more changes coming there. But that’s really the only real improvement I can think of in the past few years. In the meantime, it eliminated fixed-price mileage upgrades and took seat selection and upgrade benefits away from elites buying Basic Economy.

Some of my major complaints about the program: American offers paid upgrades to anyone on the flight while elite members wait and usually do not get upgraded. Systemwide upgrades are nearly impossible to use. Upgrades were once the major benefit of status but can no longer meaningfully be factored, of course dependent on route and dates of travel.

When you aren’t upgraded, at least elites can confirm extra legroom seats – but American has far too few of those. And when you exclude exit row seats (not eligible with young children), I often have to pick my flights carefully because there just aren’t extra legroom seats available. American says they’re adding more – but won’t start until 2028. When they first introduced Main Cabin Extra they did the whole fleet in a matter of months!

Scarce partner business class awards. British Airways guarantees award space for those redeeming Avios (whether their own, Finnair’s, Qatar’s, etc.) but those guarantee seats are unavailable for AAdvantage redemption. Qantas reserves premium cabin awards for its own members (they didn’t before the pandemic). Cathay Pacific does the same. Qatar limits access to its own premium cabin awards to those redeeming their points or those in other Avios programs. Etihad heavily limits redemptions by partners, to name just a few. These are all new restrictions in the past few years that make AAdvantage miles less valuable.

Same day changes are highly restrictive. Elites can confirm changes to their bookings, but can’t change the routing – they can’t connect through a different hub than their original reservation. What’s the use of having the best domestic network when customers aren’t allowed to use it? And from many cities there aren’t multiple flights to a given hub, effectively eliminating the benefit entirely. Here are ten changes that would make earning American miles and status more worthwhile. Most have precedents at other airlines. Some are things American has already done, and could simply bring back. Give the best customers better award pricing. American doesn’t offer a standing award discount for its top elites or credit card customers. They used to have extra availability at the saver level for Executive Platinums – by phone only – but they eliminated this when dropping the idea of saver awards for their ow flights and going all-dynamic pricing. They also used to offer an award option of a 15% redemption rebate at 175,000 Loyalty Points but they dropped this for 2024. It only applied to one American Airlines award trip, for up to two passengers, with a claim process after travel. Bring it back, make the rebate automatic, and let members use it on the awards they actually book. An annual mileage cap would control the cost without requiring a narrowly defined roundtrip. American still offers award rebates at million-plus Loyalty Point milestones. Delta and United have elite or cardmember redemption discounts. Delta mostly seemed to just raise prices on everybody else, while United’s has actually opened up more saver awards and discounts even compared to the old saver level at times. American doesn’t have anything comparable, but should. In my ideal – I don’t expect American to budget for this – I’d love to see Executive Platinum and ConciergeKey members have a limited number of opportunities to open award space each year. British Airways Gold Guest List members have “jokers” that can release awards from specified paid inventory. It doesn’t have to mean last seat avialability on every flight. It could be capacity controlled with a certain level of revenue inventory. Make partner awards easier to get, including when schedules first open American’s partner chart is very good (10 years ago the devaluation was brutal, but many airlines have devalued more since then). The challenge now is access to partner award space, with so many partners withholding inventory from American. British Airways shares revenue with American in a transatlantic joint venture that’s supposed to make them indifferent about whose aircraft a passenger flies. Yet Avios programs even outside the joint venture can get British Airways award space that American can’t. Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Qatar Airways and Etihad also give their own members or selected partners access that AAdvantage doesn’t get. American should negotiate for access, pay for additional inventory, and make reciprocal access part of its partnership discussions. Start with British Airways, despite draconian fuel surcharges that some other partners don’t even charge, simply because their close commercial relationship should produce a better result for customers – otherwise why are we allowing antitrust immunity in the first place? And keep the existing partner chart, don’t use this better inventory as an excuse to reprice the seats. American should also stop making members wait for its own booking calendar to open. American books up to 331 days ahead, while Finnair opens awards 360 days out. When a partner releases seats earlier, AAdvantage members should be able to book them then. Nearly a month’s head start matters when there are only a couple of business class awards. Many years ago that was the practice at Alaska Airlines – you could book the partner award right away, and call up later to add Alaska connecting flights when their own scheduled loaded. Give top elites priority for an empty middle seatI argued for this in 2020. It would be even more useful now, with complimentary upgrades harder to count on and not enough Main Cabin Extra seats. When a Platinum Pro, Executive Platinum or ConciergeKey member sits in a window or aisle seat in regular coach, hold the adjacent middle seat out from seat assignments. Have AgentAssist automatically release it at the gate when needed. The airline would keep selling the flight. It wouldn’t turn away a paying passenger to preserve an empty seat. Families who need to sit together and operational requirements could take priority. But when some middle seats are going to wind upempty anyway, ensuring the empty seat is beside the airline’s best customers simply makes sense. Delta already counts award travel toward its lifetime totals. Let elite households pool miles for free and share benefits easilyA family can collectively have enough miles for an award while each individual account comes up short. American should let an elite member establish a household pool, with no charge for combining miles. LifeMiles makes family pooling an elite benefit. Other programs manage pooling, too. Require verified members, put limits on how often people can join or leave, and give the household head redemption authority. Restricting the benefit to elites should make some forms of abuse less attractive, though it wouldn’t eliminate fraud. But the optimal amount of fraud is not zero anyway. American already lets members give someone status for a day. Make that benefit work like a trip benefit: select the traveler and reservation, then have the eligible seating and airport benefits apply immediately. The current terms require selecting the usage day at least seven days ahead Give Million Milers a benefit every yearAmerican deserves credit for adding lifetime Platinum Pro at four million miles and Executive Platinum at five million. It has also announced more choices for Million Miler milestone rewards. The next improvement should be something that arrives every year, including years when the member doesn’t cross another million mile threshold. Alaska gives Million Milers an annual head start toward status, which keeps them flying rather than retiring from engagement after they hit their threshold. When a Platinum Pro, Executive Platinum or ConciergeKey member sits in a window or aisle seat in regular coach, hold the adjacent middle seat out from seat assignments. Have AgentAssist automatically release it at the gate when needed.

The airline would keep selling the flight. It wouldn’t turn away a paying passenger to preserve an empty seat. Families who need to sit together and operational requirements could take priority. But when some middle seats are going to wind upempty anyway, ensuring the empty seat is beside the airline’s best customers simply makes sense. American could deliver a meaningful comfort benefit with very little displaced revenue.

Make that a regular feature of systemwide upgrades: buy premium economy, spend a certificate, and confirm business class when a seat is still for sale. Excellent article, and I agree with most of it. However, you are leaving out one major miss in AA’s Million Miler program. If you can’t chase the top tier, you’re chasing mediocrity (especially on AA today).

Excellent list. They need more MCE on their planes – it’s a competitive disadvantage compared to UA and DL. It’s the main perk of elite status these days. Software to auto-upgrade you to an MCE seat only works if there are, you know, more MCE seats.

Other than that, while most of this list would be nice to have, #1 on your list (discount award tickets for elites and cardholders) is also a need to have. It’s a competitive disadvantage compared to UA in a meaningful way, and DL in a still meaningful but somewhat more theoretical way given their often sky high redemption rates.

Bravo! Making the most of your strengths makes more sense than struggling with improving your weaknesses. I agree with all of these proposals especially better SWU options, million miler accrual and loyalty points for award tickets, and special perks for Platinum Pro and above. I’d be surprised if American adopts any of them, however.

Once again, I wish our “elites “ would just quit whining about their sorry state of life. Want first, buy first. After all, from each according to their ability (to pay).

But the airline doesn’t see both segments as part of one itinerary and doesn’t protect me if my first segment takes a delay and I misconnect. They also won’t let me check my bags all the way through. I’m literally willing to pay for part of the trip out of pocket to make it work, but the airline makes it very risky and difficult by not acknowledging that.

Lack of MCE is a big deal. I’m a lowly Gold on UA and can almost always book into Economy Plus. Flying AA this week to burn some miles earned on BA and the seat map on both flights has so few MCE seats. I booked a month out and there were none available.

Make Exec Platinums feel more valued, as there’s currently little reason to strive for the top tier given the decline in upgrade benefits.

Award discounts, additional AA inventory, and additional partner access would be a great way to do that.

Great ideas Gary. As an EXP flying out of DFW, the benefits I currently derive are almost non-existent. I’d be pleasantly shocked if AA were to implement any of these suggestions.

Better SDC changes. There’s a real no-brainer and going to make life easier for everyone including the reps.

@Common Sense — So wild to see you go “no politics” on here; at least you’re pretending to save-face by still showing up. The rest needed to submit a sick-day, apparently. (Oh, poor @This comes to mind; at least much of the rest of Ohio did their part.)

I find the 330 day calendar combined with limited partner availability to be especially galling

Confirmable SWU space at booking if seats are available for sale. Otherwise, there’s no material increased benefit for EP over Plat Pro. On a recent flight LAX-LHR I booked PE and was offered a paid upgrade price to biz class of ~$420 or ~42k miles. I’m Plat Pro and there was no confirmable space to use SWU’s on this flight despite the low paid upgrade offer, so this does not drive me to continue spending towards EP and higher LP threshholds. Upgrades were the sole reason I made sure I hit EP in the past and directly drove my spending behavior.

You make superb arguments that would strengthen AAdvantage and make more people likely to earn and retain loyalty status with American. That is valid, sensible, and would pay huge long term dividends to American. Therefore they won’t enact these badly needed changes. As a multi year EXP that’s highly unfortunate.

The issues with partner premium cabin awards is the biggest issue facing AAdvantge. American has considerable leverage here but choses not to use it. You to code share with us? Cool, our members get access to your premium cabin awards. You want to be in one of our JVs? Sweet – give us that award access. You want my booking engine to steer my passengers to your connecting flights? Wonderful – show me the award seats.

I negotiate contracts for a living and understand leverage. Give me one month and I’d have this problem solved.

#6145. Air Serbia Flight To Moscow Diverts After Politician Reportedly Skips Security

An Air Serbia flight that was supposed to fly from Serbia to Russia ended up turning around over Lithuania, in order for additional security checks to be carried out on passengers. The circumstances surrounding this sure are unusual, given who was onboard.

This incident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and involves Air Serbia flight JU134, scheduled to fly from Belgrade (BEG) to Moscow (SVO). The 1,074-mile flight was operated by an Airbus A320 with the registration code YU-APH. The flight was scheduled to depart at 6:25PM and land at 11:40PM, with a two hour time change, so it was blocked at 3hr15min.

The plane took off at 6:48PM, basically on schedule, and it started flying north, over Hungary, Slovakia, Poland, and then Lithuania. However, around 90 minutes after takeoff, while more than halfway, the plane u-turned, and flew back toward Belgrade.

The plane ended up landing in Belgrade at 9:57PM local time, a little over three hours after it first departed. The plane ended up once again taking off in the early morning hours of November 4, departing at 1:56AM, and landing at 6:43AM, over seven hours behind schedule.

Diversions happen, though it’s definitely unusual for a flight to turn around to the origin when it’s already more than halfway to its destination, especially when maintenance wasn’t to blame. Officially, the airline has shared that the decision to divert was made “in accordance with the instructions received and all applicable security rules.” That’s obviously really vague, though… so what really happened?

Here’s where the story gets really interesting. Onboard this Air Serbia flight were a few associates of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, who just recently lost an election. One of the people onboard was Aleksandar Vulin, who served as deputy prime minister until 2025, and is viewed as being very pro-Russia. The US had even imposed sanctions on him due to his close ties with Russia.

Media reports in Serbia suggest that the reason for the diversion was that security camera footage at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport had been reviewed, and it was determined that someone had helped him avoid security checks. Now, I understand the need to carry out security checks, though I’m also not sure the point of diverting when you’re already more than halfway to your destination.

Vulin denies that he was the reason that the plane diverted, claiming that it was instead a political showdown. After the diversion, he went on national TV in Serbia, to say the following:

“It’s all a lie, an act of violence and an attempt to prove to these new authorities how ready they are here at the airport, how much they are on the defensive of their ideology. So, of course it’s all a lie, of course it’s all utter nonsense. I’m really sorry and uncomfortable, so many people have returned, their lives are being ruined, their obligations are being ruined because of the attempt to politically deal with me.”

“I am completely calm, I know that I am in the right. And you know, I did not go to Moscow as a tourist, I went on business. I am going there to fight for the extension of the gas agreement. Not for me and you, but for all citizens of Serbia.”

He also said he was asleep at the time of the diversion, and had no clue what was going on until the plane landed back in Belgrade:

“We just woke up, to be honest, I fell asleep. I was sleeping on the plane, I wake up, they say: You are in Belgrade. How are you in Belgrade? When we went outside, I see the police, the special forces gathered. I say: ‘Colleagues, have you come for me?’ They laugh. They say: ‘We are not, Minister.’ I go down with all the other passengers. I go through the procedure with all the other passengers again. I go through another procedure by myself. And now, I am standing and waiting for them to let us get on the plane again.”

An Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Moscow turned around while over halfway to its destination. The decision to divert was made in accordance with “applicable security rules,” and all passengers were screened when the plane landed back in Serbia.

While it’s believed that a pro-Russia Serbian politician who was onboard may have avoided security checks at the airport, the politician denies that, and claims this was a political move.

What do you make of this unusual Air Serbia diversion?

#6144. What the FTC Wants to Know About How Airlines Set Fares

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Airline pricing has come under more scrutiny in recent years after Delta disclosed it was using AI to price some fares and a lawsuit was filed against JetBlue, alleging that the company uses personal data to price airfares. The airline industry has said it uses no personal data to determine pricing.

Airline pricing is once again under scrutiny. Last week, the Federal Trade Commission ordered Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and JetBlue to provide data on how they set fares, as part of a study of whether companies use personal information to set prices.

The agency wants details on the companies’ pricing methods. The companies have 45 days to respond.

“We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.

The FTC sent similar orders to Lyft, DoorDash, Uber, Instacart, Target and Walmart, seeking data on pricing and, for the gig companies, on worker pay.

The Federal Trade Commission has ordered Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and JetBlue to hand over data on how they set fares, part of a broader study into whether companies use personal information to price goods and services. The airlines have 45 days to respond. The same orders went to Lyft, DoorDash, Uber, Instacart, Target, and Walmart, with FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson saying the agency intends to scrutinize "opaque" pricing methodology. The inquiry lands as fares have risen sharply this year, largely because of surging jet fuel costs, and as airlines expand their use of AI in pricing. Delta, which told investors in 2024 it was working with the Israeli startup Fetcherr and said last year it was pricing about 3% of domestic routes with AI with a goal of up to 25% by the end of 2025, said it does not use personal data to set fares and has never used, tested, or planned individualized pricing. United referred questions to Airlines for America, which said it welcomes the study and that its carriers do not engage in personalized pricing. JetBlue faces a class action filed in April alleging it uses trackers to set prices dynamically. Roughly a dozen states have proposed laws this year limiting how companies collect and use customer search data, with California, Arizona, Hawaii, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Vermont proposing outright bans on surveillance pricing.

#6142. Southwest’s New Platinum Status Adds Too Little—10 Ways Rapid Rewards Should Fix Its New Program

Southwest Airlines is adding Platinum status to Rapid Rewards, but someone who already has A-List Preferred and Companion Pass won’t get much new. A third checked bag, earlier boarding, and a higher advertised earning bonus (offset by lower base-earning on higher fares) are very modest additions considering they’re launching a new top tier. Gold, the replacement for A-List Preferred, already gets the same seats. The 2027 overhaul makes things simpler by unifying qualification for elite status and Companion Pass. And they’re adding award travel on Icelandair, China Airlines and Etihad Airways beginning in the spring, including in premium cabins. We don’t yet know redemption pricing, rules or surcharges, so we don’t know how much value those will deliver. I’ve argued that Southwest’s changes follow from one another. Broader distribution puts their fares alongside everyone else’s. That creates pressure to unbundle with basic economy and paid seats and bags. Selling better seats requires assigned seating. Once they’ve given up the old differences, they need more of the benefits that make other airlines worth choosing. Southwest is inexorably becoming like the rest of the industry, but – they insist – with friendler crews. They at least need to become like everyone else without offering less. I offered ten ways to improve Rapid Rewards in 2022. Some, including partner airline redemptions and stronger credit card earning toward status, are finally being addressed. Here’s what I’d do next. Deliver Elite Members’ Bags First Southwest baggage delivery can be slow. That was easier to tolerate when checking bags was free for everyone. Once they’re charging for the service, standing around a carousel feels different. They should offer priority baggage handling for elites, with Gold and Platinum bags among the first delivered. This requires actually sorting and loading the bags so they come out first, not just a colored tag. And back it with a delivery guarantee. Delta offers 2,500 miles when checked bags take more than 20 minutes from gate arrival to the carousel. Alaska has a similar guarantee (and was actually first). Southwest could start with a guarantee for its top elites. I’d rather get my first bag promptly than have a free third one. Give Platinum Members Priority For An Empty Middle SeatSouthwest doesn’t have first class upgrades to offer. It can still make sitting in coach better. When a Platinum member selects a window or aisle in a regular legroom row, hold the adjacent middle seat out of routine seat assignments until it’s needed. Keep selling the flight, and release the seat at the gate if passengers need it. This would determine who gets the empty seat when a flight isn’t full. Someone is going to have extra space beside them. Give the customer who earned the highest status the best chance of being that person. Limiting this to ordinary coach would avoid taking some premium seats they’re trying to sell out of inventory. An empty middle can be better than a few additional inches of legroom. Introduce Lifetime Elite StatusAmerican, Delta, United and Alaska all recognize lifetime flying. Southwest now should, too. I’d base on miles or flight segments since Southwest has never had a long haul netowrk to rack up 20,000 flown miles on a roundtrip. For instance, 1,000 one-way trips could earn lifetime Silver, 2,000 could earn lifetime Gold, and 3,000 lifetime Platinum. I don’t know whether Southwest has the database to support historical flying like this. Give Elites An Award Rebate Make points worth more to the customers who earn status. A 10% rebate on Southwest awards for Gold and 15% for Platinum would make their points more valuable, and could be more easily managed than an award discount. Some Southwest credit cards already provide annual 10% or 15% discount codes. This is especially important because the new program cuts earning on expensive fares. As I laid out in comparing the new tiers, a Choice Extra ticket earns an A-List Preferred member 28 points per eligible dollar today, versus 22 for a Platinum member next year. Let Families Pool Points Free Southwest sells family travel and has one of the best benefits for traveling with someone else. Yet its program rules prohibit members from pooling points. Let a household combine its balances without paying a transfer fee. You can already use your points to book someone else’s ticket. The problem is having enough points across several accounts, but not enough in any one account for the award you want. JetBlue has offered free pooling for groups of up to seven people for years. United has family accounts, and this is a big feature in international progams. Count Award Flights Toward Status A flight paid for entirely with Rapid Rewards points doesn’t count as a qualifying flight. Southwest should change that, like Delta and Alaska do, and include partner awards as that part of the program develops. Southwest wants people to earn points from its credit cards and partners, then use them to fly. Treating that journey as less valuable to the airline makes no sense. Make Companion Pass More Useful When Traveling With Different People Companion Pass remains Southwest’s strongest benefit. But the new program keeps the old restrictions: one designated companion at a time, three changes per calendar year, and existing companion reservations must be canceled before switching people. Let Platinum members designate a small group, perhaps three people, and choose one companion for each trip. A spouse on one trip, a child on another. Still one companion per flight, still traveling with the member, with limits on changing the roster. I’d also let Platinum members use Companion Pass for an adjacent empty seat when traveling alone, an idea I included in my earlier wishlist. This would be a confirmed seat reservation, consuming inventory just as a companion booking does. A member whose travel is mostly business shouldn’t need to bring another person on the trip to get substantial value from the program’s biggest reward. Allow Confirmed Same-Day Changes On Basic Fares Southwest already lets elites use their seating benefits on Basic. That’s a real advantage over competitors, and it extends to family members on the same reservation. But even the new Platinum tier won’t receive free confirmed same-day changes on Basic. Members can stand by. They need to buy Choice or higher to confirm the change without paying a fare difference. Give Gold and Platinum confirmed changes into available seats on the day of travel, regardless of their original fare. Keep the same origin and destination, and let the member choose an available itinerary that gets them there sooner or works better with their schedule. Southwest already provides the service on more expensive fares, here earned status would supply it. Make Southwest Status Useful On Its Airline Partners The international redemption announcement addresses not being able to use Southwest points for long haul travel. The awards need solid pricing and inventory. I expect that we’ll eventually see reciprocal status recognition, but that needs to come quickly: priority check-in, baggage allowances, boarding and seat benefits and lounge access would make Gold and Platinum valuable even when member travels beyond Southwest’s route map. Give Platinum A Choice Of Benefits Southwest is building Icon Lounges, with openings planned to begin in late 2027. Access has been announced through a forthcoming premium Chase card. They haven’t announced a Platinum lounge benefit. Give members an annual choice when they earn Platinum: perhaps some lounge passes which could encourage them to try the product and get the card, or to share the passes with others. They might choose a travel credit or certificates that let friends and family select extra legroom seats when the member isn’t traveling. Southwest is already introducing two milestones, at 20,000 and 95,000 qualifying points which are below Platinum. The earlier milestone’s Preferred seat certificates aren’t extra legroom upgrades and can’t be gifted, so certificates for a friend to choose a better seat would add something different. They should continue with milestones above platinum, and continue offering choice benefits. Southwest Airlines is remaking itself in the image of the rest of the airline industry – with the same kinds of restrictions, but also adding many of the same amenities. They will have three elite tiers, but those tiers need to be competitive. I want Southwest to succeed. Are these things that would do it for you? What’s missing from my list? #6141. Is World Of Hyatt Points + Cash Worth It? The Value Varies Wildly

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night redemptions, the program also has a Points + Cash option, whereby you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay.

The reality is that the value of Hyatt Points + Cash has fluctuated significantly over the years. Going back a decade, it was the primary way that I redeemed my points. Then it was devalued significantly, and then some value was brought back. So I’d like to take a look at the current state of things… is Hyatt Points + Cash worth considering nowadays?

As the name suggests, with Hyatt Points + Cash, you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a Hyatt stay. More specifically, you’ll redeem 50% of the points required for a stay, and will receive a 30-50% discount off the standard rate for the room type chosen.

Now, there are some important things to be aware of:

Just as a reminder, below is the standard room World of Hyatt award chart, which shows the award pricing for a free night hotel stay based on which of the five pricing tiers applies for a particular night (lowest, low, moderate, upper, or top).

When booking Points + Cash, you’d pay half of the points, plus 50-70% of the flexible revenue rate, so below is that chart.

With the basics of Hyatt Points + Cash out of the way, let’s do some number crunching. Let me state upfront that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each, though I usually get quite a bit more value out of them in comparison to what a hotel stay would cost with cash.

For the purposes of the below examples, I’ll simply be comparing the cost for a free night redemption to the cost of a Points + Cash redemption. This doesn’t consider the outright cost of a stay if paying cash, so for more on that, see my post about when you should redeem points for a hotel stay.

I picked six hotels at random, belonging to different brands and in different regions. I picked totally random dates, so let’s take a look at what I found.

For the night I picked, the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay is charging 15,000 points per night, or 7,500 points plus $103 ($116 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 7,500 extra points to save $116, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.55 cents each.

The Park Hyatt Los Cabos is charging 55,000 points per night, or 27,500 points plus $500.50 ($680.68 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 27,500 extra points to save $680.68, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.48 cents each.

The Hyatt Studios Mobile is charging 3,000 points per night, or 1,500 points plus $61 ($71.98 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 1,500 extra points to save $71.98, which is like buying Hyatt points for 4.8 cents each.

The Thompson Rome is charging 35,000 points per night, or 17,500 points plus $281.20 (that includes taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 17,500 extra points to save $281.20, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.61 cents each.

The Hyatt Centric Dubai Jumeirah is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $115 ($145.14 including taxes & fees). You’re spending $145.14 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.45 cents each.

The Grand Hyatt Seoul is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $221 (that includes taxes & fees). You’re spending $221 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.21 cents each.

As you can see, the value of Hyatt Points + Cash varies significantly. In the above six examples I randomly pulled up, you’re essentially “buying” Hyatt points for anywhere from 1.45 cents to 4.8 cents each (these aren’t actually points in your account, but rather you’re spending some amount of cash in lieu of points).

So the idea is that if the “purchase” price on points were relatively low, it could be worth booking Points + Cash, rather than just redeeming outright. On the low end of the spectrum, some people might find this to be worthwhile, though I think on the high end of the spectrum, we can all agree this represents an awful deal.

Before you make a final decision, just keep in mind:

Lastly, let me just mention that in many cases Points + Cash is a better value compared to redeeming points outright in situations where the cash rate is lower than usual, and a hotel is in low season. In those situations it might not make sense to redeem points at all. This comes down to how reimbursement for these awards works between World of Hyatt and individual hotels.

For example, the single best Points + Cash deal above is at the Hyatt Centric Dubai, but if you look at the cash rate, you’ll see that redeeming points isn’t a great deal in the first place. There’s no reason to redeem 20,000 points (or 10,000 points plus $115) when the cash rate in the first place is well under $200.

Hyatt Points + Cash lets you redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay. While it’s nice to have the flexibility of this redemption opportunity, more often than not it doesn’t represent a good deal, in my opinion.

The value you’re getting per point through Points + Cash does vary wildly, but one thing that’s fairly consistent is that you won’t get outsized value. In a majority of situations where Points + Cash represents a good deal compared to the outright points cost, it’s a hotel where a points redemption isn’t a good deal in the first place.

Personally, I avoid Points + Cash redemptions, though it’s always worth checking and crunching the numbers.

What’s your take on Hyatt’s Points + Cash option? Do you ever use it?

To grayanderson’s point, the fair test is the all-in cash rate vs the cash part of P+C plus the points at your own valuation. With P+C you still pay the full % taxes on the cash portion and lose the resort fee waiver, so at a resort with a big daily fee that alone can wipe out the gain. Quick math for Beachfan’s question is (cash rate minus P+C cash) divided by half the award points, which gives you cents per point. If that’s under your ~1.4 to 1.5 cent valuation, pay cash on the refundable member rate and earn the 5x plus bonus. FWIW that cash baseline can itself differ depending on which country you search from, since hotel inventory and pricing vary by market. Arbitrica checks the same Hyatt from a ton of countries for free and finds kind of the lowest price in the world, which makes the cpp math more honest. Just remember a third party rate won’t earn Hyatt points, so compare like for like. Run the cpp number first and only use P+C when it clears your valuation

In your 5 examples the best savings using cash and points was like buying the points you for 1.45 cents. Seeing how you value Hyatt points at 1.4 that means none of the examples were valuable or good value to save the points. I agree and searched 10 properties and dates and like you could not find a single property where cash and points brought value.

So, I'd need to look at the baseline cash rates alongside these two numbers. I know I've seen a few situations at e.g. Marriott where the cash side of the points+cash rate wasn't half of the overall cash rate. Also, does this account for resort fees (or parking, if a Globalist) in the difference between the two, since those waivers apply to points-only but not points+cash?

Great Analysis thanks Lucky. Which of the hotels would be better paying all cash on a refundable member rate? In other words, what’s the point evaluation implied by the all points versus all cash rate.

This is all well and good, but Hyatt NEVER has had availability for me for any city I travel to. Not once. I've tried probably ten times, always with a flexibility of +- 2 days, and...nothing. Completely useless program.
