#6139. Expedia Expects Attractive Deals From Meta’s Muse and Google’s AI Overviews

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Expedia Group CEO Ariane Gorin, speaking at Skift Global Forum 2026 via remote video.  Skift

Will Expedia's advertising on Meta's Muse and Google AI Overviews be the new Google Search? Ariane Gorin is hopeful, citing Expedia proven track record in these sorts of deals. On the other hand, in years' past Expedia officials complained about the high cost of Google marketing.

How will big AI platforms perform as customer acquisition channels for Expedia Group and other online travel agencies, and what will they cost?

"The economics of the partnerships are being worked out," Expedia Group CEO Ariane Gorin said Wednesday about Meta's Muse and Google's AI Overviews. "You know, we have a track record of being able to work with big advertising platforms or tech platforms to use them as channels to acquire customers at attractive economics, and that's what I think we'll see."

Gorin said on Expedia’s third-quarter earnings

Expedia Group used its third-quarter earnings call to describe AI platforms as a customer acquisition channel still being priced. CEO Ariane Gorin said the economics of partnerships with Meta's Muse and Google's AI Overviews are "being worked out," and pointed to the company's history of acquiring customers through large advertising and tech platforms at attractive economics. She said Expedia is leading in citation share in the U.S. — how often its brands are cited as a source by AI chatbots — and that an integration with Muse was imminent. Gorin said the integrations are a way to learn how agents make decisions and which customers use them, and that travelers using agentic AI for discovery still want to book with a trusted brand. The underlying numbers were strong: revenue rose 12% to $4.9 billion, net income rose 7% to $1.03 billion, and room nights grew 7%, matching Booking Holdings. B2B revenue climbed 23% to $1.7 billion while the consumer brands grew 6%. Expedia raised full-year gross bookings guidance to 10% growth from 8-9%, and revenue to 11-12% from 9-10%. CFO Derek Andersen said the fourth-quarter environment is softer than the third, citing disruptions in the Middle East and unrest in some European cities.

#6138. Durbin Is Retiring, Marshall Just Lost—Why The Bill Threatening Your Credit Card Rewards Isn’t Dead

Dick Durbin is retiring and Roger Marshall just lost his Senate seat. The two most prominent champions of the Credit Card Competition Act, the law intended to regulate credit card interchange which will mean far fewer rewards for consumers, will be gone in January. The bill threatening the economics of card rewards, and the airlines that depend on them, has support from President Trump and Vice President JD Vance was an original co-sponsor so it may come back with his presidential campaign. But the thing about this legislation is that it’s more useful as a way to raise campaign money from both retailers and banks than as something Congress actually passes. Departures of Durbin and Marshall haven’t made the Durbin-Marshall bill go away. Durbin identified Vermont Senator Peter Welch as his successor on the issue. The Airline Lobby Is Right To Worry In this week’s Airlines Confidential, Airlines for America CEO Chris Sununu warns that state initiatives interfering with card fees would eliminate points-funded travel. Banks buy miles because rewards help attract customers and their spending. By reducing margins on that spending, it’s less valuable to spend to encourage consumers to use the product. In markets where government has gotten involved in interchange rates we’ve seen: smaller initial bonuses higher annual fees annual caps on awards award chart devaluations (if each mile is worth less, an airline can still award one mile per dollar on spend despite receiving less money for it from the bank) It also means less revenue for the airline. In the third quarter, American Express represented all of Delta’s profit. American Airlines is barely breaking even even with several billion net from Citibank. We’d have much shakier airlines and fewer flights, and aspirational leisure destinations like Hawaii in particular would see less air service. What The Credit Card Competition Act Actually Does The current Senate bill, S. 3623, would require covered issuers with more than $100 billion in assets to enable at least two unaffiliated payment networks. At least one would have to be outside of Visa and Mastercard. Merchants get to choose the routing. That’s meant to put downward pressure on merchant payment costs by changing who controls which network handles the transaction. Cards issued in a three-party system, such as American Express issuing its own cards, are exempt from the routing requirement. Merchants benefit from accepting cards. They get more sales, and higher average sales. It’s often less expensive to accept credit cards than to take cash (due to employee theft, incorrect change, higher insurance costs). Retailers want the service cards offer, but want the government to force Visa and Mastercard to provide it for less. Trump’s promise of $1,200 in annual family savings was completely made up and inconsistent with the bill. Currently a majority of interchange gets rebated to the customer. Regulation of interchange has never lowered prices to consumers. And card payments, funded in large part by interchange, provide services to consumers beyond just payments (and borrowings). They often fund consumer protections – not just stronger dispute resolution than debit cards, but also extended warranty, return protection, and travel protections. The Bill’s Strongest Value Is As A Threat Back in July 2023, I argued that this was an especially useful issue for opening contribution wallets on both sides. Retailers have a large, concentrated interest in lowering their acceptance costs. Banks, payment networks and airlines have a large, concentrated interest in preserving the existing economics. An unresolved legislative threat gives both sides a reason to pour dollars into campaigns and political committees. I’d still bet on another round of proposals, threatened amendments and lobbying. Durbin and Marshall are leaving but the retailers and banks with billions at stake aren’t. Politicians still want the money. #6137. Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points Double Dip Explained

The single best way to earn American AAdvantage Loyalty Points with credit card spending often flies under the radar, so I’d like to talk a little more about that in this post, especially since this tends to cause some confusion. Furthermore, this was recently made an “official” card perk, rather than something that just unofficially applied to most cardmembers.

Link: Double dip your Loyalty Points earning with the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

With the American AAdvantage Loyalty Points program, you can typically earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on a co-branded American credit card. However, there’s one card that’s an exception, and by far the best.

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more) is the co-branded Citi and American Airlines business card. There’s a quirk to the card, though, when it comes to authorized user rewards. On the surface, the authorized user ordinarily earns the Loyalty Points for their spending, and not the primary cardmember, which is an unusual policy for a small business card.

However, through December 31, 2028 (and it’s possible this will be extended again, as it has been in the past), both the primary cardmember and the authorized user earn Loyalty Points for authorized user spending. It basically means you earn two Loyalty Points per dollar spent, just in different accounts. Just to be abundantly clear here:

So the key is for the spending to be on the authorized user’s card, so that this spending unlocks double Loyalty Points (spread across two accounts).

Either way, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers several valuable perks, and also has an excellent welcome bonus, making it a good time to apply. So if you are eligible, I’d consider applying even if the double Loyalty Points opportunity doesn’t work out (though hopefully it does).

Personally, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points double dip is how I qualified for AAdvantage elite status last year. I had a hard time justifying putting spending onto co-branded American cards compared to some other cards out there, when I was only earning one Loyalty Point per dollar.

But if I can qualify for elite status for two people at once, and earn the corresponding Loyalty Point Rewards perks, the math on that spending starts to look much better:

For example, earning 250,000 Loyalty Points per account could potentially earn you a combined total of 12 systemwide upgrades or 170,000 bonus miles. That’s a pretty substantial reward, beyond just the miles you earn for spending and the status!

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers an easy opportunity to double dip Loyalty Points earning through authorized user spending. This opportunity is available to all cardmembers, and is currently valid through December 31, 2028 (though has the potential to be extended beyond that). This is a great opportunity, so if you’re pursuing AAdvantage elite status, I’d highly recommend this method.

Have you been taking advantage of this Loyalty Points double dip opportunity?

#6135. Trip.com Group Builds a Bigger Travel Business Around Concerts

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Taylor Swift The Eras Tour Wikimedia Commons / Paolo Villanueva

The concert might be the reason to travel, but Trip.com Group wants to make sure it's not the only thing fans spend money on. Tickets and hotel rooms are just the opening act.

Trip.com Group wants to turn concert trips into longer and more lucrative travel bookings. It is eyeing a move beyond tickets and hotel stays to offer fans everything from local attractions to ground transportation and dining experiences.

The company is betting that fans traveling to see their favorite artists are an opportunity to capture more of their overall travel spending, and particularly as major concerts often draw audiences across borders.

“Most concertgoers ideally wanted to spend an average of four days at the destination,” said Edison Chen, vice president of destination marketing and strategic alliances at Trip.com Group, at a media briefing in Singapore on Wednesday.

A fan flying in for a show can likely also be persuaded to spend a few extra days exploring the destination, said Chen. That creates opportunities for the company to sell attractions, transport and other experiences.

Trip.com Group is building live entertainment into a travel demand channel, moving beyond concert tickets and hotel stays to sell attractions, ground transport, and dining around shows. Edison Chen, vice president of destination marketing and strategic alliances, said most concertgoers ideally wanted to spend an average of four days at the destination, and described them as "artist-first" rather than "destination-first" travelers who pick hotels by proximity to the venue and will pay up for better seats and rooms. The company said bookings for concert travel packages rose 64% year over year in the first half of 2026, with music-related package trips up 80% in the second quarter alone. Trip.com entered live-entertainment travel in Asia about a year ago through a partnership with Live Nation, and in November 2025 began selling concert, sports, and theater tickets directly through an agreement with Dublin-based ticketing firm Coras, giving it primary inventory across European football, U.S. sports, Broadway, and the London West End. After an exclusive presale for BTS concerts in Bangkok, flight bookings from Hong Kong to Bangkok roughly tripled and bookings from Singapore rose about 200%, according to Jesse Yang, head of corporate branding and global events partnership. A new Trip Events section on the homepage lists shows even where Trip.com has no ticketing relationship, while Live Nation Asia expands its venue footprint in Bangkok, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

#6134. Priceline Faces $1 Billion Fine After Hotel Guests Were Tricked Into Paying Up To 85% More For Rooms

You search for a hotel, click what looks like its reservation page, and book a room—only to discover you’ve gone through a middleman charging hundreds of dollars more per night. That’s the deception alleged against Guest Reservations, a Priceline partner whose advertised rate could be up to 85% higher than booking directly. Now Priceline’s parent has recorded a $1 billion accounting charge toward a possible Federal Trade Commission settlement involving the partner’s practices, with the potential penalties and consumer refunds still being negotiated. A refundable room at San Francisco’s Palace Hotel was $419 on Marriott’s website. Guest Reservations wanted $775 for a comparable room with the same cancellation deadline. And the city’s lawsuit says the booking site was designed to make travelers think they were dealing with the hotel directly. The company supplying the rooms was Priceline, and its parent Booking Holdings which also owns Booking.com, has taken a $1 billion accounting hit while negotiating a possible regulatory settlement for its involvement in intercept guests who had already chosen a hotel, making them think they’d reached the hotel’s own site, and charging them more – and making it difficult to undo the purchase when they discover what happened. San Francisco’s suit includes a Google search for “palace hotel sf” on an iPhone. The top sponsored result displayed palacesanfrancisco.guestreservations.com, above Marriott’s own hotel website. Clicking led to a page devoted to the Palace Hotel. The city says the small “An independent travel network” on the site was easy to miss and ambiguous. “Guest reservations” sounds like a department of the hotel you’re trying to book. Put the property’s name in front of it, add hotel photos, and a traveler can think they’ve arrived at the hotel’s guest reservations department. The city compared prices within minutes of each other on July 1 for a July 8 stay. These were Marriott’s public nonmember rates, including taxes: King Room Cancellation Terms Marriott Direct Guest Reservations Markup Refundable for one day after booking $381 $595 56% Refundable until July 5 $419 $775 85% A separate investigation found a two-night stay at the Westin Denver Airport cost $237 more through Guest Reservations than booking the same stay directly. Guest Reservations said it clearly identifies itself as an independent platform, complies with Google’s advertising rules, and discloses its taxes and service fees before purchase. Customers also describe trouble getting refunds after discovering the intermediary. And booking through a third party means giving up hotel points and elite benefits, along with the ability to deal directly with the property when plans change. Guest Reservations isn’t owned or operated by Priceline. Priceline Partner Solutions was reportedly its exclusive hotel inventory supplier. Their operation furnished the hotel information, booking technology and payment processing, and earned revenue from completed reservations. The city’s case also targets BookOnline.com. It alleges Booking knew how the sites were acquiring customers and continued helping them sell rooms. Booking responded that it takes consumer protection seriously and believes the lawsuit lacks merit. One example of Priceline’s involvement comes from Seth Kugel’s New York Times investigation. An 85-year-old woman searching for Bologna’s Grand Hotel Majestic reached Guest Reservations and requested an eight night standard room stay. She was charged $16,559 for a suite, including $4,276 in taxes and fees. When she disputed the charge with American Express, Priceline Partner Solutions was the merchant of record and successfully sought to have the charge reinstated. Guest Reservations later told the paper it had issued her a refund. Priceline told the Times that fewer than 0.09% of Guest Reservations transactions generated complaints, that partners must comply with laws and contractual obligations, and that it takes action when it identifies violations. A low complaint rate doesn’t tell us how many people were misled. Some never discover it. Others blame the hotel. Many may think they have no recourse. Most consumers do not complain when they’re unhappy (or complain to friends and family). The odds that a complaint reaches Priceline as supplier of the inventory seem low. And they’re saying they’re getting complaints… not what they did with those! In its latest quarterly filing, Booking recorded: A $900 million reduction in revenue. A separate $100 million loss in general and administrative expenses. Booking says the FTC could seek even more. A negotiated agreement would likely include payments to the agency, money back to U.S. consumers, and changes to Priceline’s practices. There are also civil penalties for qualifying rule violations, with a current ceiling of $53,088 per violation. The government has a straightforward argument about the alleged sales process: a reasonable customer gets misled by the appearance of an ad and booking page, while the booking site says guests should have read the disclaimer more carefully. The site apparently was literally designed to create the wrong impression among customers. The FTC’s business impersonation rule covers falsely posing as another company or misrepresenting an affiliation, including by implication. #6133. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

#6131. American Airlines Dropped Trump’s Name From West Palm Beach Departure Screens

Update: This change actually happened in August. Reminder: Palm Beach airport code changing from PBI to DJT On Aug. 18, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida, will change from PBI to DJT. This is the code used on most customer- and team member-facing systems. What you can expect: Airport applications, including QIK, ACE and Falcon, will transition to using the new airport code, DJT, on Aug. 18. Customer applications, such as the American app and AA.com will also use the DJT code. Transition period: Some tools and manuals may continue to reference this airport by its previous name and airport code during a transition period. If you are unable to use DJT in these systems, revert to using PBI. If you receive any questions from customers about the change, refer to these talking points: Why is American using the DJT airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport? American follows airport codes as determined by the International Air Transport Association and other bodies. After Florida passed a law earlier this year to rename the airport, IATA announced they would change the three-digit airport code. Why is American referring to this airport as President Donald J. Trump International Airport? Earlier this year, a law was passed in the State of Florida renaming this airport from Palm Beach International Airport to President Donald J. Trump International Airport. American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments. Why does the screen behind you say, “West Palm Beach, FL”? Given that this transition is now complete and both the ICAO and IATA codes have changed, GIDS displays will once again say “West Palm Beach, FL.” American Airlines has dropped “Pres DJT” from the gate monitors of its West Palm Beach flights, going back to “West Palm Beach, FL,” as flagged by aviation watchdog JonNYC. It undoes the unusual decision to give the sitting president billing that other airport namesakes don’t get. JonNYC flagged the change Wednesday night, then added that he isn’t claiming a connection to the election results. It’s not clear exactly when American flipped the switch. so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ? — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 4, 2026 Back in July, I wrote about American breaking its usual gate screen display pattern for Trump. They generally display the city, adding an airport name where it helps distinguish between airports serving the same destination. New York’s JFK versus LaGuardia makes sense. Little Rock doesn’t get billed as Clinton airport, and Grand Rapids doesn’t get Gerald Ford. West Palm Beach got “Pres DJT.” Here’s the screen from that July coverage: American even gave agents talking points to explain the change. Their internal memo pointed to Florida’s renaming law and the change in the airport’s three-letter code, saying: American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments. That explained why the airport had a new name, but not putting the president’s name on the gate screen. And there’s no change made by the airport itself! Florida’s renaming of Palm Beach International as President Donald J. Trump International Airport took effect July 9. The passenger-facing airport code changed from PBI to DJT on August 18. American still very much needs this administration. The Department of Transportation and Federal Aviation Administration heavily regulate them. In September I wrote about Robert Isom’s praise for Trump and what American might want in return, including closer cooperation with Alaska Airlines. Just two days later, American and Alaska announced plans for Alaska to join American’s Atlantic and Pacific joint businesses. That needs DOT approval and antitrust immunity, and the administration’s help for approvals overseas. As I explained at the time, this would let them share revenue and coordinate fares and schedules with Alaska and their international partners. Reminder: Palm Beach airport code changing from PBI to DJT

On Aug. 18, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida, will change from PBI to DJT. This is the code used on most customer- and team member-facing systems.

Transition period: Some tools and manuals may continue to reference this airport by its previous name and airport code during a transition period.

If you receive any questions from customers about the change, refer to these talking points:

Why is American using the DJT airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport?

American follows airport codes as determined by the International Air Transport Association and other bodies. After Florida passed a law earlier this year to rename the airport, IATA announced they would change the three-digit airport code.

Why is American referring to this airport as President Donald J. Trump International Airport?

Earlier this year, a law was passed in the State of Florida renaming this airport from Palm Beach International Airport to President Donald J. Trump International Airport. American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments.

Why does the screen behind you say, “West Palm Beach, FL”?

Given that this transition is now complete and both the ICAO and IATA codes have changed, GIDS displays will once again say “West Palm Beach, FL.”

American Airlines has dropped “Pres DJT” from the gate monitors of its West Palm Beach flights, going back to “West Palm Beach, FL,” as flagged by aviation watchdog JonNYC. It undoes the unusual decision to give the sitting president billing that other airport namesakes don’t get.

JonNYC flagged the change Wednesday night, then added that he isn’t claiming a connection to the election results. It’s not clear exactly when American flipped the switch.

Client dinners, catered lunches and team celebrations can add up quickly. The right business credit card can turn those restaurant bills into a meaningful haul of points, miles or cash back.

From high category bonuses to uncapped flat-rate rewards, the best credit cards for dining can make every business meal work harder.

Here's how our top picks compare based on their dining returns, annual fees and reward flexibility.

The information for the U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus Visa Signature Card and the U.S. Bank Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

To determine the best business cards for dining, I looked for cards with an estimated return of at least 3% on restaurant purchases, based on TPG's valuations. I focused on ongoing earnings rather than welcome offers or dining credits, then selected cards serving distinct use cases, including high category bonuses, uncapped transferable rewards and no-annual-fee options.

Other cards that don't earn at least 3% back in value based on our valuations may still be good fits for your business within a broader rewards strategy, but are less competitive when restaurant earnings are the primary goal.

The American Express Business Gold earns valuable Membership Rewards points. Cardmembers earn 4 points per dollar spent in their top two spending categories each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in bonus category spending per year, then 1 point per dollar), with dining and restaurants falling under an available category.

That means businesses that max out their cap could earn 600,000 points each year. Even if you don't come close to that cap, 4 points per dollar is still a significant return on spend, especially when they come with all the potential of Membership Rewards.

Just be careful: Since Amex rewards extra bonus points on your top spending categories each billing cycle, if other eligible expenses overtake dining, restaurant purchases may earn only 1 point per dollar. You can use that to your advantage when your restaurant spending is low one month, but it could also catch you off guard.

To learn more, read our full review of the Business Gold.

Apply here: American Express Business Gold

The U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus earns 5% cash back in the cardholder's top eligible spending category each month on up to $200,000 in annual eligible purchases, automatically. Dining is one of the qualifying categories, and the cap is high enough that most businesses won't have to worry about it. All purchases outside the top category earn at least 2% cash back, which is also a generous return.

The $295 annual fee makes this card best for businesses with substantial, consistent restaurant spending. Otherwise, a no-annual-fee option may provide better value overall.

If you're looking for a card with no annual fee, The Blue Business Plus earns 2 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on all purchases (for the first $50,000 in spending each year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The simplicity of this card means you don't need to keep track of spending categories; it's just as great for your dining purchases as it is for shipping, advertising and other business expenses. For businesses that can stay below the cap and earn 2 points per dollar spent on all their spending, the combination of transferable points and no annual fee is difficult to beat.

To learn more, read our full review of the Blue Business Plus.

Apply here: The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express

Like the Blue Business Plus, the Capital One Venture Business earns 2 miles per dollar spent on dining and other purchases. Unlike the Amex card, however, that earning rate is unlimited. This makes Venture Business a stronger fit for businesses that expect to spend more than $50,000 each year and can take advantage of double miles well above that spending threshold, despite the $95 annual fee.

Capital One miles are highly versatile, with options to transfer to 15-plus airline or hotel partners, book travel without blackout dates through Capital One Travel and more. In fact, a different set of transfer partners could make the Venture Business a more compelling solution than an Amex, depending on your business's redemption preferences.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Business Credit Card

The Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card earns 3% cash back on eligible restaurant purchases with no annual fee, and there's no cap on total rewards.

It can't match the Business Essentials Plus card's 5% return, but there's no annual fee to recoup. A business would need to spend about $14,750 annually on dining for the 5% rate to make up for the $295 fee versus the Triple Cash card's no-annual-fee 3% return. Therefore, if you're looking for simple cash back but have more moderate restaurant spending, the Triple Cash is a stronger fit.

To learn more, read our full review of the U.S. Bank Triple Cash.

The Marriott Bonvoy Business Amex is a good fit for businesses that frequently entertain clients, host events at Marriott properties or incur dining expenses while traveling. It earns 4 points per dollar spent on eligible restaurant purchases worldwide, which represents a 3% return at TPG's November 2026 valuations. Since it doesn't impose a spending cap on its restaurant rewards, businesses can earn consistently throughout the year.

The card becomes especially valuable for businesses that regularly stay with Marriott and can put both its hotel benefits and Bonvoy rewards to use.

Of course, loyalty to one hotel brand won't work for everyone. Businesses that prioritize more flexible redemptions may prefer a card that includes Marriott as a transfer partner rather than choosing a cobranded card specifically.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bonvoy Business Amex.

Apply now: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card

The right business card option depends on more than earning rates. You'll also need to account for how much your business spends, whether you prefer cash back or travel rewards and whether you're willing to pay an annual fee.

Start with the net value, not the largest number in the table. The Amex Business Gold and Business Essentials Plus only deliver their highest dining returns when restaurant purchases rank among the business's top eligible categories. But cards that earn lower rates of return on dining might be a better value once you factor in annual fees and spending caps.

In addition to considering the type of rewards best for your business, think about what else these cards offer. Secondary benefits like travel protections, cellphone insurance, lounge access or elite status might make up for a lower earning rate on meals when you consider the whole package.

A large welcome offer can improve a card's first-year value, but it shouldn't outweigh its long-term fit. Compare ongoing rewards after the annual fee, along with the protections, credits and other benefits your business will realistically use. That said, when two or more cards are equally strong long-term fits, a welcome bonus can be a useful tiebreaker. Especially since some credit cards currently offer welcome bonuses of 100,000 points or more.

Lastly, confirm your spending will count toward elevated earning rates if the bonus rate affects which card you pay with. Dining bonuses depend on how the merchant categorizes the purchase, and not all food vendors are considered a restaurant. For example, a hotel cafe may code as travel, while a bar might code as nightlife or entertainment.

The Amex Business Gold offers the highest potential dining return based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, but its earning rate alone likely doesn't settle the decision. Spending caps, annual fees, redemption flexibility and other card benefits will also factor into which card delivers the most value for your business.

Businesses with large, predictable restaurant expenses will come out ahead by choosing premium cards, even after budgeting for an annual fee. When your dining spending is more moderate or inconsistent, though, a no-annual-fee card may produce the same net value with less monitoring. Don't pay for an earnings rate your business won't regularly trigger.

#6129. Minor Hotels Puts Its New Wellness Brand Inside a St. Regis It Owns

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Minor Hotels properties featured in The White Lotus have seen a surge in bookings.  Minor Hotels

Owning the building made this easy. Minor didn’t need anyone’s money to put its wellness brand inside a Marriott-run hotel. Getting an outside owner to pay for one, and agreeing with another brand on who keeps the client, will be harder.

Minor Hotels has put the first city outpost of its new wellness brand inside a hotel it owns but doesn’t run. It is a test case meant to show other hotel owners that the concept can work under brands other than Minor’s own.

Bangkok Life, which was announced last month, pairs medical diagnostics with traditional medicine, nutrition and fitness. The new offering sits inside The St. Regis Bangkok, which Marriott manages under its St. Regis brand. The hotel is one of several Minor owns but other companies operate.

Thailand-headquartered Minor launched Life Longevity as a standalone wellness brand in October, building out its flagship, Layan Life by Anantara, at Anantara Layan Phuket Resort. Opting for a Bangkok roll-out in a hotel it owns also lets Minor invest its own capital first.

Minor Hotels has opened the first urban location of its Life Longevity wellness brand inside The St. Regis Bangkok — a hotel Minor owns but Marriott operates under its own brand. The move follows Layan Life by Anantara at Anantara Layan Phuket Resort, which Minor spent more than $11 million developing, and replaces the property's former Longevity Hub by Clinique La Prairie. Minor Chief Commercial Officer Ian Di Tullio said the brand was designed from the start to work independently of Anantara, giving Minor the freedom to place it in its own luxury properties or someone else's. Minor still owns or leases almost 70% of its portfolio under what it calls an asset-right strategy, and Di Tullio said that lets the company fund a concept itself, test the economics, and then approach third-party owners. He named three formats for the brand: a resort retreat, an urban hub, and eventually a residence. Di Tullio declined to say whether Marriott approved the concept under its brand standards or shares in revenue, citing confidentiality. Marriott did not immediately respond to Skift's request for comment.

#6128. Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways Sale: Save Up To 50% On Award Flights

Alaska Atmos Rewards offers the Global Getaways promotion, whereby members can save on award tickets in select regions. Atmos Rewards launches this promotion on the first Wednesday of each month (which the program calls “Atmos Members Day”), so we just saw the one for November launched.

Let’s go over the opportunities, as you can save up to 50% on award tickets. There are some cool markets in which you can save miles, though unfortunately only economy travel qualifies.

For the new Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways promotion, you can save up to 50% on award travel to nine destinations, with the following restrictions:

The theme for this Global Getaways promotion is “lights, camera, departure,” with the idea being to “roll out the red carpet for the destinations that have starred in your favorite films and shows.” With this sale, you can save on one-way redemptions to the following destinations (these savings are up to 50%, but not always that high):

I very much appreciate Alaska Atmos Rewards’ creativity with this promotion, as nowadays it’s pretty rare to see programs offer award sales that are also valid for travel on partner airlines. Now, admittedly I wish there weren’t quite as many restrictions in terms of the booking window, travel period, the class of service limitations, and the one-way discount, but still, there will be value here for some, and it’s better than nothing.

If you’re simply looking for the lowest cost award, some of these award prices are very tough to beat. For example, getting from the mainland to Hawaii for 11,500 points is a great deal, as is getting from the United States to India for 30,000 points. Keep in mind that with Atmos Rewards, award flights even earn status points, so could help you qualify for status.

I do hope that over time we see some first and business class award sales as well (it’s probably not happening, but we can dream, right?). Many of us have historically loved the program for the value it offers for premium cabin travel, so this promotion doesn’t help us much with that.

This is basically Alaska’s version of Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards or Singapore KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes, except it applies for travel on partner airlines (rather than just for travel on the program’s airline), and is exclusive to economy (while the other promotions are mixed).

Alaska Atmos Rewards has launched its latest Global Getaways promotion, which is a monthly redemption deal offering up to a 50% discount on awards. This time around, you can save points on economy redemptions to select destinations. You need to book by November 7, 2026, mostly for travel in early 2027. While this won’t be useful for everyone, I imagine some people will get value from this.

#6125. Amex Gold Card Review: Benefits & Points For Those Who Like To Eat

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse if you spend a lot on food, whether it’s at restaurants or supermarkets (or a combination of both). While the card has a somewhat steep annual fee, the good news is that it offers credits that can largely help offset it. We’re also currently seeing an exceptional welcome offer, making it the ideal time to pick up this card. Anyway, enough of an intro, let’s get into my in-depth Amex Gold Card review.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before I get into my full Amex Gold Card review, let me summarize some of the most important features:

Here are my thoughts on the major pros and cons of the Amex Gold Card:

For someone looking to earn Membership Rewards points, the Amex Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there. To start, let’s take a look at the welcome offer on the card, along with the eligibility requirements and fees. After all, these are important factors people consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $8,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard credit pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each. So if you are eligible for a bonus of 100,000 points, those are worth $1,700, by my valuation.

This is a huge bonus, and on top of that, you have a full six months to complete the minimum spending requirement, which should be easy enough for many people to accomplish, as that translates to roughly $1,333 per month in required spending. Personally I’d only apply for the card if I got a welcome offer of at least 60,000 points (or ideally 80,000 points), but everyone has to decide for themselves what they’re willing to “settle” for.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who have or have had the card, or those who have had the Premier Rewards Gold Card in the past. Furthermore, those who have or have had an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) may also not be eligible for the welcome offer on the card.

However, if you have had one of these cards before, you’re still eligible for the card, but you’re just not eligible for the welcome offer (which is “once in a lifetime”). In some circumstances, it could still be worth getting the card in those situations, if you’d benefit from it on an ongoing basis.

Let me emphasize that you’ll want to apply for the Amex Gold before you apply for the Amex Platinum. That’s because if you have the Amex Gold, you’re still eligible for the Amex Platinum offer, while the inverse isn’t true.

See this post for all the rules on applying for Amex cards, and see this post for details on getting approved for the Amex Gold Card.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee. There is no annual fee for up to five additional cards. Meanwhile, the annual fee for six or more additional cards is $35 for each card (Rates & Fees).

Note that Amex Gold Card authorized users don’t receive some of the same benefits as the primary cardmember, but their spending does count toward the rewards that the primary cardmember earns.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally. That’s especially useful when you consider that you can earn 4x points on dining abroad, all with no foreign transaction fees.

What makes the Amex Gold Card so valuable is the bonus categories it offers, in the form of Membership Rewards points. The bonus categories include the following:

This is an outstanding return on spending. Based on my valuation of Amex points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like an 8.5% return on eligible prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights.

Now let’s take a closer look at just how those bonus categories are defined.

The Amex Gold Card offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

With the Amex Gold Card you’ll earn 4x points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year at restaurants worldwide, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar spent.

Generally speaking, restaurants are defined pretty broadly, and the category includes everything from fast food to cafes to fine dining. This even includes delivery and takeout, given the popularity of that nowadays.

Just note that convenience stores, nightclubs, and restaurants located within other establishments won’t typically qualify for bonus points. Furthermore, eligibility for bonus points is determined based on how the merchant chooses to be categorized. There’s a chance that some merchants may not be categorized as a restaurant, even though you might consider them a restaurant.

For dining, this card even beats the 3x points that the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) offer — this is one of the best rewards cards for dining purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 4x points on the first $25,000 spent every calendar year at U.S. supermarkets, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar. This excludes superstores and warehouse clubs, so don’t expect you’ll be able to earn those bonus points at Sam’s Club, for example. This is one of the best rewards cards for grocery store purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 3x points on airfare, with no limits on how many bonus points you can earn. This only applies when booking directly with an airline, through the Amex Travel App™ or through amextravel.com. Furthermore, charter flights and private jet flights are excluded.

Officially, booking through online travel agencies (except Amex Travel) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice, it may still sometimes code for 3x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them. This is one of the best rewards cards for airfare purchases.

The Amex Gold Card also offers 2x points on prepaid car rentals and cruises booked through Amex Travel. This bonus category doesn’t make or break the card, but it’s a nice extra, especially if you already make these bookings occasionally.

The Amex Gold Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to about 20 partners, consisting primarily of airline loyalty programs, but also of some hotel loyalty programs.

The reason this represents such a good deal is that you can get outsized value toward first and business class travel. These tickets are often disproportionately expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal on points. On top of that, Amex often has transfer bonuses, which can stretch your points even further.

While you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than 1.0 cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

In general, I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Gold Card offers a variety of benefits that can help offset the annual fee of the card. In particular, the Amex Gold offers statement credits for eligible purchases, which could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee. Let’s take a closer look at how these work (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The first perk is that the Amex Gold Card offers a dining credit of up to $120 per year. There are some restrictions to be aware of with this credit:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

This is a fantastic benefit and should be worth face value for anyone who uses Uber at least once a month. Even if you don’t use Uber, this can be useful for getting food delivery through Uber Eats.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

One thing I’d mention is that anecdotally this also works for Dunkin’ reloads, so you can always get the Dunkin’ app, and then load $7 onto your account each month, and that should trigger the credit. That’s a great way to use this to “bank” credit with Dunkin’ toward a future purchase.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards. Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year — just note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection. Benefits include a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade, if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum Card.

Holding the Amex Gold Card entitles you to a complimentary upgrade to Hertz Five Star status (enrollment required). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals. If you already rent cars through Hertz, this is a nice extra. It’s one of the more recently added benefits on the Amex Gold Card, too, since it was introduced in celebration of the card’s 60th anniversary.

The Amex Gold Card comes with a handful of travel insurance benefits that can protect your trip when you pay with your card. Check the card’s benefits guide for exact exclusions and limits, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Gold Card is a great card for anyone who spends a lot of money on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets), and who is looking to earn Membership Rewards points. Furthermore, the card potentially offers over $400 in annual credits, between the dining credit, Resy credit, Dunkin’ credit, and Uber Cash.

I’d argue that if you value earning Membership Rewards points, if you spend a lot on dining, and if you can use a decent number of the card’s credits, then picking up this card is a slam dunk. It’s hard to beat this kind of return on dining and supermarket spending, and it’s a great complement to some other Amex cards.

The great welcome offer that’s available is the icing on the cake, and makes applying for the card all the more tempting. I’d recommend confirming you’re eligible for a welcome bonus on the higher end of the spectrum with the current offer of as high as 100,000 points, especially because you can only get an Amex Gold Card welcome bonus once.

I will say, the Amex Gold Card might not be for you if you don’t spend a lot on dining, if you don’t live in a major city where you can easily use the credits, if you value airport lounge access as a card perk, or if you’d rather earn cash back than travel rewards, since those are all potential considerations with the card.

It’s also worth comparing the Amex Gold Card to other options. Here’s how the Amex Gold Card stacks up against some of the most popular alternatives.

The Amex Platinum Card (learn more) has a higher annual fee than the Amex Gold and comes with many more perks and annual credits. Here are the biggest differences to know about:

If you travel many times a year and want as many benefits as possible, the Amex Platinum Card is hard to beat. That said, the Amex Gold Card still offers a better return on spending when it comes to dining out and shopping at U.S. supermarkets. As I see it, the cards serve different purposes — one is about the perks, and the other is about the return on spending.

If you’re looking for a rewards card with a lower annual fee, the Chase Sapphire Preferred Card (learn more) is worth comparing against the Amex Gold Card as well. It has a much lower annual fee of $95 and fewer perks, but it still earns very strong rewards:

Between the Amex Gold Card and the Chase Sapphire Preferred, the best option for you could come down to whether you prefer Amex Membership Rewards points or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Make sure to compare your welcome bonus offers between both cards before making a final decision as well.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) is another great rewards card with useful bonus categories at the $95 annual fee level:

If you want just one rewards card in your wallet, the Citi Strata Premier makes a strong case for itself with its bonus categories. I value both Amex points and Citi ThankYou points at 1.7 cents apiece, but some travelers might prefer one rewards program over the other depending on their favorite airline and hotel partners.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is one of my favorite cards for those looking for a simple strategy, and who don’t want to focus on a bunch of credits, maximizing bonus categories, etc.

The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers a minimum of 2x miles per dollar spent, making this one of the best cards for everyday spending. The reasonable annual fee plus the flat 2x miles is ideal for someone who doesn’t maybe spend a huge amount in categories that are otherwise eligible for bonus points.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points. With 4x points on dining and supermarkets, earning Membership Rewards points is easy.

The card also offers some credits that are potentially useful, which for many will help offset the annual fee. The card offers up to $120 dining credits, up to $120 in Uber Cash annually, up to $100 in Resy credits annually, and up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually — a total of $424 in annual credits if you take advantage of all of them. If you don’t yet have the card, it’s seriously worth considering.

If you want to learn more about the Amex Gold Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: American Express® Gold Card (Rates & Fees), and American Express Platinum Card® (Rates & Fees).

At face value it sound like not a bad deal, but when you get into the details, it is a typical Amex limitation of how to use the credits. $120 dining divided monthly and need to be done via a certain platform for example or $100 hotel credit through their platform that is usually more expensive than direct and requires a two night stay, etc. One of biggest points is that the memebership points is not worldwide. #6123. KLM to Cut Workforce by Nearly 15% in Major Cost-Saving Drive

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: A KLM Boeing 737 at Amsterdam Schiphol Airport. KLM/Capital Photo

Despite improving profits, the Dutch airline says its future is far from guaranteed, with big changes needed to bring costs under control and restore competitiveness.

KLM is preparing to shrink its workforce by almost 15% as part of a major restructuring aimed at cutting costs and improving its long-term competitiveness.

The Dutch flag carrier announced the measures on Thursday alongside parent company Air France-KLM's third-quarter earnings. Around 5,000 positions have already been or will be affected, with jobs eliminated, outsourced or transferred within the wider airline group.

The overhaul aims to deliver an additional €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in annual earnings improvements, bringing the total targeted improvement to €1.4 billion.

Speaking on Thursday, Marjan Rintel, KLM's CEO, delivered a stark message about the need for change: "KLM's future is not guaranteed… That's why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we're taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute."

Tags: air france-klm, airlines, earnings, jet stream, klm

Skift provides the insights. You make the decisions.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

KLM will cut, outsource, or transfer about 5,000 positions — close to 15% of its workforce — in a restructuring announced Thursday alongside Air France-KLM's third-quarter results. The plan targets an additional €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in annual earnings improvements, lifting the total goal to €1.4 billion. Roughly 1,250 catering jobs have already moved to Gategroup, 800 ground services roles are expected to go to third-party providers at Schiphol and for KLM Cityhopper, and 2,000 positions, including 1,500 at contact center Cygnific, will transfer to parent Air France-KLM. Another 1,000 reductions are planned through productivity gains, and KLM is seeking union agreements covering at least an 8% productivity improvement by 2028 and restrained wage growth. The fleet is being resized too: A321neos stay, Embraer E195-E2s replace previously planned A320s, and older 737s and E190s will be phased out, giving Cityhopper a bigger role in Europe. The cuts come despite improving numbers — KLM's third-quarter operating profit rose €106 million to €458 million, and group operating profit hit €1.35 billion, sending shares up about 12% — with CEO Marjan Rintel saying the cost base remains too high and that "KLM's future is not guaranteed."

#6122. ENDING SOON: 100,000 Points Plus A Companion Award—Why Alaska’s Best Credit Card Beats Those From Bigger Airlines

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is probably the best airline cobrand credit card, and it has a limited-time offer – 100,000 bonus points. Get 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award with this offer. To qualify, spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account. The annual fee is $395.

The offer gives you two different things. The 100,000 bonus points and the 25,000 point Global Companion Award that reduces the points needed for a second passenger’s award ticket.

I think the strongest reasons to consider it are the annual companion award and earning 3 points per dollar on eligible foreign purchases. Alaska has also put a substantial reward at $60,000 in annual spending.

Each account anniversary brings another 25,000-point Global Companion Award, with no annual spending requirement. Spending $60,000 in your card anniversary year earns a separate 100,000 point Global Companion Award. You can earn both. These work on eligible Alaska, Hawaiian and partner awards available through Alaska’s website, in any cabin. Suppose an award costs 35,000 points per passenger. Two tickets would normally require 70,000 points. Applying a 25,000-point certificate brings that down to 45,000 points, plus applicable taxes and fees. If each ticket costs 100,000 points apiece, the larger certificate brings the combined price down from 200,000 to 100,000 points, plus taxes and fees. Things to know: Book both travelers together on the same itinerary. The certificate applies to a new booking, not an existing reservation. You can use it for one-way or roundtrip travel. Multi-city and open-jaw itineraries are excluded. If the companion’s ticket costs more than the certificate covers, pay the difference in points. If it costs less, you lose the unused value. Book within one year of issuance. Travel can take place later, but changes after certificate expiration forfeit the discount. Partially used tickets can’t be changed. Only one certificate can be applied per reservation, and it can’t be combined with another discount. Pay taxes, fees and surcharges with the Summit card. The cardholder doesn’t need to travel – you can book for any two travelers. You still need award space for two. Using all 25,000 points of the anniversary certificate would cover the $395 fee if those saved points are worth 1.58 cents each to you. At 1.5 cents, it’s $375. That’s close enough that using another benefit can put you ahead. But don’t give the certificate full value if you’d otherwise let it expire or use it to save only 10,000 points. Foreign Purchases Are The Standout Earning Category The card earns: 3 points per dollar on eligible dining, foreign transactions, and Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. 1 point per dollar on other purchases. A 10% relationship bonus on purchase points when you have a qualifying Bank of America or Merrill account. That makes the rates 3.3 and 1.1 points per dollar. Dining and airline bonuses are something offered by numerous cards. Getting a bonus on eligible shopping and other purchases abroad that wouldn’t ordinarily fall into a bonus category is much more interesting. (Generally Chase buys points at a discount from its cobrand partners on foreign transactions, effectively subsidized by the program, making it uneconomic to offer something like this.) The relationship bonus triggers with qualifying checking accounts, consumer savings and certificates of deposit, as well as Merrill investment accounts. A new account can take up to 60 days to trigger the bonus. The Card Can Save Money On American Award Tickets Atmos charges a $20 partner award booking fee per person, each way. Summit waives it when you redeem points from the primary cardholder’s account and pay the award’s taxes and fees with that card. The primary cardholder doesn’t have to be traveling. That saves $80 on a roundtrip partner award for two. Five such bookings would save $400, more than the annual fee, without assigning any value to the companion award or lounge passes. This is a fee Alaska imposes and then lets its premium cardholders avoid. I’d prefer they didn’t charge it in the first place. But if you’re booking these awards anyway, the savings are great. Free points sharing helps, too. The primary cardholder can establish a network with up to ten other Atmos members and move redeemable points between linked accounts without a transfer fee. Each member can belong to only one network, and the primary cardholder can change each linked account only once every 12 months. Status points can’t be transferred. Being able to combine balances is useful when several family members have points but no one has enough for the award you want. Lounge Access, Bags And Travel Benefits The card’s travel benefits include: Eight Alaska Lounge passes annually, issued two per calendar quarter. They expire at the end of that quarter. Each covers one adult and up to two accompanying children under 21, with access to Alaska Lounges for the travel day. You need an eligible same-day boarding pass, and access is subject to capacity. These don’t admit you to Hawaiian’s lounges or partner lounges. Eight Alaska Wi-Fi passes annually, also two per quarter. Each is for one flight, and unused passes expire at quarter-end. A first checked bag free and preferred boarding for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights, when airfare is purchased with the card. Include the primary cardholder’s Atmos number. 20% back on eligible onboard purchases. This is for Alaska food, beverages and Wi-Fi, and Hawaiian food and beverages, when paid with the card. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years when charged to the card. Complimentary upgrade waitlist priority for eligible elite members. A same-day confirmed change fee waiver. Alaska’s benefits page includes eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights. Saver fares are excluded, and routing and same day travel restrictions apply. For a family of two adults and two children under 21, two lounge passes can cover everyone for a travel day. There’s also a $50 delay voucher. For an eligible Alaska booking purchased directly with the Summit card, a departure delay of at least two hours or a cancellation within 24 hours of departure can qualify. It’s for the primary cardholder, limited to one per calendar day, and expires 48 hours after issuance. Activation instructions arrive by email, and eligible spending is reimbursed as a statement credit. There’s also trip and baggage delay coverage, trip cancellation and interruption protection, and lost luggage reimbursement. along with primary rental car collision coverage. The $60,000 Spend Strategy Summit earns one status point per $2 in purchases, plus 10,000 status points each account anniversary beginning with your first anniversary. Atmos Gold requires 40,000 status points and comes with oneworld Sapphire. So $60,000 of spending produces 30,000 status points. An anniversary deposit of 10,000 in the same qualification year gets you to Gold which is oneworld sapphire. Status qualification runs by calendar year. The $60,000 companion award threshold runs by card anniversary year. Spending split between two calendar years can earn the certificate without producing Gold in either year. And a new cardholder doesn’t receive the anniversary status points immediately upon opening the account. Suppose you put $60,000 of purchases that earn the base rate on Summit. With the relationship bonus, you’d earn 66,000 redeemable points and the 100,000-point companion certificate. A card earning 2 points per dollar would generate 120,000 points on that same spending. You’re giving up 54,000 points in the alternative program in exchange for the certificate and the status credit. That can definitely be worth it even aside from the status. #6121. Defiant Ritz-Carlton Singapore Joining Marriott Bonvoy… Finally!

The world’s only Ritz-Carlton that doesn’t participate in the Marriott Bonvoy program will finally be joining, which seems long overdue. I can’t imagine the hotel will be particularly generous, but we’ll see!

The 608-key Ritz-Carlton Millenia Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program as of December 1, 2026. So as of that date, Bonvoy members will be able to earn and redeem points, and take advantage of Bonvoy elite perks, when staying at the hotel (admittedly Bonvoy elite perks at Ritz-Carlton properties are fairly limited, as breakfast isn’t a benefit for any elite tier).

As I covered in late 2025, this property is the only Ritz-Carlton in the world that doesn’t participate in the Bonvoy program. The backstory here is that the hotel opened back in 1996, and at the time, Ritz-Carlton didn’t have any sort of a loyalty program that awarded points.

In 2010, the Ritz-Carlton Rewards program started awarding points for hotel stays, as a parallel program to Marriott Rewards. The ability to earn and redeem points came at a cost to individual hotels, but it was intended to boost occupancy and average daily rates.

Initially, hotels had the option of whether they wanted to opt in or out of the program. Most hotels bought into the concept, though the Ritz-Carlton Osaka and Ritz-Carlton Singapore were the two hotels that opted out. The Ritz-Carlton Osaka eventually decided to participate, leaving the Ritz-Carlton Singapore as the only hotel that’s not participating.

Ultimately when the Marriott Bonvoy program formed as the combination of Marriott Rewards and Starwood Preferred Guest, the hotel could still stick to its legacy contract of not having to participate in the program. Clearly the owners of the hotel have now had a change of heart… or something!

Obviously we don’t have any sort of an official explanation for the reason that this Ritz-Carlton property is finally backtracking. I can’t imagine that Marriott gave the owners an ultimatum, given that Marriott is known for letting hotel owners get away with anything, as long as they get paid.

My guess is that the competitive realities just finally caught up with this hotel — Singapore is an increasingly competitive hotel market, this is a massive hotel with 600+ rooms to fill every night, and the hotel is also a bit past its prime.

The truth is that loyalty programs exist for a reason, as they’re a great tool for getting heads into beds. Obviously the hotel will be on the hook for some additional loyalty fees, but I imagine this will make the hotel more appealing to people who otherwise wouldn’t have considered it.

I also have to imagine that even though the hotel did a decent job communicating its lack of participation in Marriott Bonvoy, I still suspect many guests didn’t realize this, and ended up being disappointed.

As of December 1, 2026, the Ritz-Carlton Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program. This is the only Ritz-Carlton hotel in the world that hasn’t participated in Bonvoy, so this is great to see.

The backstory is that the hotel opened before Ritz-Carlton had a loyalty program, and then when a program was finally formed, participation was optional. Literally every other Ritz-Carlton in the world saw value in this… except this one, apparently.

Fortunately they’ve now come to their senses, or something, so it’s great to see that this will be changing.

What do you make of the Ritz-Carlton Singapore joining Bonvoy?

#6120. Fuel Hedges Kept Emirates Profitable as Earnings Fell Two-Thirds

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: An Emirates Airbus A380-800. Vincenzo Pace / Vincenzo Pace

Fuel hedges turned a likely loss into a profit for Emirates. The war’s full cost will show only once that cover runs out.

Emirates airline’s first-half net profit fell 66% to AED 3.3 billion ($899 million), with the result resting on AED 7.1 billion ($1.93 billion) in fuel hedging-derived gains. At open-market fuel prices, the airline would have lost money after the U.S.-Iran war closed regional airspace and caused jet fuel costs to soar.

The Dubai-based carrier’s revenue fell 13% to AED 56.9 billion ($15.5 billion) in the half, despite what it described as strong cargo performance and enduring travel demand across its markets.

“It has been a demanding six months,” Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum, chairman and CEO, said in a statement on Thursday, citing “unprecedented regional challenges and high fuel prices.”

The first six months of fiscal 2026–27, to end-September, posed significant challenges to its operations due to air

Emirates posted a 66% drop in first-half net profit to AED 3.3 billion ($899 million), and the result rested on AED 7.1 billion ($1.93 billion) in fuel hedging gains. The airline said that without those gains, at open-market fuel prices, it would have lost money after the U.S.-Iran war closed regional airspace and sent jet fuel costs soaring. Revenue fell 13% to AED 56.9 billion ($15.5 billion). Passenger traffic dropped 22% to 21.8 million, capacity fell 17%, and seat factor slipped to 72% from 79.5%, as connecting traffic moved to Istanbul, Singapore, and other hubs. Pre-hedge fuel costs rose 60% year over year; hedging cut the net increase to 13%, with fuel still 34% of operating cost. Cargo was the bright spot: tonnage fell 1% but revenue rose 52% as conflict squeezed airfreight capacity and shipping disruption pushed volume to air. Emirates kept spending through the downturn, taking nine A350s, refitting 12 aircraft under a $7 billion-plus retrofit program, and adding Starlink to 36 more aircraft. Linus Benjamin Bauer of BAA & Partners said the core flying business was likely loss-making on an unhedged basis and that the second half will show whether the operating model has recovered. Emirates has not disclosed its hedging position for the fiscal second half.
