If you have yet to take a solo trip, there are many reasons why you really should. Solo travel helps you build confidence and new skills. It also provides time to reflect, recharge and reconnect with yourself — so you can return home the best version of yourself for the people who rely on you day-to-day.

I know it can be daunting to embark on your first big trip alone. But never fear, intrepid soloist. I've rounded up the top solo travel mistakes so that you can avoid them to ensure your trip goes smoothly.

Related: Travel mistakes that could ruin your next trip

One of the perks of solo travel is that you get to decide where to stay and what to do, so put some thought into it. This will ensure you have the best trip possible.

A good starting point is to check the State Department travel advisory for your destination, which will help you understand any safety concerns and identify neighborhoods you may want to avoid. It's also a good idea to enroll your trip in STEP, so you'll be alerted to things like natural disasters and security threats.

Safety isn't the only thing to consider. Are you looking for a quiet, relaxing getaway or a bustling neighborhood with endless things to do? Would you rather stay close to the action or save money by staying in a less popular area? Choose your accommodations accordingly.

Don't make the mistake I made on my first solo trip and not plan any activities. Spontaneity sounded fun, but I found making decisions on my own much harder than expected. You don't need to have your entire itinerary planned out to the minute, but doing some planning before you travel will reduce your stress during the trip.

Plus, many popular tourist attractions and trendy restaurants fill up quickly — and waiting in long lines is even less fun with no one to talk to. Do your research, and if needed, make a reservation or book a timed-entry ticket ahead of time.

Sometimes, the difference between traveling solo and with others really shines through in the little things...like using an airport bathroom.

You can't simply ask a companion to hold your luggage while you run to the restroom or figure out how to operate a metro ticket machine; you must keep track of it at all times. So think twice about packing that extra-large checked bag or hauling a not-so-ergonomic shoulder duffel on an international trip, as you will have to take it with you literally everywhere.

I personally prefer a backpack and small rolling carryon, which I can easily maneuver through crowded airports and over cobblestoned streets — without reaching my destination with a backache. Plus, it's big enough to accommodate sufficient clothing for a week (or more). My carryon is expandable, so if I buy too many souvenirs, I can unzip the extender and check it on the way home.

Related: How to pack your carryon right and avoid checking a bag

Connecting with new people is one of the many joys of solo travel, but that doesn't mean you should completely let your guard down. You may run into pickpockets, con artists and worse on your journey, and as a solo traveler, you're more likely to be targeted.

One simple step to reduce your risk is by not broadcasting your solo status. Err on the side of caution when chatting with new friends — and if they start getting nosy, tell them you're meeting up with friends later.

One way to prevent hotel staff from knowing your single status is opting for mobile check-in so that you can bypass the front desk completely. Or, you can ask the concierge for an extra key and allude that someone will be joining you shortly. And when catching a ride to or from your accommodation, it's a good idea to be picked up or dropped off down the street from your hotel.

Related: Solo travel safety tips every traveler should know

You only want to be incognito to the locals.

Let your actual friends and family know your travel plans: flight numbers, where you'll be staying on which dates, contact info for your tour operator, etc. You'll be glad you did if you hit a snag and need help rebooking on the fly. You can go a step further by sending them a copy of your passport or ID, in case you lose your documents while traveling.

You'll probably want to stay in contact with loved ones through text messages, phone calls or social media posts every so often. But you can also share your location continuously with apps like Find My, which can help ease their minds as well as give you an added layer of security. That way, both you and your loved ones can enjoy your trip stress-free.

Some things are must-haves no matter how many people you're traveling with, but they become even more critical when you're on your own — because if you forget something, you can't just reach into a companion's suitcase.

For instance, do you have a backup plan in case your phone dies while you're navigating a new city or road-tripping through an unfamiliar country? You can't simply borrow someone else's phone, so a charged power bank or old-fashioned map can come in clutch.

The same goes if you wind up at a store that doesn't accept your credit card. Always pack a couple of backup cards (preferably ones that don't charge foreign transaction fees) and keep some cash on hand.

Similarly, if you catch a cold on your flight or get food poisoning during a solo trip, there's no one else to run to a drugstore. And if you hurt yourself while out hiking alone, it may take a while for help to arrive. Prepare yourself for anything with a travel-ready first-aid kit.

Related: Travel essentials that can save your trip when things go wrong

One of the downsides of solo travel is that it can start to feel lonely, especially on longer trips. Making new friends is a great way to combat loneliness, as well as learn more about local culture and/or meet likeminded travelers.

If striking up a conversation with a stranger sounds more stressful than fun, you're not alone. Thankfully, there are plenty of ways for even the shyest travelers to make connections, including cruises and small-group tours designed specifically for solo travelers.

Female Travel Buddies is one of many Facebook groups ideal for those flying solo: Members post open invitations for fellow travelers in the same area to join you for brunch, sightseeing or a show. If this type of thing interests you, consider joining a handful of groups a few months ahead of your trip to get familiar with the members and learn how they work.

Related: 6 tips for meeting people when traveling solo

Just because you're traveling alone doesn't mean you can't take photos along the way — but capturing memories can be trickier by yourself.

The good news is you don't have to be limited by the length of your arm. Be sure to pack a selfie stick, mini tripod with remote shutter or selfie monitor screen. You'll find it well worth the investment, as having the right tools will make it far easier to snap the perfect selfie. (Just remember: safety first, especially when hiking, taking selfies near cliff edges, etc.!)

If, like me, you feel a little awkward or uncomfortable taking selfies alone, the best advice I can give you is to do it anyway. The more you do it, the more comfortable you'll get and the better your photos will turn out.

Solo travel doesn't have to be daunting. Follow these tips to embark on your first solo trip with confidence and ensure it goes smoothly, and before you know it, you'll be a seasoned solo traveler.

#6117. American Airlines Quietly Removes Trump From West Palm Beach Gate Monitors

American Airlines has updated the gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach, and they no longer mention President Trump. This seems like a sensible change (unrelated to politics), and the timing sure is… interesting.

Over the summer, we saw Palm Beach International Airport (PBI) renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport. We knew that Trump wanted an airport named after him, and some conservative politicians in Florida came together to make it happen.

It’s interesting to see how airlines handled this. At the time, American updated its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The monitors initially read “West Palm Beach, FL.” American then updated the monitors to say “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach.” Now JonNYC reports that as of this week, the airport name listed on the monitors has been changed again, and is back to the original name, with no mention of Trump.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ? https://t.co/IG2mPA3zgG

JonNYC specifically emphasizes that he’s not claiming there’s any connection between this and the election results, though the timing of it happening this week sure is interesting.

Personally I’m not a fan of airports being named after even semi-controversial figures, and particularly politicians. It’s something I’ve said over and over, regardless of the party affiliation of the person. Unless a city has multiple airports, I think it’s also stupid to identify the airport based on the name rather than the place.

Like, it makes sense to clarify London Heathrow (LHR) vs. London Gatwick (LGW), but it’s not like there are multiple airports in West Palm Beach. For that matter, saying you’re “flying to President Trump” just sounds a little weird, in my opinion.

JonNYC notes that he’s not suggesting that this had anything to do with the recent election, though everything about the timing here is interesting:

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom: "From a commercial aviation perspective, the eyes of the world have been on us, and we've certainly delivered… No doubt, it's a result of the economy and the job market." https://t.co/28JzoEf4Z3 pic.twitter.com/BcgYJbChNz

American Airlines seems to have quietly reversed course on how it refers to West Palm Beach’s airport on its gate monitors. In recent months, the airline has referred to the airport as “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach,” while now it seems to be back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

This change comes the same week as the midterm elections, though everyone can decide for themselves to what extent these points are related…

What do you make of this American gate monitor change?

#6116. Southwest Airlines Now Runs Late Nearly A Third Of The Time

Southwest Airlines was late nearly a third of the time in October, and its cancellation rate was more than twice Delta’s. It finished last for punctuality among the ten North American airlines in aviation analytics company Cirium’s new monthly report, while Delta led on both. For the past two months, I’ve pointed out that Southwest’s poor on-time rankings were offset by canceling fewer flights than anyone else. They weren’t on-time but they reliably got passengers to their destinations. In October, though, Delta, United and even Frontier cancelled a smaller share of flights than Southwest. Here are Cirium’s North American results. On-time means arriving at the gate within 15 minutes of schedule. Airline   September On-Time   October On-Time   October Canceled Delta   82.52%   86.86%   0.24% United   78.65%   84.06%   0.31% WestJet   85.31%   83.56%   0.90% JetBlue   74.64%   82.27%   0.57% Alaska   80.73%   81.06%   1.10% American   77.11%   80.10%   0.63% Allegiant   Not listed   77.89%   1.13% Frontier   75.49%   77.62%   0.38% Air Canada   73.19%   75.74%   2.80% Southwest   71.14%   68.90%   0.51% Southwest’s Fixes Extend Into January Southwest’s on-time performance fell 2.24 percentage points from September. Every other U.S. airline improved. And Southwest was nearly seven points behind even Air Canada, the next airline up the list. They’re also way down from last October when they were 75.5% on time versus 68.9% this year. Delta improved year-over-year from 84.5% to 86.9%. Southwest’s cancellation rate increased from 0.38% to 0.51%. That’s still only about five cancellations per thousand flights, but Delta was at 2.4 per thousand and United at 3.1. There was no longer a cancellation advantage in October to offset the Dallas-based carrier’s greater likelihood of arriving late. Management knows there’s a problem. On the October 22 earnings call, chief operating officer Andrew Watterson said the weakness was concentrated in delays between roughly 15 and 45 minutes. He described the airline consistently starting aircraft turnarounds well, then losing time at the end. Changes to gate checking bags and closing flights are supposed to begin in November. Southwest gate checks a lot more bags now that passengers want to carry more belongings onboard, since checked bags have a fee. Agents will finally be able to close flights using an iPad at the aircraft. And adjusted schedules begin in January. Fast turns let Southwest get more flying out of each airplane. But those savings shrink when those produces delays, and CEO Bob Jordan acknowledged that poor punctuality is adding to costs including from misconnecting passengers. Delta Leads, United Closes In, And JetBlue Recovers Delta took first place from WestJet, ending the Canadian airline’s five-month run at the top of North America. Delta also ranked third on Cirium’s global list. Their cancellation rate has fallen from 1.77% in August to 0.92% in September and 0.24% in October. That’s real improvement compared to their abysmal summer operation. United is getting improving, too. Delta’s punctuality lead over United narrowed from 3.87 percentage points to 2.80. Delta canceled less often this time, but the difference was just 0.07 percentage points or seven flights per 10,000 scheduled. I wouldn’t pay much extra for Delta over United based on that operational gap. Against Southwest, Delta was nearly 18 percentage points more likely to arrive within the on-time window. American improved, too, but fell further behind both of its major competitors. Delta’s lead over American widened from 5.41 to 6.76 points. United’s lead widened from 1.54 to 3.96 points. American’s better month left them sixth in North America. And JetBlue went from 63.85% on time in August to 74.64% in September and 82.27% in October. Their 7.63-point gain was the largest of any North American airline. JetBlue finished ahead of both Alaska and American on punctuality, and canceled less often than either. Their cancellation rate fell from 5.09% in August to 0.57% in October. Even Newark Made The On-Time Airports List The airport report measures on-time departures, rather than arrivals. Six U.S. airports made Cirium’s top 20 large airports worldwide, up from just two in September: Minneapolis–St. Paul: 87.00%, eighth Washington Dulles: 86.25%, eleventh Detroit: 86.13%, twelfth Salt Lake City: 85.69%, thirteenth Newark: 85.64%, fourteenth Atlanta: 85.17%, eighteenth Four are Delta hubs. The other two are United hubs. No American hub made the list. This is partly another view of the airlines themselves, since a hub’s results depend heavily on its dominant carrier. I never expect to see Newark doing well! And this data can be useful to some degree in choosing between otherwise similar connecting options, although can also be seasonal due to weather. #6115. KLM Plans 15% Workforce Reduction And Simpler Fleet: “Future Not Guaranteed”

It’s obviously a tough time for aviation in general, given the impact of high jet fuel prices. For that matter, Dutch national carrier KLM has faced its own unique challenges, given increasing limits placed on the carrier’s Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS) hub, plus all the competitive challenges (increased competition from regional low cost carriers, Gulf carriers, etc.).

In recent years, we’ve seen KLM introduce initiatives intended to improve economics. The airline is now taking that to the next level, and has just announced an absolutely massive project intended to improve economics by €1 billion per year.

KLM has unveiled the details of a project that it expects will contribute to annual earnings improvements of €1 billion per year, which it hopes will allow the company to invest in fleet, customer experience, and people.

KLM’s plan is to focus on its core strengths, which it describes as a global network of 160 destinations served nonstop from Schiphol, and reliable operations supported by a modern fleet. The company wants to become a smaller, simpler, and more agile organization, through restructuring, outsourcing, and closer collaboration with Air France-KLM.

Here’s how KLM CEO Marjan Rintel describes this initiative:

“Every day, we all work with incredible dedication, commitment, and pride. But KLM’s future is not guaranteed. The environment we operate in is becoming increasingly complex, with global instability, high fuel prices, and growing pressure on the aviation industry. That’s why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we’re taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute.”

“We’re doing this with a clear vision for the future: one where KLM remains a great airline that connects customers to the world, a company people want to work for, and one the Netherlands can be proud of.”

How does KLM plan on improving economics by so much over the coming years? For one, the airline will simplify its fleet.

The long term plan is to have a fleet of 185 Airbus, Boeing, and Embraer aircraft. The latest changes particularly center around the European network, where just about all network carriers in Europe struggle to make money, given the costs and competitive landscape.

KLM plans to change the balance between larger and smaller aircraft on European routes. In the long run, the airline will fly a mix of 227-seat Airbus A321neos and 132-seat Embraer E195-E2s. The company no longer plans to acquire Airbus A320neos, which were part of a larger Air France-KLM order, as those planes are instead going to Transavia. Furthermore, in the coming years, we’ll see Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s retired.

Next, the airline hopes to achieve greater flexibility, higher productive, and lower costs, with its labor agreements. As you’d expect, this will be the most painful change. For one, KLM plans to reduce its workforce by around 15%, meaning that around 5,000 positions will be “reorganized.”

This follows the company’s number of staff already declining in recent years. The good news is that there aren’t expected to be mass layoffs — KLM expects to limit the impact on employees through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements, and transfers to other positions.

The airline also emphasizes that employment terms and conditions need to become simpler and more competitive, noting that “continuing on the current path is not sustainable.” KLM wants to work with unions to establish new collective labor agreements, and the company aims to achieve a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028.

This decrease in headcount will come through a combination of Air France and KLM cooperating more closely, outsourcing catering and maintenance, and reducing planned growth of the fleet.

The airline industry is tough in the first place, and among the major network carriers, KLM is perhaps in the toughest spot, when you consider the overall industry dynamics:

KLM is planning to majorly cut costs and simplify things, which is probably necessary in light of how the situation has evolved.

As part of this, the carrier’s short haul fleet will eventually consist of just Airbus A321neos and Embraer E195-E2s. On top of that, we’ll see the airline reduce its workforce by around 15%, through a combination of increasing efficiency, outsourcing jobs, and more. The company will also be looking for some concessions from existing employees.

In total, the company hopes that these changes will contribute €1 billion per year. While aviation is tough across the board, it’s especially tough to be KLM, where you’re reliant on one hub (which regulators keep trying to shrink) with very high costs, and that hub isn’t a market that’s as lucrative as somewhere like London, Paris, etc. I’m a fan of KLM, and I hope these changes don’t do too much to change the quirky spirit of the airline.

What do you make of these major KLM changes?

Tripadvisor said Thursday that CEO Matt Goldberg and the board agreed to his departure, effective February 16, and that Chief Financial Officer Michael Noonan resigned to pursue another opportunity. The exits come 16 months after Starboard Value took a 9% stake in Tripadvisor and eight months after the activist investor won four of 10 board seats. That campaign has coincided with Chairman Greg Maffei's exit, a 20% workforce cut, and the $700 million sale of TheFork to American Express. Tripadvisor did not announce a CEO search process, and the company has said no option is off the table for monetizing Viator, its experiences booking business, and its non-core hotel metasearch business. Kristen Dalton, chief strategy and operations officer, becomes interim CFO on January 1, 2027, after Noonan stays through December 31, 2026. The leadership vacancy arrives as the board entertains strategic alternatives, which leaves the structure of the company — and the ownership of Viator — unresolved.

#6112. Emirates Profits Plunge Due To War… But The Airline Still Made Money?!

It goes without saying that it has been a tough year for airlines, due to the United States getting into a war with Iran. All airlines have been dealing with higher jet fuel prices, but airlines in the Gulf region have of course been dealing with additional issues, as all kinds of airports in the region have been attacked, making some people reconsider traveling through the region.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note that Emirates has just released its financial results for the first half of the fiscal year (April 1 through September 30, 2026). Yes, Emirates’ profits decreased massively, but surprisingly, the airline still turned a healthy profit, and the numbers look much better than I would’ve guessed.

Prior to this year, Emirates was the world’s most profitable airline for two years in a row, as the carrier really is incredibly well run.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note how the airline performed over the first six months of the current fiscal year, which coincides entirely with the current Iran conflict. While there are results for the overall Emirates Group (which also includes dnata, etc.), I’m focusing on the airline specifically, since I find that to be most telling.

Emirates reported a half-year profit of $1 billion, down 68% compared to the previous year. Interestingly, revenue was $15.5 billion, down “only” 13% compared to the same period the previous year. The airline didn’t actually cut back its total capacity that much — available seat kilometers (ASKM) decreased by 17% compared to the previous year, while the passenger load factor decreased to 72%, from 79.5% the previous year. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers over the six months, down 22% from the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, Emirates is operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, with the passenger and cargo network spanning 150 airports in 78 countries. However, that reflects the number of destinations, rather than the total actual capacity (in other words, many destinations are being operated with reduced frequencies).

Emirates CEO Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum reflected on this as “a demanding six months,” and said that “once again our business model and our people stood up to the test.” He explained that the company is entering the second half of the fiscal year “with measured optimism,” “while keeping a close watch on costs and geopolitical developments.”

One would think that Gulf carriers are in the toughest spot of any airline, given that they’ve been so reliant on connecting people traveling between other regions, and at least among some people, their willingness to travel through the region has decreased, assuming it can be avoided.

Admittedly many people also just live in this region, so it’s not like there are endless options. But when you consider all factors, I’d say these are very encouraging results, much better than I would’ve expected.

I know there’s often a lot of skepticism when it comes to the reported financials of Gulf carriers. I do think at some Gulf carriers, there’s reason to be skeptical about the math, based on what is and isn’t reported.

In the case of Emirates, though, the airline is legitimately very profitable and well run. The airline has managed to efficiently scale its operation in a way that no other airline really has, and that’s where credit goes for the carrier’s success.

Of course we have to acknowledge that there’s a difference in underlying economics. Dubai (DXB) is much lower cost to operate out of than somewhere like London Heathrow (LHR) or New York Kennedy (JFK), and Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company. Furthermore, the cost of jet fuel is lower in Dubai than it is in somewhere like London, and I imagine the airline also has access to more attractive financing opportunities, given that it’s owned by the government.

However, that’s hardly anything that’s super hidden or secret. I mean, economics in US aviation are also sort of lopsided. Airline profits are largely reliant on everything except actually flying, which is a privilege and upside that most foreign carriers can’t fully unlock.

I think it’s also interesting to note how well Emirates’ yields have held up during this time. For example, just based on looking at fares through Google Flights, it seems like Etihad’s strategy has just been to publish incredibly low fares to fill seats, including in premium cabins. I haven’t found that to be the case with Emirates, though, as the airline has managed to maintain pricing power despite reduced demand.

Emirates has reported its financial results for the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. As you’d expect, this was a generally tough time for a Gulf carrier, given the current war with Iran. While Emirates’ profits were cut by around two-thirds, the airline still turned a healthy profit of around $1 billion.

Honestly, the actual operating figures don’t at all reflect what you’d expect during a crisis, so it seems like the airline is weathering this story pretty well, all things considered. I do feel like Emirates is uniquely positioned among its competitive set, and I’d be shocked if the story is similar at Etihad or Qatar Airways.

What do you make of Emirates’ financial results?

I've been saying this for many years, but companies earnings whether foreign or domestic are not what they seem. You can have a big 4 accounting firm checking your numbers all you want but it's all just numbers on a computer screen.

Profit was accounted for by their fuel hedges, and the accounting treatment they gave those.

"Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company" - So could airlines based at LHR or JFK ;) It's their own decision to outsource everything. Ultimately, the main benefit EK has is that they're not publicly traded so they can have a long term strategy.

Hot take, but… profits aren’t everything. Like, maybe, safety is more important (missiles and drones still hitting airports in the region). I don’t care if there are ‘deals’ or bonus points, I won’t personally route through DXB, DOH, etc. anytime soon, and I used to, plenty. (UAE, etc. shouldn’t have trusted Trump and Jared…)

#6110. Chase Adds 10,000 Vacation Homes To The Edit In 2027—Use Your Hotel Credits, But No Points Boost

Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) cardmembers will be able to use their hotel credits at more than 10,000 vacation homes starting January 1, 2027. And Chase tells me consecutive bookings at the same home can each trigger a credit, potentially letting someone use the personal card’s full $500 annual allowance on one trip. There’s a significant limitation, though: Points Boost won’t apply to these homes at launch. The Edit name also won’t bring breakfast or upgrades. The home benefits require four nights, while the statement credit only requires two. Two Night Bookings Qualify For Credits, And Back-To-Back Bookings Are Allowed Chase already added Plum Guide to Chase Travel in April. The January expansion moves a selection of those homes into The Edit, alongside more than 1,500 hotels and resorts. The annual Edit statement credits available for bookings made in 2027 is: Chase Sapphire Reserve® and J.P. Morgan Reserve: up to $500, with a maximum of $250 per eligible booking. Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business: up to $1,000, with a maximum of $250 per eligible booking. The business card’s increase to $1,000 was announced in September. And Chase confirms that a prepaid two- or three-night home booking qualifies for the statement credit, even though it receives none of the vacation home benefits because those require a minimum four night stay (and individual properties can impose longer minimum stays). Bookings will be instantly confirmed, and full prepayment is required for The Edit benefits. I also asked whether you could book consecutive reservations at the same property. A Chase spokesperson tells me: Yes. Cardmembers can book back-to-back stays at the same property. Each eligible booking of two or more prepaid nights can qualify for the annual Edit statement credit, subject to the annual credit limit. For on-property benefits, however, consecutive reservations at the same property are considered a single stay, so only the first eligible stay will receive The Edit benefits. Two eligible two-night reservations could use both $250 credits from a personal Reserve card on a single four-night trip, or book a two-night and four-night reservation for a six night trip to use both credits and receive The Edit benefits on the stay. But you only get benefits on one four-night mininum stay. Back-to-back bookings aren’t entitled to benefits twice even if each reservation is for four nights. Chase commits to matching Plum Guide’s pricing. Asked about the identical home, dates and occupancy, the spokesperson replied: Yes. For the same home, dates and occupancy, the total price and cancellation policy offered through Chase Travel will match those available through Plum Guide. The credit shouldn’t get eaten up by a higher price than Plum Guide charges for the same reservation. Chase says it worked with Plum Guide to select homes based on design, guest ratings and distinctive features. Plum Guide does the vetting, not Chase. Chase isn’t sharing representative homes or pricing examples yet, so we can’t compare actual bookings. No Points Boost At Launch I’d hoped putting these homes into The Edit would create better opportunities to redeem Ultimate Rewards points. I asked and was told: No. Points Boost will not be applicable to vacation homes in The Edit at launch. Cardmembers can still redeem points, as they already can for Plum Guide through Chase Travel. But joining The Edit won’t bring better redemption value. This follows American Express adding Airbnb Luxe to its Platinum lodging credit. Eligible prepaid Luxe stays of at least two nights can use up to $300 each half-year, and a qualifying booking opens access to a separate $250 annual Airbnb Experiences credit. Amex doesn’t allow Pay with Points for those Airbnb bookings. Chase does allow points, but without Points Boost that’s not useful. It’s really just a new way to use the $250 statement credits. Four Nights Gets A $150 Credit, But No Breakfast Or Upgrades I asked Chase to confirm exactly which hotel benefits would carry over. At launch in January, the vacation-home benefits will include a $150 in-stay credit, plus early check-in and late checkout when available. Breakfast, room upgrades and welcome amenities are not part of the vacation-home benefit package. The benefits have been designed specifically around the vacation-home experience and how travelers use these properties. I’ve found The Edit credits useful on two-night hotel stays priced below $300 per night, with breakfast and a $100 property credit included. The home package adds $50 to the service credit but requires at least four nights, and drops breakfast and upgrades. Not surprising – there’s little to upgrade into when you’re booking a unit of one. And there’s nobody to make you breakfast! The $150 credit actually sounds better than just private chefs and massages highlighted in the announcement. Here’s what guests can buy and whether they’ll see prices before booking: Cardmembers will be able to see the eligible services available for a vacation home on the Chase Travel booking page before booking. Offerings vary by property and can include services such as fridge stocking, babysitting and dry cleaning. Pricing will depend on the specific service and request and will not be displayed at booking, however cardmembers can work with Reserve Travel Designers to understand available options and obtain pricing estimates for the services they are interested in. Fridge stocking and babysitting are things a family might actually buy. But the booking page won’t show what the credit buys. After booking, guests will receive an email explaining how to use the credit. Reserve Travel Designers can help arrange services, and Chase recommends doing so at least 72 hours in advance. Early check-in and late checkout don’t actually seem like a Chase value add. A hotel has a pool of rooms. A house with guests leaving that morning needs to be cleaned before the next guests arrive. If another group is coming that afternoon, there isn’t much room for a late departure. So late checkout is either available or not, based on whether other reservations butt up against yours. Plum Guide already accommodates early check-in and late check-out requests subject to availability, albeit sometimes with fees. I asked whether Chase would waive those charges, require hosts to grant requests when possible, prioritize cleaning or offer earlier confirmation. Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance. We Don’t Know Yet If We Can Double Dip With Loyalty Credit Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits. What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals). Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though! For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less. Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance. We Don’t Know Yet If We Can Double Dip With Loyalty Credit Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits. What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals). Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though! For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less. This follows American Express adding Airbnb Luxe to its Platinum lodging credit. Eligible prepaid Luxe stays of at least two nights can use up to $300 each half-year, and a qualifying booking opens access to a separate $250 annual Airbnb Experiences credit.

The EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy sits on top of existing tourism strategies released by the economic bloc’s Commission. But it still falls short of presenting measurable targets that would actually support its implementation.

The European Commission wants to spread tourism across more destinations and seasons, according to its tourism strategy — which does not allocate new funding or set numerical targets.

The EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy released Wednesday sets out Brussels’ vision for tourism across its economic bloc: it would like tourists spread across lesser-traveled destinations throughout the whole year. The Commission said that, on average, 42% of nights spent in a destination fall in its three busiest months.

The long-awaited strategy and its supporting documentation are designed to further the EU’s competitiveness, sustainability and resilience. They come against a backdrop of backlash about overtourism and a summer of extreme heat and wildfires in parts of Europe.

The European Commission released its EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy on Wednesday, setting out a vision to spread visitors across lesser-known destinations and across the full year — without new funding, binding mandates, or numerical targets. The Commission said 42% of nights spent in a destination fall, on average, in its three busiest months, and the strategy arrives after a summer of extreme heat, wildfires, and continued overtourism backlash. Its sustainability pillar rests on three voluntary instruments: the EU Model for Tourism Management, a proposed Council Recommendation for Balanced Tourism, and an EU Toolbox for Balanced Tourism that will include shared approaches to short-term rentals. A Cruise Cooperation Dialogue was also proposed. The Commission said €18 billion in EU support is expected to have benefited tourism from 2021 to 2027 but committed no fresh money, pointing instead to the 2028–2034 budget still under negotiation and to combining private investment with financial instruments. Industry voices quoted by Skift welcomed the volume-to-value direction while pressing for measurable targets, simpler funding access, and practical fixes such as interoperable transport ticketing, which the Commission said it would only "explore" by 2028. The strategy also flags that AI trip-planning tools could reinforce existing tourism hubs if destinations stay passive.

#6106. 15 lessons from the midterms as Democrats rebound with historic wave

ANALYSIS — It wasn’t exactly a surprise that Democrats did well on Tuesday, but the breadth and depth of their victory was stunning. Votes are still being counted, but it’s looking like a massive blue wave with very few Republican survivors.

Just two years ago, Donald Trump delivered one of the biggest Republican victories in recent history. The GOP won back the White House, finished ahead in the national popular vote, recaptured the Senate majority and held on to the House. But what Republicans thought was a permanent realignment of the party coalitions crumbled under the weight of an unpopular war in the Middle East and voter frustrations over the economy and president’s economic policies.

The complete analysis will come in the weeks and months ahead, but here are a few initial thoughts.

Trump is a political mortal. Despite the pervasive narrative that normal political rules don’t apply to the president, election night showed that is simply not true. Sure, he was a surprise victor in 2016, but as an unpopular sitting president in 2018, his party lost a net of 40 House seats. When he ran for reelection in 2020, again as an unpopular president, he lost. When he got to run against an unpopular Democratic administration in 2024, he won again. And when his job approval rating sank to historic lows, his party was routed in the midterms.

Polls pointed in the right direction. Despite a decade of ridicule and abuse, the polling industry had a good cycle. Of course, there were a few outliers, but much of the public and private data (at least on the Democratic side) pointed to a good midterm for Democrats. Surprise outcomes on Tuesday were likely more due to a lack of data than poor data. And, if anything, some surveys underestimated the support for Democratic candidates. Pollsters still have methodological challenges, particularly with low response rates, but it’s time to ditch the narrative that polls always underestimate Republicans.

Democrats captured the Senate. Democrats are going to gain at least seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. They might gain up to nine with wins in Alaska and Mississippi. (Both races haven’t been called as yet by The Associated Press). They needed to gain four seats for a majority. Our projection of a Democratic gain of four to six seats was directionally accurate but will fall at least slightly below the final tally.

It could have been worse for Republicans. While it’s almost hard to believe, the night could have been a bigger catastrophe for the Senate GOP. Louisiana Rep. Julia Letlow won the open seat by 2 points; appointed Florida Sen. Ashley Moody won by 3 points; and Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts was leading by 7 points as of Wednesday morning. If Sens. Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi or Dan Sullivan of Alaska survive, they’d do so by narrow margins. Meanwhile, Democrats didn’t really have any close calls, as they held Michigan (6 points as of Wednesday morning), Minnesota (10 points), New Hampshire (14 points) and Georgia (18 points).

Democrats captured the House. While dozens of races remain uncalled by the AP, Democrats will gain the House majority as expected. But the size of the wave is going to be bigger than expected. Democrats will likely clear our projection of a net gain of 20 to 30 seats and could approach their 40-seat gain during Trump’s first midterm.

Redistricting flopped for Republicans. Republicans are struggling to gain any of the seats they intentionally redrew to elect new members of their own party. Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas ended up as debacles for the GOP with near total domination by Democrats up and down the ballot, all in states Trump won just two years ago. North Carolina Republican Tim Moore is on track to lose a district that he helped draw for himself.

It didn’t have to be this way. Even though Republicans are placing the early blame on history and inevitability, Tuesday’s results were not a foregone conclusion. Things could have been very different had Trump not started the conflict with Iran, which resulted in domestic economic hardship, or waged a tariff war with friendly countries. Or if he had limited his immigration policy to closing the border and deporting violent criminals in the country illegally. Republicans would have held the Senate, and it would have been an extremely close fight for the House. No matter who or what Republicans choose to blame, the party is here because of Trump.

Sometimes history repeats itself. Twenty years ago, there was an unpopular Republican president in the White House with a war in the Middle East that was driving up fuel prices. Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress as Republicans lost 30 House seats and six Senate seats — a remarkably similar outcome to this cycle.

Midterms portend the future, except when they don’t. Democrats had a great night this week but that’s no guarantee the success will continue. In their best-case scenario, 2026 could be the first part of a two-cycle wave, similar to 2006 and 2008, when Democrats expanded their House majority and won the White House. But 2028 could also look like 2012 in reverse, with Republicans bouncing back from a disastrous midterm as Democrats did after the 2010 tea party wave.

Candidate quality is only a fraction of the story. Republicans can try to blame their candidates or campaigns, whether it’s Hyde-Smith, Ken Paxton in Texas or Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, but all of them would have won in a political environment in which the president was even modestly popular. Without Trump’s self-inflicted policy wounds, candidate quality would not have mattered as much for Republicans, and they could have exploited Democrats with vulnerabilities, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Gina Hinojosa’s victory over GOP Greg Abbott in Texas, where Democrats also appear on track to sweep every other statewide race, is proof that Republican problems in the Lone Star State extended beyond Paxton’s baggage.

The Trump coalition collapsed. The coalition that brought Republicans to the mountaintop didn’t stick around very long as the party lost ground among a host of key demographic groups that were supposed to be a permanent part of its voter bloc. Trump finished behind Kamala Harris by just 11 points among voters aged 18-29. Republican candidates lost those voters by 47 points on Tuesday, according to the exit polls. Trump finished 5 points behind Harris among Latino voters, but Republicans lost them by 27 points this year. Trump lagged Harris by just 3 points among independent voters but Republicans lost them by 17 points this week. Trump bested Harris among male voters by 12 points in 2024, but Republicans ran even with Democrats with this group on Tuesday. Republicans even lost ground among voters without a college degree. Trump was +13 against Harris in 2024, but Republicans were just +4 in the midterms.

Personal brands matter until they don’t. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania’s 1st District came into the cycle with stellar reputations about bucking partisan trends, but both Republicans went down to defeat. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York’s 17th could join them. It’s just evidence that voters have a limited tolerance for voting against their own partisan tendencies.

Pay attention to special elections. For two years, Democratic candidates significantly overperformed in special elections and regularly scheduled off-year elections. Republicans dismissed the results as “special,” finding excuses to explain them away. But that was a mistake. Their turnout problem was right in front of everyone for more than a year.

Elections are humbling. Losing twice to Trump was a humbling experience for Democrats. Seeing most of those gains wiped out in a single night should be humbling for Republicans. But we’ll see what lessons each party chooses to take from these results.

White evangelicals couldn’t save Republicans. White evangelical voters continue to be one of the most reliable pieces of the GOP coalition. After supporting Trump with 76 percent in 2020 and 82 percent in 2024, and Republican candidates with 83 percent in 2022, white evangelicals supported GOP candidates once again, with 82 percent. But turnout did not keep pace. According to the exit polls, white evangelicals made up 17 percent of the midterm electorate after consistently comprising around a quarter of voters for more than a decade.

#6104. A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

Argument: A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

“A very good morning,” I said in Spanish, smiling at the young director of the Colombian National Land Agency as we exchanged congratulatory handshakes. It was 2024, and my U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) team and I had just arrived to inaugurate new offices for the land agency in downtown Bogotá, where fresh staff and IT systems would help speed the laborious and typically yearslong process of turning paperwork into official land titles.

It had taken years of hard work and millions of dollars of aid to bring reform to Colombia’s dysfunctional land administration system, in which more than 40 percent of rural landowners lacked proper titles. Over several years, we had carefully researched ownership in several key counties, and now it was the land agency’s turn to convert our surveys into official titles.

“A very good morning,” I said in Spanish, smiling at the young director of the Colombian National Land Agency as we exchanged congratulatory handshakes. It was 2024, and my U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) team and I had just arrived to inaugurate new offices for the land agency in downtown Bogotá, where fresh staff and IT systems would help speed the laborious and typically yearslong process of turning paperwork into official land titles.

It had taken years of hard work and millions of dollars of aid to bring reform to Colombia’s dysfunctional land administration system, in which more than 40 percent of rural landowners lacked proper titles. Over several years, we had carefully researched ownership in several key counties, and now it was the land agency’s turn to convert our surveys into official titles.

Looking at the elaborate setup, I turned to my program manager and asked under my breath, “How much did we pay for this?” USAID contractors always footed the bill for such events, in my experience. “Nothing,” he replied. “This is their show.”

This memory epitomized for me both the promise and dysfunction of my 21 years at USAID. We existed to bring such transformational reform to life, within the governments of our host countries. Yet we were hampered by our own systems and practices.

The end of USAID’s operations in September 2025 was a tragedy—for U.S. soft power and influence, for the lives in developing countries that have been lost, and for the shameful treatment of USAID’s foreign and American staff. But the agency was not perfect, and as we look toward building back something better, we need to think sharply about how to make a system more interested in transformation than paper-clip counting.

I recognized much of what frustrated me with USAID in the pages of Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s 2025 bestseller, Abundance—too much paperwork, pursuing low-risk and low-impact approaches when we knew better ones, and stymied by process over outcomes.

USAID generally spent its funding through competitively awarded grants and contracts to NGOs and for-profit contractors. These entities would, in turn, hire experts, rent out offices, and buy vehicles and equipment to provide expertise to the host-country organization.

In this case, our contractor was a big, for-profit U.S. firm. Staffed by very capable Colombians, it was always a struggle to get our contractors to see why the real goal was for the local government to take over. The contract required deliverables, such as 20,000 land titles issued, not the deeper reforms that the inauguration of the new offices represented.

The whole system of measurement and incentives within USAID worked against these moments. Our standard indicators counted units, such as the number of people trained, but had no way to measure transformation. The auditors were notorious for only finding fault and lack of compliance, not handing out kudos. Nothing in any of our systems awarded us for the host country, rather than ourselves, taking on responsibility for a project.

These are not entirely new questions. In former USAID Administrator Andrew Natsios’s widely read 2010 essay, “The Clash of the Counter-Bureaucracy and Development,” he detailed how USAID had become consumed by compliance and paperwork, spending “as much money on oversight and control as on implementation.” Worse, it had strayed from its mission of creating transformational partnerships with developing countries in favor of low-risk, countable outputs.

I moved to Washington in 2000 and worked as a management consultant for federal agencies until 2004, when I became a foreign service officer with USAID. The practices and acronyms Natsios described were our bread and butter—inspector general audits, performance measurement, and strategic planning. I naturally carried that skillset over when I began my USAID career. My last tour was as deputy director in Colombia, the largest USAID program in the Western Hemisphere. As I became a senior USAID officer, Natsios’s critique rang truer and truer to me.

A perennial directive during my 21 years at USAID was to push us, working in the field missions, to work more with local partners. Most recently, the goal of former Administrator Samantha Power’s localization initiative was to provide 25 percent of USAID’s total funding in direct contracts and grants to local partners. The Biden administration ended with still a long way to go to meet that goal, reaching only 12 percent of funding.

The development theory was simple; partners more involved in designing and managing programs would produce more sustainable programs that they saw as their own, not as the donor’s. To be sure, done poorly, there were plenty of potential downsides to giving direct grants to local partners, such as heightened corruption, aid dependency, and exacerbating local power dynamics as local elites would often control this funding.

But there were other potential advantages, too. Locals tend to understand how to get things done in their own country and may devise more appropriate solutions, and grants to local partners often cost less to implement.

Despite all these efforts, most of our funding went to grants to large international NGOs, the United Nations, or to big contracts with for-profit firms that had developed around implementing specialized USAID funding, known as “Beltway bandits.” Most USAID staff instinctively knew that local partners would have a better angle on problems. But we also knew that it was just too complicated and time-consuming to do it at scale.

Natsios described the situation in 2010 as one where the complexity of working with USAID, “restricted newer, smaller, and local organizations from competing for grants and contracts, because these organizations lack the business systems to follow U.S. federal law and regulation, to account properly for all funds, to disburse money quickly, and to produce measurable and auditable results.”

In 2025, 15 years after Natsios published his essay, the situation was about the same or perhaps marginally better with regard to the proportion of USAID funding globally going to local organizations, probably increasing by a couple of percentage points, from 10 to 12 percent.

In Colombia, the proportion going to local organizations was far less than the global average—only about 5 percent of our funding went to local partners. The rest went to large international NGOs, the U.N., and Beltway bandits. Speaking as someone partly responsible for this situation, this was insane.

Colombia, while having significant development challenges and needs, is considered by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development to be an upper-middle-income country. It has a highly developed private sector and state. The challenges noted by Natsios of “lack of business systems” were much less an issue in a place such as Colombia, yet we provided very little of our funding to local partners. Our complicated design and contracting processes were the same whether the grant was $100,000 or $10 million, disincentivizing smaller projects—while USAID’s complexity put off local partners. We had clear incentives to spend but no penalties for not working with locals. And we had the staff to manage 20 large grants but not 100 small ones.

When I ask myself how we could move from the bureaucratic, risk-averse, and process-focused USAID to a new and redesigned foreign assistance that is bold and transformative, my answers stem from my own experience—and the limited number of projects I felt were truly successful. In my 21-year career, I probably worked on or led just five or six projects I would consider to be absolutely transformative out of dozens of projects. Other work was good, but it did not have the same feeling of real change.

I felt that difference powerfully one night in Kabul in 2016. We were running a virtual online auction at the U.S. Embassy, where private sector investors from around the world would bid on a new 10-megawatt solar farm project in Kandahar. The CEO of the Afghan utility and his senior staff accompanied us in person, and we watched on a TV monitor as bids came in from companies. The numbers slowly got better and better as the night progressed. When bidding closed, the Afghan government had a deal at a world-class price from the winning company.

This moment meant that the Afghan government could negotiate with the global private sector, equal to equal, without donors as intermediaries. The teary-eyed CEO hugged me and immediately called the Afghan president to tell him the good news.

No standard indicator can capture that moment, and it was not featured as a headline in the next audit report. Yet that moment was so transformative that this approach to infrastructure was repeated to great effect by the Afghans on their own. The Afghan government used the private investor approach we piloted with them that night to triple the output of Kajaki Dam with Turkish investors over the next few years.

Models exist within USAID and federal foreign assistance to pull from. Down the hall from me in Bogotá sat the lead for USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) program. I was envious of the fact that she wasn’t there that often but instead out in the field working directly with communities on small infrastructure or community projects. OTI’s model was completely different than the rest of USAID. Field managers were expected to be in the field, bonding with counterparts, adjusting programs, and making things happen. Back-office contract and finance work was done in Washington. If I wanted to get a read on the political dynamics at a key counterpart agency, my first stop was to speak to the OTI rep.

The Inter-American Foundation (IAF), a much smaller U.S. federal body, also worked with those small communities and NGOs doing truly grassroots development work. In Colombia, it worked with small Indigenous-led NGOs serving their community or women’s groups helping them to start small businesses—organizations often without offices or full-time staff.

How did IAF do it? Its procedures were completely different from ours, its funding scale was generally under $100,000, and it included a key condition in making these grants. It generally requested that an NGO’s own contribution be at least as much as IAF’s, ensuring that this was the NGO’s project and the NGO owned it.

Global problems are landing on U.S. shores in unprecedented numbers. The right focuses on migration and illegal drugs, while the left sees climate change and pandemics. However you weigh each of these threats, they could all be mitigated by well-designed foreign assistance.

I know this is the case because I managed such programs in Colombia just prior to the mission’s closure. We helped Venezuelan migrants take advantage of generous policies that would allow them to stay in Colombia, rather than start their hike to the United States through the Darién Gap. Other programs incentivized coca farmers to stop growing coca and make their livelihood legally. Climate finance preserved hundreds of thousands of acres of virgin forest to slow climate change. Funding helped Colombia’s health ministry prepare for the next pandemic. Foreign assistance is not a panacea but remains an essential tool to protect the United States.

As Natsios reminds us, development is about building institutions “in poor and fragile states, with the ultimate goal of developing a capable state, market economy, and civil society.” It’s not about bean-counting. It is time to think boldly about how we could redesign foreign assistance around that objective and help solve the threats facing the United States.

Jeremiah A. Carew was the deputy mission director of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in Colombia from 2021 until the mission’s closing in August 2025. Over his 21-year career with USAID, he served in Peru, Afghanistan, Uganda, Vietnam, South Sudan, and Washington, D.C. He retired at the rank of counselor in the U.S. Senior Foreign Service, and his final assignment was as mission director of USAID in Somalia. He currently resides in Ecuador, where he writes on international development topics for Razón Pública in a monthly column; his work has also appeared in El Tiempo and the Foreign Service Journal.

#6102. Washington Is Debating the Wrong AI Risk

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Washington Is Debating the Wrong AI Risk

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Washington is gripped by an artificial intelligence (AI) panic, driven by the prospect of superintelligent models delivering our doom. Today’s Nostradamuses include whistleblowers from frontier AI companies—who put the odds of AI killing all humans at greater than one in 10 and warn that insiders expect it could happen before the end of the decade—and anti-nuclear activists, who note that it wouldn’t be the first time humanity built something that could kill us all. The doomsayers may yet be right, but their scenario rests on a long chain of assumptions, each highly unlikely on its own and far less likely to align all at once.

This doesn’t mean AI isn’t dangerous. But by fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios, we miss the forest for the trees: the common, mundane AI dangers already present and actively causing harm. The pressing AI risk Washington should focus on more is automation bias, the phenomenon where humans over-rely on or over-delegate to AI relative to the accuracy of AI models, off-loading cognition to the machine, sometimes even in the face of contradictory evidence.

Washington is gripped by an artificial intelligence (AI) panic, driven by the prospect of superintelligent models delivering our doom. Today’s Nostradamuses include whistleblowers from frontier AI companies—who put the odds of AI killing all humans at greater than one in 10 and warn that insiders expect it could happen before the end of the decade—and anti-nuclear activists, who note that it wouldn’t be the first time humanity built something that could kill us all. The doomsayers may yet be right, but their scenario rests on a long chain of assumptions, each highly unlikely on its own and far less likely to align all at once.

This doesn’t mean AI isn’t dangerous. But by fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios, we miss the forest for the trees: the common, mundane AI dangers already present and actively causing harm. The pressing AI risk Washington should focus on more is automation bias, the phenomenon where humans over-rely on or over-delegate to AI relative to the accuracy of AI models, off-loading cognition to the machine, sometimes even in the face of contradictory evidence.

The high-profile insistence on AI safety to address the risk of extinction from AI superweapons created by the most advanced large language models (LLMs) distracts attention from the urgent risks we should and can begin to solve now: human errors in operational usage of AI today due to automation bias.

A Chinese-flagged container ship transits the Gulf of Oman on Oct. 13. AFP via Getty Images

This spring, during the U.S. war with Iran, it appears that an intelligence report suggested that China was sending nuclear weapons components on a ship in the Middle East toward Iran. The U.S. military immediately began surveillance and made plans to intercept and board the vessel. Just before the operation began, officials reexamined the original report. They discovered it came from an analyst who forwarded an AI model’s output that stitched together intelligence to suggest the ship carried nuclear components. The report was false, with the AI model either incorrectly identifying or hallucinating the nature of the vessel’s cargo.

It’s easy to blame the AI for the false report. But what matters more is that the analyst didn’t check what the model had generated, and neither did the planners who received the report. The analyst entered the fabricated AI claim into a standard intelligence report that went up the chain of command, and no one checked until it was almost too late. Better AI or guardrails on AI models would not have solved the problem.

For those who know their Cold War history, this should ring alarm bells. In September 1983, Soviet early-warning satellites reported that the United States had launched nuclear missiles. The duty officer, Stanislav Petrov, judged it a false alarm and declined to report it up the chain as an attack. He was right, and he likely averted nuclear war. This spring’s episode was, in essence, a Petrov incident without a Petrov. In 1983, a machine raised a false alarm and a human had the presence of mind to question it. This time, a machine raised a false alarm, and the human analyst passed it along. The error surfaced only on a last-minute second look.

It’s evident to anyone how close of a call this was, and how near to danger we came. Sen. Mark Warner recently stated that for Congress to take real action, we will need a “holy heck moment.” This near-miss incident probably won’t qualify—it drew a fraction of the attention and news coverage given to this summer’s Hugging Face incident, in which OpenAI models escaped their testing environment and breached the company’s servers—but it should. The episode did not go unnoticed, on the other hand, in China, where one news outlet described the failure as one wherein the machine “merely handed over a crooked ruler,” but humans were the ones who ultimately did the measuring.

Talk of “super intelligence” distracts from frequent screwups.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”

Just as British people did with steam power, the American public can shape how this technology spreads.

The near-miss regarding the Chinese ship is not the only example. Airline pilots fall prey to automation bias when they ignore their instruments and training and trust the autopilot too much, causing tragic plane crashes that have killed hundreds over the past three decades. Automation bias in drivers occurs when navigation software routes them onto a closed road (as in the famous Allstate commercial); instead of using their eyes and judgment, they follow it anyway. For the military, a classic example happened in 2003, when Patriot missile systems in Iraq classified friendly aircraft as incoming missiles, and operators approved engagements that killed British and American troops.

Despite its prevalence today, this type of human error does not feature heavily in the AI argument now consuming Washington. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for slowing frontier development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warns that humanity could lose control of AI, while U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed the push for restrictions as a “conspiracy.” The current debate focuses on guardrails for what labs build and the potential for doomsday scenarios. One explanation for the focus on doomsday scenarios is that      they capture the public imagination. Another is that they distract from the complicated reasons that real-world accidents often occur. Accidents regularly result from the interactions among people, organizations, and technologies. The tendency in the non-AI accident realm (think a plane crash) is to blame the pilot, rather than the complex system and interaction among the pilot, their training, and the technology that leads to the accident. We could be seeing the AI version of that dynamic, where the AI becomes the scapegoat.

But the near-miss with the Chinese ship shows what can happen if we continue to ignore the risks with AI systems that already exist and are already being (mis)used.

In January, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released an Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy designed to put AI tools in the hands of 3 million military and civilian personnel at every classification level. Scaling AI adoption is essential to U.S. military power, but it must happen responsibly to be effective. The new strategy emphasizes expanding access to data, compute, and AI tools from warfighting to intelligence to enterprise, and even special hiring authorities for AI talent. The next step, conspicuously missing from the AI Acceleration Strategy, is training to ensure commanders and operators understand the advantages and risks of the AI systems they use.

Automation bias is not inevitable, and if the American government, including but not limited to the military, can address it, the United States can lead the world in AI adoption with responsible speed. Based on our experience working in the Pentagon and doing research on practical AI risks, two changes would help the United States capture the benefits of AI and mitigate much of the risk.

U.S. Army cadets take notes during a lecture on terrorism at the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York, on March 30, 2007. Don Emmert/AFP via Getty Images

First, create standard operating procedures for managing AI outputs. For example, any finished intelligence product that used a generative AI tool should say so, visibly, to everyone who reads it. The analyst in this recent incident reportedly used AI to both query intelligence reports and then to package the findings, and in this final report failed to disclose AI use, making the report’s content look human-generated. Furthermore, AI inferences in intelligence reports should require confirmation beyond the AI model for high-risk decisions. Boarding a Chinese vessel during an ongoing war would have been incredibly risky. Speed that leads to operational failure isn’t useful. One additional operational check can make a huge difference without substantially slowing things down. This does not only apply to intelligence products, though there is a unique risk there—but also to any output aided by AI tools, including in the use of AI decision-support systems.

The second is training. In co-authored research, we found that people with the least experience with AI models were the most likely to defer to them, a version of the Dunning-Kruger effect applied to machines. Familiarity built through structured training, including exposure to these systems failing, produces better, more effective AI users. In more recent work, we found that West Point cadets exhibited automation bias in 3.9 percent of trials, compared with 9 percent in a matched sample of the American public, suggesting that military education can help produce personnel who interrogate algorithmic outputs to maximize their effective usage instead of merely accepting them.

The danger of automation bias will not be engineered away by better models or models that never hallucinate, because the failure comes from how people use them. The military is not helpless here. Solving AI risk is more about people and organizations than engineering, and it’s not an imagined problem for tomorrow.

Michael C. Horowitz is the director of Perry World House and the Richard Perry professor at the University of Pennsylvania, and a senior fellow for technology and innovation at the Council on Foreign Relations. X: @mchorowitz

Lauren Kahn is a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

#6100. The strange new math behind the price of your groceries

Walmart recently published a list of things it promises not to do to its customers.

âWe price the product, not the person,â Walmart CEO John Furner announced in a September letter to customers. âYour income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay wonât change the price,â he promised. Nor, he said, would the retailerâs AI shopping assistant, Sparky, use information customers shared to raise prices or conceal cheaper options.

This was nice to hear. I hadnât previously considered that telling a computer I needed toilet paper might result in an emergency toilet-paper rate. There is something faintly unnerving about the specificity of a corporate reassurance, particularly when it introduces several possibilities you hadnât thought to worry about.

It made me preemptively nostalgic for the little paper price tag beneath a box of cereal. Thereâs something reassuringly stupid about it. It tells you what the cereal costs. It doesnât know how much money you make, whether youâre in a hurry or what the temperature is outside. Unless an employee comes along with a new sticker, the person reaching for the same box ten minutes later sees the same number. A modest achievement, perhaps, but one Iâm growing increasingly fond of.

The appeal isnât really the paper. Itâs the transparency of the arrangement. As retailers gather more information about their customers and acquire increasingly sophisticated pricing tools, shoppers risk knowing less about why theyâre paying what theyâre paying. The problem isnât simply higher grocery bills. Itâs the possibility of a transaction in which one side can examine the other in exquisite detail, while the other can barely see the rules.

What prompted the letter from Furner is that Walmart is expanding its use of electronic shelf labels, little screens that let employees update prices digitally from a central computer instead of replacing stickers by hand. The change makes sense. Furner points out that updating paper tags is tedious work, and heâd rather employees spend their afternoons helping customers than tending to a small forest of adhesive rectangles. Digital labels can also help ensure the price on the shelf matches the price at checkout.

And electronic labels arenât, in themselves, surge pricing. Walmart says it doesnât use them to change prices according to who is shopping or the time of day. But efficiency is a different question from trust. Making a price easier to change isnât necessarily a problem. Making it harder to understand how that price was reached might be.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

Weâve already accepted a surprisingly elaborate set of conditions for saving money on groceries. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Clip the digital coupon before you leave home. After handing over our personal information and completing several minor administrative tasks, weâre permitted to save 75 cents on yogurt. The store, meanwhile, gets a rather detailed account of our preferences. What happens when that bargain runs in reverse?

Last December, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that shoppers using Instacart were sometimes shown different prices for identical groceries from the same store at the same time. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., an 18-ounce box of Signature SELECT Corn Flakes appeared for $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69, depending on whose screen you were looking at.Â

Instacart said the shoppers were assigned to pricing experiments randomly, not sorted by income, demographics or browsing history. It ended the tests after the investigation. That distinction matters, especially because the research didnât establish that anyoneâs personal habits were being used against them. But it demonstrated how quietly prices can diverge when the shopper sees only the number assigned to her. You canât question a difference you have no way of seeing.

I buy a lot of black beans. Enough, presumably, that a supermarketâs software could identify me as a woman with firm opinions about legumes. If that earns me a coupon, wonderful. Iâm considerably less enthusiastic about the possibility of an algorithm deciding that my apparent dependence on black beans means I could stand to pay another 30 cents per can. Itâs one thing to recognize a loyal customer. Itâs another to recognize a captive audience.

Other pricing algorithms raise different questions (McDonaldâs, for instance, faces a lawsuit alleging AI-assisted price coordination among franchises, which the company denies). Prices have always fluctuated; coupons have always rewarded some shoppers more than others. Nor should computers be banished from the business of deciding what things cost. But the supermarket is not an airline, and dinner should not require the same vigilance as booking a flight.

Walmartâs promise is worth taking seriously. The company has drawn a clear line around how it says it will use customer information, and thatâs preferable to leaving shoppers guessing. But itâs a corporate commitment, not a rule every retailer must follow. And the fact that a supermarket now feels obliged to assure us it wonât charge extra because we seem hurried or financially comfortable suggests how strange our expectations have become.

Perhaps itâs naive to want a supermarket not to use what it knows about me against me. Still, I donât need the price tag to know me. I need it to tell me what the cereal costs.
